41723.q: On which night did the worst of the November pogroms take place?
41723.e: On the night of 9 to 10 November 1938 Jews were attacked all over the German Reich. The violence continued in the following days.
41723.m: The November pogroms began on 9 November 1938.

41724.q: Which name that plays down the November pogroms was widely used for a long time?
41724.e: The term “Kristallnacht” (Night of Broken Glass) plays down the violence. That is why people today speak of the November pogroms.
41724.m: Instead of “Kristallnacht”, people now say November pogroms.

41725.q: What did the Nazis use as a pretext for the November pogroms of 1938?
a: An assassination attempt on a German diplomat
41725.e: The young Jewish man Herschel Grynszpan shot a German diplomat in Paris. The Nazis used the act as a pretext for the violence.
41725.m: An assassination in Paris served as a pretext for the pogroms.

41726.q: Which places of worship were set on fire during the November pogroms?
41726.e: More than 1,000 synagogues and prayer rooms were destroyed or set on fire. The fire brigade was only supposed to stop the fire spreading to neighbouring houses.
41726.m: During the November pogroms the synagogues burned.

41727.q: About how many Jewish men were taken to concentration camps after the November pogroms?
41727.e: After the pogrom more than 30,000 Jewish men were arrested. They were sent to the camps at Dachau, Buchenwald and Sachsenhausen.
41727.m: After the pogroms tens of thousands of Jewish men were deported.

41728.q: Who had to pay for the damage after the November pogroms?
41728.e: The victims were blamed for the damage. On top of that they had to pay one billion Reichsmarks.
41728.m: After the pogroms the victims were robbed as well.

41729.q: Who gave the inflammatory speech in Munich on the evening of 9 November 1938 that set off the pogrom?
41729.e: At a party meeting in Munich the propaganda minister called for violence. After that the orders went out to party offices throughout the Reich.
41729.m: The pogroms were planned by the party leadership and were not spontaneous.

41730.q: Where does the word “Kristall” (crystal) in the old name for the pogrom night come from?
a: From the broken panes of glass
41730.e: Countless shop windows of Jewish shops and homes were smashed. The broken glass on the streets gave the night its glossed-over name.
41730.m: The shards of smashed shop windows lay on every street.

41731.q: Which office did Joseph Goebbels hold from 1933?
41731.e: Goebbels was Reich Minister of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda. He controlled newspapers, radio and films.

41732.q: Which action took place on 10 May 1933 in Berlin and many university towns?
41732.e: Students burned books by Jewish authors and critics of the regime. In Berlin Goebbels gave a speech at the event.
41732.m: During the book burning unwanted books were destroyed.

41733.q: Which question did Goebbels ask in his famous speech at the Berlin Sportpalast in 1943?
41733.e: After the defeat at Stalingrad Goebbels wanted to push the population into an even greater war effort. The hand-picked audience cheered on command.
41733.m: In the Sportpalast speech Goebbels called for total war.

41734.q: What was the cheap radio set that brought propaganda into many homes called?
41734.e: The People's Receiver (Volksempfänger) was cheap so that as many families as possible could afford a radio. That way millions heard the speeches of the party leaders.
41734.m: The People's Receiver brought propaganda into people's living rooms.

41735.e: With propaganda Goebbels tried to win people over to the Nazis. He used newspapers, radio, films and parades to do so.
41735.m: Propaganda influences people in a one-sided way.

41736.q: Which media did Goebbels mainly use for his propaganda?
41736.e: In the 1930s there was no internet yet and hardly any television. So Goebbels controlled radio, newspapers and cinema.
41736.m: Goebbels spread propaganda through radio, newspapers and films.

41737.q: What happened to artists and journalists the Nazis did not like?
a: They were no longer allowed to work in their profession
They were allowed to earn more
41737.e: Anyone who wanted to work had to be a member of Goebbels' Reich Chamber of Culture. Jews and critics were not admitted and lost their jobs.
41737.m: Goebbels controlled who was allowed to make art and culture.

41738.q: How did Joseph Goebbels' life end?
a: He took his own life in Berlin in May 1945
He was sentenced to death in Nuremberg
41738.e: On 1 May 1945, shortly before the end of the war, Goebbels took his own life in the Führer's bunker in Berlin. So he never had to answer for his actions in court.
41738.m: At the end of the war Goebbels escaped all responsibility.

41739.q: What does the abbreviation SS stand for?
41739.e: The SS was founded in 1925 as a protection troop for Hitler. Later it became the most powerful organisation in the Nazi state.
41739.m: The SS was the Protection Squadron of the Nazi Party.

41740.e: Heinrich Himmler built the SS up into a huge apparatus of power. He was one of those chiefly responsible for the Holocaust.
41740.m: Heinrich Himmler was the head of the SS.

41741.q: Who was the SS originally a protection troop for?
41741.e: The SS was founded in 1925 as a bodyguard for Hitler. Later it became the most powerful organisation in the Nazi state.
41741.m: The SS began as a protection troop for Hitler.

41742.q: What colour was the well-known uniform the SS wore from 1932?
41742.e: Before that the SS wore the brown SA shirt with a black cap and tie. With the black uniform it wanted to set itself apart from the SA as an elite.
41742.m: From 1932 the SS wore black uniforms.

41743.q: Which organisation ran and guarded the concentration camps?
41743.e: The camps were run by SS units, the so-called Death's Head units. The SS was therefore responsible for countless crimes.
41743.m: The SS ran the concentration camps.

41744.q: What does the word “Gestapo” stand for?
41744.e: Gestapo is short for Geheime Staatspolizei, the Secret State Police. It was the political police of the Nazi state.
41744.m: The Gestapo was the Secret State Police.

41745.q: What was the main task of the Gestapo?
a: Tracking down and persecuting political opponents
Collecting customs duties at the border
41745.e: The Gestapo watched the population and persecuted everyone regarded as an opponent. It tortured prisoners and sent them to camps.
41745.m: The Gestapo persecuted opponents of the regime.

41746.q: Could the Gestapo lock people up without a court ruling?
a: Yes, for as long as it liked
41746.e: With so-called protective custody the Gestapo could imprison people without a verdict. No court could review this.
41746.m: The Gestapo could imprison people without a verdict.

41747.q: Where did the Gestapo get a great many of its tip-offs from?
41747.e: The Gestapo had relatively few officers. Many arrests came from denunciations by neighbours, colleagues or acquaintances.
41747.m: Denunciations helped the Gestapo persecute people.

41748.q: What stands today in Berlin where the Gestapo headquarters used to be?
a: A museum about the Nazis' crimes
41748.e: Today the Topography of Terror on the site informs visitors about the crimes of the Gestapo and the SS.
41748.m: In Berlin a museum remembers the Gestapo perpetrators.

41749.q: About how many European Jews were murdered in the Holocaust?
41749.e: The Nazis murdered about six million Jews. That was about two thirds of the Jews in Europe.
41749.m: About six million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust.

41750.q: What is the Holocaust called in Hebrew?
41750.e: Shoah means “catastrophe” or “great disaster” in Hebrew. Many Jewish people use this word.
41750.m: Shoah is the Hebrew word for the Holocaust.

41751.q: At which conference in January 1942 did senior Nazi officials organise the mass murder of the Jews?
41751.e: On 20 January 1942 representatives of ministries and the SS met in a villa on Berlin's Wannsee lake. They discussed carrying out the so-called “Final Solution”.
41751.m: The genocide was organised at the Wannsee Conference.

41752.q: In which city was the largest Jewish ghetto in occupied Europe?
41752.e: At times more than 400,000 people were crammed into the Warsaw Ghetto. In 1943 the inhabitants fought back in the ghetto uprising.
41752.m: The Warsaw Ghetto was the largest ghetto.

41753.q: Which sign did Jews in the German Reich have to wear on their clothes from September 1941?
41753.e: The yellow star with the word “Jude” (Jew) had to be worn where it could be seen. In this way Jews were publicly marked and excluded.
41753.m: The yellow star marked Jews in public.

41754.q: Which group, besides the Jews, was also the victim of a Nazi genocide?
41754.e: Hundreds of thousands of Sinti and Roma were persecuted and murdered. Many Roma call this genocide the Porajmos.
41754.m: The Sinti and Roma were also victims of genocide.

41755.q: Which St Gallen police commander saved Jewish refugees in 1938 and was later honoured as “Righteous Among the Nations”?
41755.e: Paul Grüninger let hundreds of refugees into Switzerland despite a ban. He was dismissed and convicted, and only cleared in 1995.
41755.m: Paul Grüninger saved refugees and was punished for it.

41756.q: Which Swiss diplomat saved tens of thousands of Jews in Budapest with letters of protection?
41756.e: Carl Lutz was vice consul in Budapest and issued letters of protection in 1944. In this way he saved tens of thousands of people from deportation.
41756.m: Carl Lutz saved tens of thousands of lives in Budapest.

41757.q: In which present-day country is the Auschwitz memorial?
41757.e: Auschwitz is near the town of Oświęcim in southern Poland. At that time the area was occupied by Germany.

41758.q: Who liberated the Auschwitz camp in January 1945?
41758.e: Soviet soldiers reached the camp and found about 7,000 survivors. The SS had driven most of the prisoners away on death marches beforehand.

41759.q: On which day is International Holocaust Remembrance Day?
41759.e: 27 January is the anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz in 1945. The UN declared it a day of remembrance in 2005.
41759.m: On 27 January the victims of the Holocaust are remembered worldwide.

41760.q: What was the part of Auschwitz called where most people were murdered in gas chambers?
41760.e: Auschwitz II, called Birkenau, was an extermination camp. Most of the victims there were murdered straight after they arrived.
41760.m: Auschwitz-Birkenau was the largest extermination camp.

41761.q: Which words are written over the gate of the Auschwitz main camp?
41761.e: The sentence “Arbeit macht frei” was a cruel lie. It was meant to deceive and mock the prisoners.
41761.m: Over the gate of Auschwitz stood “Arbeit macht frei”.

41762.q: About how many people were murdered in Auschwitz?
41762.e: About 1.1 million people were murdered in Auschwitz, the vast majority of them Jews. No other camp had so many victims.
41762.m: Auschwitz has become the symbol of the Holocaust.

41763.q: What was tattooed on the forearm of many prisoners in Auschwitz?
41763.e: Auschwitz was the only camp where prisoners were systematically tattooed with numbers. People were meant to be nothing but numbers.
41763.m: In Auschwitz people were turned into numbers.

41764.q: Which Nazi organisation ran the Auschwitz camp?
41764.e: The SS ran the concentration and extermination camps. The first commandant of Auschwitz was Rudolf Höss.
41764.m: The SS ran the Nazis' camps.

41765.q: Who formed the core of the resistance group White Rose?
41765.e: The White Rose consisted mainly of young students at the University of Munich. They wanted to call on people to resist.
41765.m: The White Rose was a group of young students.

41766.q: What was the name of Sophie Scholl's brother, who also belonged to the White Rose?
41766.e: Hans Scholl studied medicine and founded the group with Alexander Schmorell. His younger sister Sophie joined later.
41766.m: Hans and Sophie Scholl fought the regime together.

41767.q: By what means did the White Rose resist?
41767.e: The group wrote, printed and handed out leaflets against Hitler. It wanted to make people think.
41767.m: The White Rose fought with words.

41768.q: What did the White Rose leaflets call for?
41768.e: Six leaflets were produced between 1942 and 1943. They urged people to stand up against Hitler and the war.
41768.m: The White Rose used leaflets to call for resistance.

41769.q: Where were Hans and Sophie Scholl discovered and arrested in February 1943?
a: At a printing works in Vienna
41769.e: On 18 February 1943 they threw leaflets into the atrium of the university. A caretaker saw them and reported them to the police.
41769.m: Hans and Sophie Scholl were arrested at their university.

41770.q: How old was Sophie Scholl when she was executed in February 1943?
41770.e: Sophie Scholl was born on 9 May 1921 and executed on 22 February 1943. So she was 21 years old.

41771.q: What was Sophie Scholl when she joined the White Rose?
41771.e: Sophie Scholl began studying biology and philosophy in Munich in 1942. There she joined her brother's group.
41771.m: Sophie Scholl was a student in Munich.

41772.q: What did the Allies do with the last leaflet of the White Rose?
a: They dropped millions of copies over Germany
They banned it in their countries
They sold it as a book
41772.e: The leaflet reached England. In 1943 British planes dropped it over Germany as the “Manifesto of the Munich Students”.
41772.m: In this way the White Rose's message reached millions of people.

41773.q: Who helped the White Rose students with the last leaflet?
41773.e: Kurt Huber was a professor of philosophy and musicology in Munich. He helped write the last leaflet and was executed in 1943.
41773.m: A professor also belonged to the White Rose.

41774.q: Which officer planted a bomb on 20 July 1944 to kill Hitler?
41774.e: Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg placed the bomb at a briefing meeting. He wanted to end the war and the crimes.
41774.m: Stauffenberg dared to try to assassinate Hitler.

41775.q: What was the name of the Führer's headquarters where the bomb of 20 July exploded?
41775.e: The Wolf's Lair was in East Prussia, in present-day Poland. Hitler stayed there for much of the war.
41775.m: The assassination attempt took place at the Wolf's Lair.

41776.q: What did Stauffenberg hide the bomb in?
41776.e: At the meeting Stauffenberg put the bag with the explosives near Hitler. Then he left the room on a pretext.
41776.m: The bomb was hidden in a briefcase.

41777.q: What was the name of the plan the conspirators meant to use to take power after the assassination?
41777.e: The “Valkyrie” plan was really meant for an emergency at home. The conspirators wanted to use it to take over the government.
41777.m: Operation Valkyrie was meant to seize power.

41778.q: What protected Hitler from the full force of the explosion?
41778.e: The explosive was behind a solid table support. Also, the meeting was held in a wooden hut, so the blast could escape.
41778.m: Hitler survived the assassination attempt with only slight injuries.

41779.q: What did the conspirators of 20 July 1944 want to achieve?
a: Kill Hitler and end the war
41779.e: The conspirators wanted to get rid of Hitler, take power and end the war. The plan failed.
41779.m: The conspirators of 20 July wanted to overthrow Hitler.

41780.q: What happened to Stauffenberg after the failed assassination attempt?
a: He was shot that same night
41780.e: Stauffenberg was arrested in Berlin and shot during the night. Today a memorial there remembers the resistance.
41780.m: Stauffenberg was shot that same night.

41781.q: How did the Nazi regime react to the assassination attempt of 20 July 1944?
a: It had many of those involved arrested and executed
41781.e: After the assassination attempt thousands were arrested. Many were sentenced to death in show trials.
41781.m: The Nazi regime took brutal revenge on the conspirators.

41782.q: When did the main war crimes trial in Nuremberg begin?
41782.e: The trial began on 20 November 1945. The verdicts were announced on 1 October 1946.
41782.m: The Nuremberg trials began in autumn 1945.

41783.q: How many victorious powers together formed the court in Nuremberg?
41783.e: The USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France formed the International Military Tribunal. Each country provided judges and prosecutors.
41783.m: Four victorious powers sat in judgement in Nuremberg.

41784.q: Which highest-ranking defendant took his own life before his execution?
41784.e: Hermann Göring was commander-in-chief of the air force and was sentenced to death. Shortly before the execution he poisoned himself in his cell.

41785.q: What was the harshest sentence the Nuremberg court imposed on several of the main defendants?
41785.e: The court passed twelve death sentences. Others received prison sentences, and three were acquitted.
41785.m: In Nuremberg several of the main defendants were sentenced to death.

41786.q: In which building did the trial in Nuremberg take place?
41786.e: The Palace of Justice had hardly been damaged in the war and had a prison. Courtroom 600 is a memorial today.
41786.m: The trial took place in the Nuremberg Palace of Justice.

41787.q: Which charge was used for the first time in an international trial at Nuremberg?
41787.e: For the first time leading politicians had to answer for crimes against humanity. That was a milestone in international law.
41787.m: In Nuremberg crimes against humanity were charged for the first time.

41788.q: Which present-day court in The Hague follows in the tradition of the Nuremberg trials?
a: The European Court of Human Rights
41788.e: The International Criminal Court has been working since 2002. Like the court in Nuremberg, it prosecutes individuals for the most serious crimes.
41788.m: The Nuremberg trials are a model for today's international criminal law.

41789.q: Which deputy of Hitler stayed in prison after the Nuremberg trials until his death in 1987?
41789.e: Rudolf Hess was sentenced to life imprisonment. In the end he was the only prisoner in Berlin's Spandau prison. Goebbels, Hitler and Göring were no longer alive in 1946.
41789.m: Rudolf Hess stayed in prison until his death.

41790.q: What did the Fascists want to achieve with the March on Rome in 1922?
41790.e: At the end of October 1922 Mussolini's supporters headed towards Rome. Shortly afterwards Mussolini became head of government.
41790.m: The March on Rome brought Mussolini to power.

41791.q: Who led the movement that organised the March on Rome?
41791.e: Benito Mussolini was the leader of the Italian Fascists. With the March on Rome he put pressure on the government.
41791.m: Mussolini used the March on Rome to come to power.

41792.q: Who appointed Mussolini head of government in 1922?
41792.e: King Victor Emmanuel III asked Mussolini to form a government instead of using the army against the Fascists.
41792.m: In 1922 the king handed the government to Mussolini.

41793.q: Why did the Italian army not stop the March on Rome?
a: The king gave no order to do so
The Fascists were already in Rome
41793.e: The government wanted to use the army against the Fascists. But the king did not sign the necessary state of emergency.
41793.m: Because the king did not act, nobody stopped the Fascists.

41794.q: How did Mussolini himself travel to Rome to become head of government?
a: On foot at the head of the march
41794.e: Mussolini waited in Milan to see how things would develop. Only when the king summoned him did he travel to Rome in a sleeping car.
41794.m: Mussolini did not march himself but came to Rome by train.

41795.q: What were Mussolini's supporters called because of their clothes?
41795.e: The fighting squads of the Italian Fascists wore black shirts. The Nazis' SA later wore brown shirts.

41796.q: Which German coup attempt of 1923 took the March on Rome as its model?
41796.e: In November 1923 Adolf Hitler wanted to march from Munich to Berlin, much as Mussolini had marched on Rome. However, the putsch failed in Munich itself.
41796.m: Hitler's putsch of 1923 copied the March on Rome but failed.

41797.q: Which title did Mussolini give himself as leader of the Fascists?
41797.e: “Duce” comes from the Latin “dux”, which means leader. In propaganda Mussolini was only ever called “il Duce”.

41798.q: Which job, among others, had Mussolini done before he became a politician?
41798.e: Mussolini was a teacher and above all a journalist. He edited the socialist newspaper “Avanti!” and later founded “Il Popolo d'Italia”.
41798.m: Before his dictatorship Mussolini was a newspaper journalist.

41799.q: What colour were the shirts of the Italian Fascist fighting squads?
41799.e: The Fascist gangs of thugs wore black shirts. That is why they are called Blackshirts.
41799.m: The Blackshirts were the fighting squads of the Italian Fascists.

41800.q: Who was the leader of the Italian Fascists and their Blackshirts?
41800.e: Benito Mussolini founded the Fascist movement in Italy. The Blackshirts helped him to power with violence.

41801.q: How did the Blackshirts deal with political opponents?
41801.e: The Blackshirts beat up and humiliated opponents, for example socialists and trade unionists. In this way they spread fear.
41801.m: The Blackshirts relied on violence against people who thought differently.

41802.q: Which striking weapon was the typical tool of the Blackshirts?
41802.e: The squadristi beat opponents with wooden clubs, called “manganello” in Italian. The club became the sign of their violence.
41802.m: The club was the best-known weapon of the Blackshirts.

41803.q: What happened in 1924 to the MP Giacomo Matteotti, who had criticised the Fascists in parliament?
41803.e: Giacomo Matteotti had denounced electoral fraud and Fascist violence in parliament. Shortly afterwards he was kidnapped and murdered by Blackshirts.
41803.m: The murder of Matteotti in 1924 showed how brutal the Fascists were.

41804.q: With which march did the Blackshirts put pressure on the Italian government in 1922?
41804.e: In October 1922 thousands of Blackshirts headed for the capital. The king then appointed Mussolini head of government.
41804.m: After the March on Rome in 1922 Mussolini came to power.

41805.q: What were the uniformed men of the German Nazis, who resembled the Blackshirts, called?
41805.e: The Storm Detachment (SA) of the Nazi Party wore brown shirts. Like the Blackshirts, it used violence against political opponents.
41805.m: The SA in Germany were the Brownshirts.

41806.q: What happened to the Blackshirts in Italy in 1923?
41806.e: In 1923 the fighting squads were made part of a state militia. In this way the party troop became part of the state.
41806.m: In 1923 the Blackshirts became a state militia.

41807.q: What does the Italian word “fascio”, from which “fascism” comes, mean?
41807.e: “Fascio” means bundle or league in Italian. The term stood for a closely united group.
41807.m: Fascism comes from the Italian word “fascio”, meaning bundle.

41808.q: What were the “fasces” in ancient Rome?
a: Bundles of rods with an axe
41808.e: The fasces were rods of wood tied together, often with an axe inside. They showed the power of the highest officials to punish.
41808.m: In ancient Rome the bundle of rods with an axe was a sign of official power.

41809.q: Who were the first to use a bundle of rods as a sign of power?
41809.e: In ancient Rome attendants carried a bundle of rods in front of the senior officials. It showed their power to punish.
41809.m: The bundle of rods was already a sign of power in ancient Rome.

41810.q: What does the bundle stand for as a symbol of the Fascists?
41810.e: A single rod breaks easily, but a whole bundle does not. The Fascists wanted to show that the people should be united under one leader.
41810.m: The bundle was meant to represent unity and strength.

41811.q: Which Swiss cantonal coat of arms shows a bundle of rods with an axe, with no connection to fascism at all?
41811.e: The coat of arms of the canton of St Gallen has shown a bundle of rods since the canton was founded in 1803. It stands for the unity of the districts of that time.
41811.m: The St Gallen coat of arms shows a bundle of rods that is much older than fascism.

41812.q: Who founded the Fascist movement in Italy in 1919?
41812.e: In 1919 Benito Mussolini founded the first Fascist fighting leagues in Milan. In 1921 they became the Fascist Party.
41812.m: Mussolini founded the Fascist movement in 1919.

41813.q: Which feature belongs to a fascist state?
a: A personality cult around a dictator
41813.e: Fascist states put one leader above everything and tolerate no opposition. The press and the courts are controlled.
41813.m: In fascism a leader stands above the people, the law and the parties.

41814.q: What is the salute with the right arm stretched out that the Italian Fascists used called?
41814.e: The Fascists claimed the salute came from ancient Rome. They wanted it to recall the greatness of the Roman Empire.
41814.m: The Fascists used the so-called Roman salute.

41815.q: What did the Lateran Treaties settle?
a: The relationship between Italy and the Pope
The peace after the First World War
The border between Italy and Switzerland
41815.e: The Lateran Treaties were signed in 1929. They settled the relationship between Italy and the Pope.

41816.q: Which new state was created by the Lateran Treaties?
41816.e: With the treaties Italy recognised the Vatican as a separate, independent state. The Pope is its head of state.
41816.m: Since 1929 Vatican City has been a state of its own.

41817.q: Who signed the Lateran Treaties for Italy?
41817.e: Mussolini signed as head of government. Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Gasparri signed for the Holy See.
41817.m: In 1929 Mussolini concluded the Lateran Treaties with the Pope.

41820.q: Which religion became Italy's state religion through the Lateran Treaties?
41820.e: The Catholic religion was laid down as the only state religion. This was only abolished in 1984 by a new agreement.
41820.m: Through the Lateran Treaties Catholicism became Italy's state religion in 1929.

41821.q: In which building in Rome were the Lateran Treaties signed?
41821.e: The treaties are named after the place where they were signed. The Lateran Palace stands next to the Lateran Basilica in Rome.
41821.m: The Lateran Treaties take their name from the Lateran Palace.

41822.q: Which Swiss troop still protects the Pope in Vatican City today?
41822.e: The Pontifical Swiss Guard has existed since 1506. Its guards must be Swiss citizens and Catholic.
41822.m: The Pope has been protected by the Swiss Guard for over 500 years.

41823.q: From when to when did the Spanish Civil War last?
41823.e: The war began in July 1936 with a military coup. It ended on 1 April 1939 with Franco's victory.
41823.m: The Spanish Civil War lasted from 1936 to 1939.

41824.q: Which two sides fought each other in the Spanish Civil War?
41824.e: The Republicans defended the elected government. The Nationalists under Franco had risen up against it.
41824.m: In the Spanish Civil War Republicans fought against Nationalists.

41825.q: Who began the coup in 1936 that started the Spanish Civil War?
a: Parts of the army under General Franco
41825.e: Generals around Francisco Franco rose up against the Republic in July 1936. This turned into a three-year civil war.
41825.m: A coup by generals around Franco started the Spanish Civil War.

41826.q: Which countries supported Franco in the Spanish Civil War with troops and weapons?
41826.e: Hitler sent the Condor Legion, and Mussolini sent tens of thousands of soldiers. Both also tested new weapons there.
41826.m: Hitler and Mussolini helped Franco win the civil war.

41827.q: Which country mainly supported the Spanish Republic with weapons?
41827.e: The Soviet Union supplied planes, tanks and advisers. France and Great Britain, on the other hand, held back with a policy of non-intervention.
41827.m: The Soviet Union was the Spanish Republic's most important helper.

41828.q: What were the units of volunteers from many countries who fought for the Republic called?
41828.e: Tens of thousands of volunteers from more than 50 countries joined the International Brigades. Many wanted to stop fascism.
41828.m: The International Brigades fought on the side of the Republic.

41829.q: What happened to many Swiss men who had fought in the Spanish Civil War after they came home?
41829.e: About 800 Swiss went to Spain, most of them on the side of the Republic. Back in Switzerland many were convicted for serving in a foreign army.
41829.m: Swiss fighters in Spain were punished for serving in a foreign army.

41830.q: Which city did the Republicans defend with the cry “No pasarán” (They shall not pass)?
41830.e: The Republicans defended the capital Madrid against Franco's troops for a long time. The politician Dolores Ibárruri made the cry famous.
41830.m: “No pasarán” became the battle cry of Madrid's defenders.

41831.q: Which English writer fought in Spain and wrote the book “Homage to Catalonia” about it?
41831.e: George Orwell fought in a militia in Catalonia and was wounded. Later he also wrote “Animal Farm” and “1984”.
41831.m: George Orwell wrote about his experiences in the Spanish Civil War.

41832.q: In which Spanish region is the town of Guernica?
41832.e: Guernica, Gernika in Basque, is a particularly important town for the Basques. The tree under which the Basque assemblies used to meet stands there.
41832.m: Guernica is a town in the Basque Country.

41833.q: During which war was Guernica bombed in 1937?
41833.e: In the Spanish Civil War General Franco fought against the Republic. On 26 April 1937, a market day, Guernica was destroyed from the air.

41834.q: Planes from which country mainly bombed the town of Guernica in 1937?
41834.e: The German Condor Legion supported General Franco. Italian planes also took part.

41835.q: Which artist painted the famous picture “Guernica”?
41835.e: Pablo Picasso painted the picture in 1937 as a protest against the bombing. It is one of the best-known anti-war paintings.
41835.m: Picasso painted “Guernica” as an accusation against war.

41836.q: Why did Picasso paint the picture “Guernica”?
a: As a protest against the bombing of the town
As a present for General Franco
41836.e: Picasso was horrified by the attack. He painted the huge picture in 1937 and showed it at the World's Fair in Paris.

41837.q: In which colours is Picasso's “Guernica” painted?
a: Every colour you can think of
41837.e: Picasso did without bright colours. The shades of grey are reminiscent of newspaper photos and make the effect even gloomier.
41837.m: Picasso's “Guernica” is painted only in black, white and grey.

41838.q: In which city does Picasso's “Guernica” hang today?
41838.e: Since 1992 the picture has been on show in the Reina Sofía museum in Madrid.

41839.q: Why did Picasso's “Guernica” only come to Spain in 1981?
a: Picasso wanted to give it only to a free Spain
The painting was lost during the war
Spain could not pay the price
The painting needed a long restoration
41839.e: Picasso decided that the picture could only return to a democratic Spain. That is why it was in the Museum of Modern Art in New York until 1981.
41839.m: “Guernica” only returned to Spain after the end of the dictatorship.

41840.q: Which tree in Guernica is an ancient symbol of Basque liberties?
41840.e: Representatives of the Basques used to meet under the Oak of Gernika. The tree survived the attack of 1937.
41840.m: The Oak of Guernica is a symbol of the Basques.

41842.q: About how long did Franco rule Spain as a dictator?
41842.e: Franco ruled from 1939 until his death in 1975. That is almost 40 years.
41842.m: Franco ruled Spain for almost 40 years.

41843.q: How many parties were allowed in Spain under Franco?
41843.e: All other parties were banned. Only the Falange, which Franco controlled, was allowed.
41843.m: Under Franco only one party was allowed.

41844.q: What was Spain's official position in the Second World War under Franco?
a: It declared war on the USA
41844.e: Franco did not enter the war, although he was close to Hitler. However, he sent the volunteer Blue Division against the Soviet Union.
41844.m: Spain officially stayed neutral in the Second World War.

41845.q: Which languages were heavily suppressed in public under Franco?
41845.e: Franco wanted a united Spain with only one language. Catalan and Basque were banned in schools and offices for a long time.
41845.m: Under Franco Catalan and Basque were suppressed.

41846.q: Which branch of the economy grew especially strongly in Spain from the 1960s?
41846.e: Millions of tourists from northern Europe travelled to Spain's beaches. That brought a lot of money into the country.
41846.m: In the 1960s Spain became a popular holiday destination.

41847.q: What did the Basque underground organisation ETA want to achieve through violence?
41847.e: From 1959 ETA carried out many attacks to separate the Basque Country from Spain. It dissolved itself in 2018.
41847.m: ETA used violence to fight for an independent Basque Country.

41848.q: Who had to help build Franco's huge memorial, the “Valley of the Fallen”, near Madrid?
41848.e: Franco had the memorial with its tall cross built partly by political prisoners. Today it is called Valle de Cuelgamuros.
41848.m: Political prisoners had to help build Franco's memorial.

41849.q: How did Spain become a democracy after Franco's death?
a: Largely peacefully, through reforms and elections
41849.e: After 1975 the government and the parties agreed on reforms step by step. There were free elections in 1977 and a new constitution in 1978.
41849.m: After Franco, Spain became a democracy largely peacefully.

41850.q: Who decided from 1977 who sat in the Spanish parliament?
41850.e: In 1977 Spaniards were allowed to vote freely for the first time in decades. Since then the people have decided the make-up of parliament.
41850.m: Since 1977 the Spanish people have elected their parliament freely.

41854.q: What was banned in Spain under Franco and allowed again in 1977?
41854.e: Under Franco almost only his own movement was allowed. In 1977 many parties were permitted again, even the Communist Party.
41854.m: In 1977 many parties were allowed to stand in Spain again.

41855.q: What did the peaceful change of government in Spain in 1982 show?
41855.e: In 1982 the Socialists won the election and took over the government peacefully. This was seen as a sign that the young democracy was stable.
41855.m: The peaceful handover of power in 1982 showed that Spain's democracy was stable.

41856.q: Which military alliance did Spain join in 1982?
41856.e: Spain became a member of NATO in May 1982. In 1986 the people confirmed in a referendum that they wanted to stay in the alliance.
41856.m: Spain has been a member of NATO since 1982.

41858.q: What did Juan Carlos I do after he became king in 1975?
a: He carried on the dictatorship unchanged
He left the country at once
41858.e: Franco had expected Juan Carlos to continue his dictatorship. But the king supported free elections and a democratic constitution.
41858.m: Juan Carlos I helped Spain on its way to democracy.

41859.q: Who chose Juan Carlos in 1969 as Spain's future head of state?
41859.e: Franco named Juan Carlos as his successor in 1969. He expected Juan Carlos to continue his regime.
41859.m: Franco made Juan Carlos his successor.

41860.q: How did Juan Carlos I act during the attempted coup of February 1981?
a: He backed the constitution on television
He fled abroad with his family
He stayed silent until the next day
41860.e: During the night the king appeared on television in uniform. He ordered the army to protect the constitution, and the coup collapsed.
41860.m: In 1981 Juan Carlos helped stop the coup against democracy.

41861.q: What does it mean when a king abdicates, as Juan Carlos I did in 2014?
a: He gives up his office voluntarily
41861.e: Juan Carlos I gave up the crown voluntarily in 2014. His son became the new king as Felipe VI.
41861.m: Someone who abdicates gives up their office voluntarily.

41862.q: Who succeeded Juan Carlos I as king after his abdication in 2014?
41862.e: Juan Carlos abdicated in June 2014. His son became the new King of Spain as Felipe VI.
41862.m: Felipe VI has been King of Spain since 2014.

41863.q: Which city is the capital of Spain, where the king also has his seat?
41863.e: Madrid is the capital of Spain. The royal palace and parliament are there.
41863.m: Madrid is the capital of Spain.

41864.q: Why did Juan Carlos I leave Spain in 2020?
a: Because of accusations about his finances
Because he became president of another country
41864.e: Juan Carlos faced accusations about secret money dealings. That is why he left Spain in 2020 and then lived in Abu Dhabi.
41864.m: Juan Carlos left Spain in 2020 because of financial accusations.

41865.q: Which country did António de Oliveira Salazar rule as a dictator?
41865.e: Salazar ruled Portugal as prime minister from 1932 to 1968. That made him one of the longest-ruling dictators in Europe.
41865.m: Salazar was the dictator of Portugal.

41866.q: What were people in Portugal not allowed to do under Salazar?
a: Speak their minds freely and found parties
41866.e: Salazar ruled without free elections and without free parties. Anyone who criticised the regime was persecuted.
41866.m: Under Salazar there was no freedom of opinion.

41867.q: What existed in Salazar's Portugal so that newspapers wrote nothing against the government?
41867.e: With censorship the state controls what may be published. Criticism of Salazar was cut out.
41867.m: Salazar controlled the newspapers with censorship.

41868.q: What did the secret police do in Salazar's Portugal?
a: It watched and arrested opponents of the regime
41868.e: The secret police, PIDE, watched the population and arrested and tortured opponents. It was dissolved in 1974.
41868.m: Salazar's secret police persecuted opponents of the regime.

41869.q: Against whom did Portugal under Salazar fight a colonial war from 1961?
41869.e: In Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau movements fought for independence. The long war cost Portugal many lives and a lot of money.
41869.m: Portugal wanted to keep its African colonies by force.

41870.q: How did the dictatorship in Portugal end in 1974?
a: Through an almost bloodless revolution by soldiers
By a decision of the UN
41870.e: In the Carnation Revolution soldiers overthrew the dictatorship. People put carnations in the barrels of their rifles.
41870.m: The Carnation Revolution ended the dictatorship in Portugal in 1974.

41871.q: What was Salazar's attitude towards Portugal's colonies in Africa?
a: He wanted to keep them at any price
He gave them their freedom straight away
41871.e: Portugal had colonies such as Angola and Mozambique. Salazar fought long wars so as not to lose them.
41871.m: Salazar clung to the colonies in Africa.

41872.q: What did Portugal under Salazar do in the Second World War?
41872.e: Portugal did not enter the war. Lisbon became an important port for refugees on their way to America.
41872.m: Portugal was neutral in the Second World War.

41873.q: What was the movement of officers that led the Carnation Revolution in 1974 called?
41873.e: In Portuguese it was called “Movimento das Forças Armadas”, or MFA for short. Many officers were tired of the colonial war.
41873.m: The Armed Forces Movement overthrew the dictatorship in Portugal in 1974.

41874.q: Who was overthrown by the Carnation Revolution?
41874.e: Marcelo Caetano was the last head of government of the dictatorship. He surrendered on 25 April 1974 and went into exile.
41874.m: The Carnation Revolution overthrew the dictatorship in Portugal.

41875.q: What was special about the song played on the radio as the starting signal on the night of the Carnation Revolution?
a: It had been banned by the dictatorship
It was the Spanish national anthem
41875.e: Shortly after midnight a radio station played the banned song “Grândola, Vila Morena”. For the officers this was the signal to strike.
41875.m: A banned song gave the starting signal for the Carnation Revolution.

41876.q: Where did the soldiers go on 25 April 1974 to overthrow the government?
a: To an island in the Atlantic
41876.e: Captain Salgueiro Maia came to Lisbon with his troops. There they surrounded the building where the head of government had taken refuge.
41876.m: The soldiers of the Carnation Revolution went to Lisbon.

41877.q: Who first became head of state of Portugal after the Carnation Revolution?
41877.e: The overthrown head of government handed power to General António de Spínola. He had criticised the colonial war.
41877.m: After the Carnation Revolution a general led Portugal at first.

41878.q: According to tradition, who handed out the first carnations to the soldiers?
41878.e: Celeste Caeiro worked in a restaurant and had brought carnations with her. She put a flower in a soldier's rifle barrel, and others copied her.
41878.m: Celeste Caeiro gave the Carnation Revolution its flowers.

41879.q: When did the first free elections in Portugal after the Carnation Revolution take place?
41879.e: Exactly one year after the revolution, on 25 April 1975, Portugal voted. More than 90 per cent turned out to vote.
41879.m: One year after the Carnation Revolution Portugal held free elections.

41880.q: How much blood was shed in the Carnation Revolution compared with other uprisings?
a: Very little, there were only a few deaths
It led to a long civil war
41880.e: The revolution took place almost without violence. Only outside the headquarters of the secret police were a few people shot.
41880.m: The Carnation Revolution was an almost bloodless overthrow.

41881.q: About how long did the military dictatorship in Greece last from 1967?
41881.e: On 21 April 1967 officers staged a coup. In July 1974 their regime collapsed.
41881.m: Greece was a military dictatorship from 1967 to 1974.

41882.q: What is a military dictatorship, like the one in Greece from 1967 to 1974?
a: The people elect the government every year
A king rules with a parliament
41882.e: In Greece army colonels took power in a coup. People speak of the regime of the colonels.
41882.m: In a military dictatorship army officers rule.

41883.q: What is a junta, like the one that ruled Greece from 1967?
a: A group of officers who rule a country
41883.e: A junta is a group of officers who rule after a coup. In Greece Colonel Georgios Papadopoulos led the junta.
41883.m: A junta is a ruling group of officers.

41884.q: What happened at the Athens Polytechnic in November 1973?
a: A student uprising was crushed with a tank
41884.e: Students occupied the Polytechnic and protested against the junta. On 17 November a tank broke through the gate, and people were killed.
41884.m: The uprising at the Athens Polytechnic in 1973 was ended by force.

41885.q: Which event led to the collapse of the Greek military dictatorship in 1974?
41885.e: The junta had the President of Cyprus overthrown. Turkey then attacked Cyprus, and the regime in Athens collapsed.
41885.m: The Cyprus crisis of 1974 ended the rule of the colonels.

41886.q: What did Greece have again after the end of the military dictatorship in 1974?
41886.e: Konstantinos Karamanlis returned from exile and organised free elections. In this way Greece became a democracy again.
41886.m: After 1974 Greece became a democracy again.

41887.q: What did the Greek people decide in a vote in December 1974?
41887.e: About two thirds voted against the king's return. Since then Greece has been a republic.
41887.m: Since 1974 Greece has been a republic without a king.

41888.q: What did the Greek military government do with the music of the composer Mikis Theodorakis?
a: It played it at every festival
It made it the national anthem
It had it sung in all schools
41888.e: Mikis Theodorakis was arrested and exiled. His songs became symbols of resistance against the junta.
41888.m: Mikis Theodorakis' music was banned under the junta.

41889.q: Why did Greece leave the Council of Europe in 1969?
a: The military government was accused of torture
The Council of Europe was dissolved
41889.e: The Council of Europe accused the junta of torture and human rights violations. Greece left before it could be expelled and returned in 1974.
41889.m: Because of torture Greece left the Council of Europe in 1969.

41890.q: Which profession had Salvador Allende trained in before he became a politician?
41890.e: Salvador Allende studied medicine and worked as a doctor. Later he became one of the best-known politicians of Chile's Socialist Party.
41890.m: Salvador Allende was a doctor by profession.

41891.q: Which office did Salvador Allende hold in Chile from 1970?
41891.e: Allende narrowly won the presidential election in September 1970 and took office in November 1970.
41891.m: Allende became President of Chile in 1970.

41892.q: With what kind of alliance did Salvador Allende come to power?
41892.e: Unidad Popular (Popular Unity) was an alliance of left-wing parties. With it Allende wanted to transform Chile into a socialist country by democratic means.
41892.m: Allende came to power with an alliance of left-wing parties.

41893.q: Which important raw material did Allende's government nationalise in 1971?
41893.e: The big copper mines belonged mainly to US companies. In 1971 the Chilean parliament voted unanimously to nationalise them.
41893.m: Allende nationalised the Chilean copper mines.

41894.q: What was special about Allende's election victory in 1970?
41894.e: Allende was an openly Marxist politician who became president through a democratic election. At the time this was almost unique in the world and caused a great stir.
41894.m: Allende was a Marxist who became president in a free election.

41895.q: What did Allende's government promise every child in Chile each day?
41895.e: A well-known Unidad Popular programme planned for every child to receive half a litre of milk a day. This was meant to fight malnutrition.
41895.m: Allende wanted to give every child half a litre of milk a day.

41896.q: Where did Salvador Allende die on 11 September 1973?
a: In the La Moneda presidential palace
41896.e: During the military coup Allende stayed in the La Moneda presidential palace in Santiago. He died there as soldiers stormed the building; investigations later found that he had taken his own life.
41896.m: Allende died in the La Moneda presidential palace.

41897.q: Did Allende win more than half the votes in the 1970 election?
41897.e: Allende received only about 36 per cent of the vote and therefore no absolute majority. That is why parliament had to confirm him as president.
41897.m: Allende won in 1970 with only about a third of the vote.

41898.q: In which country did the military stage a coup against President Allende on 11 September 1973?
41898.e: On 11 September 1973 the armed forces took power in Chile. That is why people in Chile often speak of the “other 11 September”.
41898.m: The coup in Chile took place on 11 September 1973.

41899.q: How was the La Moneda presidential palace attacked during the 1973 coup?
a: It was bombed by fighter planes
Not at all, it was sold
41899.e: Air force fighter planes dropped bombs on the presidential palace in Santiago. The pictures of the burning palace went round the world.
41899.m: During the coup fighter planes bombed the presidential palace.

41900.q: Which place in Santiago served as a huge prison camp after the coup?
41900.e: After the coup thousands of people were held in the Estadio Nacional, the big football stadium. Many were interrogated and tortured there.
41900.m: In 1973 the National Stadium in Santiago became a prison camp.

41901.q: The singer Víctor Jara was murdered after the coup in Chile. What did his songs become a symbol of?
41901.e: The songwriter Víctor Jara was arrested and killed after the coup. His songs became a symbol of resistance.
41901.m: Víctor Jara's songs became a symbol of resistance in Chile.

41902.q: What do you call the group of military chiefs that ruled Chile after the coup?
41902.e: A military junta is a government made up of the heads of the armed forces. In Chile it included the leaders of the army, navy, air force and police.
41902.m: A government of military chiefs is called a junta.

41903.q: Which country supported Allende's opponents during the Cold War, among other things through the CIA?
41903.e: The US government did not want a socialist government in South America. So the CIA funded Allende's opponents and helped to destabilise the country.
41903.m: The USA worked against Allende's government through the CIA.

41904.q: Which general ruled Chile as a dictator for many years after the coup of 1973?
41904.e: General Augusto Pinochet led the military government. The dictatorship lasted until 1990.
41904.m: Pinochet was dictator of Chile from 1973 to 1990.

41905.q: The military government in Chile had a new constitution written in 1980. What does a constitution set out?
a: The most important rules of a state
41905.e: A constitution lays down who has which powers in the state and what rights people have. Chile's 1980 constitution secured a great deal of power for the military.
41905.m: A constitution contains the most important rules of a state.

41906.q: What did people in Chile vote on in October 1988?
a: Whether Pinochet could carry on ruling
Whether Chile would become a monarchy
Whether Chile would join the EU
Whether the capital would be moved
41906.e: The population could decide with “Sí” or “No” whether Pinochet should rule for another eight years. The vote was provided for in the 1980 constitution.
41906.m: In 1988 Chile voted on whether Pinochet should carry on ruling.

41907.q: Which side won the referendum in Chile in 1988?
41907.e: The majority voted “No” to another term for Pinochet. This cleared the way back to democracy.
41907.m: In the 1988 vote in Chile, No won.

41908.q: What did Pinochet have to do after losing the vote of 1988?
a: Accept the result and give up power
41908.e: No won with about 56 per cent. Pinochet had to accept the result and in 1990 handed the presidency to an elected successor.
41908.m: After the No vote of 1988 Pinochet had to give up power.

41909.q: Which sign did the No campaign in Chile use as its symbol in 1988?
41909.e: The colourful rainbow stood for the many different parties that had joined together against Pinochet. The campaign relied on cheerfulness instead of fear.
41909.m: The rainbow was the symbol of the No campaign in Chile.

41910.q: Which message did the No campaign spread in its well-known song?
41910.e: The song “Chile, la alegría ya viene” means “Chile, joy is on its way”. The campaign deliberately relied on hope.
41910.m: The No campaign promised that joy was coming.

41911.q: What is the 2012 feature film about the advertising campaign for the 1988 vote in Chile called?
41911.e: The film “No” by the director Pablo Larraín tells the story of an advertising man who creates the TV adverts for the No campaign. It was nominated for an Oscar.
41911.m: The film “No” tells the story of the 1988 vote in Chile.

41912.q: How was the new president chosen in Chile in 1989?
41912.e: In December 1989 the people of Chile voted freely. Patricio Aylwin won and took office in March 1990.
41912.m: In 1989 Chile once again elected its president freely.

41913.q: Which post did Pinochet keep until 1998 after his presidency ended?
41913.e: Pinochet remained head of the army until 1998. After that he became a senator for life and so kept his influence for a long time.
41913.m: Pinochet remained head of the Chilean army until 1998.

41914.q: In which city is the Plaza de Mayo?
41914.e: The Plaza de Mayo is the most important square in the Argentine capital. The seat of government, the Casa Rosada, stands on it.
41914.m: The Plaza de Mayo is in Buenos Aires.

41915.q: Who were the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo looking for?
41915.e: The women demanded information about their sons and daughters who had been abducted by the military dictatorship. The authorities gave no answers.
41915.m: The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo searched for their missing children.

41916.q: Who was ruling Argentina when the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo began to protest?
41916.e: The first women met on the square in 1977. At that time Argentina was ruled by a military dictatorship.
41916.m: The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo protested against the military dictatorship.

41917.q: What do the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo wear on their heads as their mark?
41917.e: The white headscarf was originally a reminder of their children's cloth nappies. Today it is also painted on the ground of the square.
41917.m: The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo wear white headscarves.

41918.q: On which day of the week do the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo traditionally walk around the square?
41918.e: For decades the women have met every Thursday afternoon. They walk in a circle round the May Pyramid in the middle of the square.
41918.m: The Mothers walk round the square every Thursday.

41919.q: Why did the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo walk in a circle instead of standing still?
a: It was too cold to stand
They wanted to collect donations that way
41919.e: The military government banned gatherings. So the police told the women to keep moving, and that is how the walk began.
41919.m: Because gatherings were banned, the Mothers walked in a circle.

41920.q: What happened to Azucena Villaflor, one of the founders of the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo?
41920.e: Azucena Villaflor was kidnapped and murdered in December 1977. Her remains were only identified in 2005.
41920.m: The founder Azucena Villaflor herself became a victim of the dictatorship.

41921.q: Who are the Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo looking for?
41921.e: Many babies of abducted women were born in captivity and given to other families. With the help of DNA tests the grandmothers have found more than 130 of these grandchildren.
41921.m: The Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo search for their stolen grandchildren.

41922.q: Which language does the word “desaparecidos” come from?
41922.e: “Desaparecido” is the Spanish word for “disappeared”. It became the term for the victims of enforced disappearance.

41923.q: According to estimates by human rights organisations, how many people disappeared in Argentina during the dictatorship?
41923.e: Human rights groups speak of up to 30,000 disappeared people. A state commission was able to document about 9,000 cases individually.
41923.m: Up to 30,000 people disappeared in Argentina during the dictatorship.

41924.q: Who ruled Argentina at the time when thousands of people disappeared?
41924.e: Argentina was ruled by a military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983. During this time it made thousands of opponents disappear.
41924.m: The desaparecidos disappeared during the military dictatorship.

41925.q: What does “enforced disappearance” mean in a dictatorship?
a: The state secretly abducts people and hides where they are
The state sends people on holiday
41925.e: The families never found out what happened to their relatives. Many of the disappeared were tortured and murdered.
41925.m: In enforced disappearance the state secretly abducts people.

41926.q: What were the so-called death flights in Argentina?
a: Prisoners were thrown from planes into the sea
41926.e: Many prisoners were drugged and dropped from planes over the Río de la Plata or the sea. This was so that their bodies would never be found.
41926.m: On the death flights prisoners were dropped over the sea.

41927.q: Who bravely protested in Argentina against the disappearance of their relatives?
41927.e: From 1977 the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo went every week to the government palace in Buenos Aires. They wore white headscarves.
41927.m: The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo fought for their missing children.

41928.q: What can be found today at many former torture sites in Argentina?
41928.e: The sites remember the victims of the dictatorship. The former navy school ESMA in Buenos Aires is now a museum and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
41928.m: Memorials at former torture sites now remember the victims.

41929.q: Why did the military junta give families no information about the disappeared?
a: So that nobody could prove its crimes
Because it did not know itself
Because the disappeared were on holiday
Because a UN law forbade it
41929.e: Without bodies and files the murders were never to be solved. To this day families are searching for their relatives.
41929.m: Enforced disappearance was meant to cover up the crimes.

a: Cooperation between dictatorships against their opponents
A rescue mission in the Andes
41930.e: In Operation Condor the secret services of several South American dictatorships worked together. They persecuted, kidnapped and murdered opponents, even across national borders.
41930.m: Operation Condor was a conspiracy of South American dictatorships against their opponents.

41931.q: During which period did South American dictatorships jointly persecute their opponents (Operation Condor)?
41931.e: Operation Condor was agreed in Santiago de Chile in 1975. It continued into the 1980s.
41931.m: Operation Condor existed in the 1970s and 1980s.

41932.q: Which country did the secret service that drove Operation Condor come from?
41932.e: DINA was the secret service of the Pinochet dictatorship in Chile. Its head invited the others to the founding meeting in Santiago.
41932.m: Chile's secret service was behind Operation Condor.

41933.q: Which of these countries was NOT one of the founding countries of Operation Condor?
41933.e: The founding members were Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia; Brazil and others joined later. Mexico was not a military dictatorship at the time and took in many refugees.
41933.m: Operation Condor mainly involved countries in the south of South America.

41934.q: Which animal is Operation Condor named after?
a: A large vulture of the Andes
41934.e: The Andean condor is one of the largest flying birds in the world. It is the heraldic animal of Chile and several other Andean countries.
41934.m: The Andean condor gave Operation Condor its name.

41935.q: What are the “Archives of Terror” that were found in 1992?
41935.e: In 1992 the teacher Martín Almada found tonnes of files in a police building near Asunción. They prove Operation Condor and are now part of UNESCO's Memory of the World.
41935.m: The Archives of Terror in Paraguay prove Operation Condor.

41936.q: Where did Pinochet's secret service murder a Chilean politician living in exile in 1976?
41936.e: Secret service agents killed Orlando Letelier with a car bomb in the middle of the US capital.
41936.m: Operation Condor also hunted opponents abroad.

41937.q: Which of these countries took part in Operation Condor?
41937.e: Besides Chile, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, Bolivia under the dictator Hugo Banzer was also involved.
41937.m: Dictatorships in South America took part in Operation Condor.

41938.q: Which country did Alfredo Stroessner rule as a dictator?
41938.e: Alfredo Stroessner was a general and ruled Paraguay. His dictatorship was one of the longest in South America.
41938.m: Alfredo Stroessner was dictator of Paraguay.

41939.q: About how long did Alfredo Stroessner rule?
41939.e: Stroessner came to power in 1954 and was overthrown in 1989. So he ruled for about 35 years.

41940.q: Where did Alfredo Stroessner's father come from?
41940.e: His father was an immigrant from Hof in Bavaria. That is why Stroessner has a German surname.
41940.m: Stroessner's father was a German immigrant.

41941.q: What was Alfredo Stroessner before he became a dictator?
41941.e: Stroessner was commander-in-chief of the army. In 1954 he seized power in Paraguay in a coup.
41941.m: Stroessner was a general before he became a dictator.

41942.q: How did Alfredo Stroessner's rule end in 1989?
41942.e: In February 1989 he was overthrown by General Andrés Rodríguez, a close confidant. Stroessner then went into exile.
41942.m: Stroessner was overthrown in a coup in 1989.

41943.q: Which country did Alfredo Stroessner flee to after he was overthrown?
41943.e: After 1989 Stroessner lived in exile in Brasília. He died there in 2006 without ever being put on trial.
41943.m: Stroessner lived in exile in Brazil until his death.

41944.q: On which continent is Paraguay, the country Stroessner ruled?
41944.e: Paraguay is in South America, between Argentina, Brazil and Bolivia. It has no access to the sea.

41945.q: How did Stroessner's government treat its opponents?
a: They were persecuted, tortured or killed
They were brought into the government
They received money from the state
41945.e: Under Stroessner there was no real opposition. Critics were watched, locked up and often tortured.

41946.q: What did Paraguay under Stroessner build together with Brazil on a border river?
41946.e: The Itaipú power station was built on the Paraná river. It is still one of the largest hydroelectric power stations in the world.
41946.m: Paraguay and Brazil built a huge hydroelectric power station together.

41947.q: Who seized power in Brazil in a coup in 1964?
41947.e: In 1964 the armed forces overthrew the elected government. After that generals ruled for more than 20 years.
41947.m: In 1964 the military seized power in Brazil.

41948.q: What happened to Brazil's elected president in 1964?
41948.e: President João Goulart was planning reforms. The military saw this as a danger and overthrew him.
41948.m: In 1964 the military in Brazil overthrew the elected president.

41949.q: Who was president of Brazil from 1964 to 1985?
41949.e: After the 1964 coup five generals ruled one after the other. There were no free presidential elections.

41950.q: What did the military government in Brazil do with parliament in 1968?
a: It allowed it to be freely elected
41950.e: In 1968 a decree closed parliament and tightened censorship. The harshest period of the dictatorship began.
41950.m: In 1968 the dictatorship in Brazil became even harsher.

41951.q: Who was kidnapped by rebels in Rio de Janeiro in 1970?
41951.e: Left-wing rebels kidnapped the Swiss ambassador in December 1970. He was freed after the government let 70 political prisoners leave the country.
41951.m: In 1970 the Swiss ambassador in Brazil was kidnapped.

41952.q: What did millions of people demand on the streets of Brazil in 1984?
41952.e: The movement “Diretas Já” means “Direct elections now”. People wanted to elect the president themselves instead of the generals.
41952.m: In 1984 people in Brazil demanded free presidential elections.

41953.q: Who took over the office of president in Brazil again in 1985?
a: A civilian instead of a general
41953.e: In 1985 a civilian became president for the first time since 1964. That ended the military dictatorship.
41953.m: The military dictatorship in Brazil ended in 1985.

41954.q: What did a woman who had been tortured as a young opponent of the dictatorship in Brazil later become?
41954.e: Dilma Rousseff spent almost three years in prison during the dictatorship. From 2011 to 2016 she was President of Brazil.
41954.m: After the dictatorship Dilma Rousseff became President of Brazil.

41955.q: Which country did Rafael Trujillo rule as a dictator?
41955.e: Rafael Leónidas Trujillo ruled the Dominican Republic in the Caribbean. He had himself called “El Jefe”, meaning “the boss”.
41955.m: Rafael Trujillo was dictator of the Dominican Republic.

41956.q: About how long did Rafael Trujillo rule the Dominican Republic?
41956.e: Trujillo came to power in 1930 and remained the country's strongman until his death in 1961.

41957.q: What was the capital Santo Domingo called during the Trujillo dictatorship?
41957.e: In 1936 the capital was renamed in honour of the dictator. After his death it got its old name back in 1961.
41957.m: Under Trujillo, Santo Domingo was called Ciudad Trujillo.

41958.q: How did Rafael Trujillo's rule end in 1961?
41958.e: On 30 May 1961 Trujillo was shot in his car by conspirators. Soon afterwards his regime collapsed.
41958.m: Trujillo was killed in an assassination in 1961.

41959.q: Against which people was the massacre of 1937 under Trujillo directed?
41959.e: In the border region Trujillo had thousands of Haitians murdered. Estimates vary widely; many experts assume about 20,000 deaths.
41959.m: In 1937 Trujillo had thousands of people from Haiti murdered.

41960.q: Which plant is the 1937 massacre in the Dominican Republic named after?
41960.e: Soldiers are said to have made people say “perejil”, the Spanish word for parsley. Anyone who pronounced it with a French Creole accent was identified as Haitian.
41960.m: The 1937 massacre is called the Parsley Massacre.

41961.q: Why were the three Mirabal sisters murdered in the Dominican Republic in 1960?
a: They fought against the dictator Trujillo
41961.e: Patria, Minerva and María Teresa Mirabal fought against the dictatorship. Trujillo's men murdered them on 25 November 1960.
41961.m: The Mirabal sisters were murdered by Trujillo's men.

41962.q: Which day of remembrance is linked to the day the Mirabal sisters died?
41962.e: The UN declared 25 November the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. In doing so it also honours the murdered sisters.
41962.m: 25 November is the International Day against violence against women.

41963.q: What is “The Feast of the Goat” by Mario Vargas Llosa?
a: A novel about the dictator Trujillo
A law against cruelty to animals
41963.e: The novel came out in 2000 and tells of Trujillo's last days. Its author came from Peru and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2010.
41963.m: Mario Vargas Llosa wrote a novel about Trujillo.

41964.q: Which country did the Somoza family dominate for decades?
41964.e: The Somoza family ruled Nicaragua from the 1930s until 1979. It also owned a large part of the country's economy.

41965.q: How many members of the Somoza family were President of Nicaragua?
41965.e: Anastasio Somoza García and his sons Luis and Anastasio Somoza Debayle ruled one after the other. That is why people speak of a family dynasty.
41965.m: Three Somozas, a father and two sons, ruled Nicaragua.

41966.q: How did Anastasio Somoza García, the founder of the dynasty, die in 1956?
a: He was shot in an assassination
He died in a plane crash
41966.e: The young poet Rigoberto López Pérez shot him in León. Somoza García died of his injuries a few days later.
41966.m: Somoza García was killed in an assassination in 1956.

41967.q: Which movement overthrew the Somoza dictatorship in 1979?
41967.e: The Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN) led an uprising against Somoza. On 19 July 1979 its fighters entered Managua.
41967.m: The Sandinistas overthrew the Somoza dictatorship in 1979.

41968.q: Who are the Sandinistas in Nicaragua named after?
41968.e: Augusto César Sandino fought against the US occupation of Nicaragua. In 1934 he was murdered on the orders of Somoza García.
41968.m: The Sandinistas bear the name of the rebel Augusto César Sandino.

41969.q: What did Anastasio Somoza Debayle do with a lot of the aid money after the Managua earthquake of 1972?
a: He made himself rich with it
He gave it to the victims
41969.e: The earthquake destroyed the capital Managua and killed thousands. A large part of the international aid disappeared into the pockets of the family and its associates.
41969.m: Somoza Debayle enriched himself with the aid money after the earthquake.

41970.q: What did the murder of the critical journalist Pedro Joaquín Chamorro in Nicaragua in 1978 trigger?
a: A victory for Somoza in elections
41970.e: Chamorro was a fierce critic of Somoza. After his murder in January 1978 there were general strikes.
41970.m: The murder of Pedro Joaquín Chamorro in 1978 triggered protests against Somoza.

41971.q: What did Anastasio Somoza Debayle do after he was overthrown in 1979?
a: He became a teacher in Managua
41971.e: Somoza Debayle fled into exile, finally to Paraguay. He was killed there in an attack in 1980.
41971.m: Somoza Debayle fled into exile in 1979.

41972.q: Which country did Nicolás Maduro rule as president from 2013?
41972.e: Maduro took over the presidency of Venezuela in 2013 after his predecessor died. In January 2026 he was captured in a US military operation and taken to New York.
41972.m: Nicolás Maduro became President of Venezuela in 2013.

41973.q: Whose successor did Nicolás Maduro become in 2013?
41973.e: Hugo Chávez died of cancer in March 2013. He had earlier named Maduro as the successor he wanted.
41973.m: Maduro was the successor of Hugo Chávez.

41974.q: What job did Nicolás Maduro do before he became a politician?
41974.e: Maduro worked as a bus driver in Caracas and was a trade unionist. Later he became speaker of parliament and foreign minister.
41974.m: Nicolás Maduro used to be a bus driver.

41975.q: What did Venezuela's economy go through under Maduro from about 2016?
41975.e: Prices rose extremely fast, at times by many thousands of per cent a year. Many people could hardly afford food and medicine any more.
41975.m: Under Maduro Venezuela went through hyperinflation.

41976.q: About how many people have left Venezuela since 2014 (as of 2025)?
41976.e: According to the United Nations, almost 8 million Venezuelans have emigrated. It is one of the largest refugee movements in the world.
41976.m: Almost 8 million people have emigrated from Venezuela.

41977.q: What happened in Venezuela in January 2019?
a: An opponent of Maduro declared himself president
There was no government any more
41977.e: The speaker of parliament, Juan Guaidó, considered Maduro's re-election invalid. Many states recognised him, but Maduro kept power.
41977.m: In 2019 Venezuela had two men who called themselves president.

41978.q: Why is the presidential election in Venezuela in July 2024 so strongly disputed?
a: The opposition presented evidence of its victory
41978.e: The electoral authority declared Maduro the winner without publishing detailed results. The opposition showed polling records according to which Edmundo González had clearly won.
41978.m: The 2024 election in Venezuela is considered impossible to verify.

41979.q: Which prize did the Venezuelan opposition politician María Corina Machado receive in 2025?
41979.e: Machado was honoured for her work for democracy in Venezuela. She herself was not allowed to stand in the 2024 election.
41979.m: María Corina Machado received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2025.

41980.q: What is the task of a truth commission?
a: To shed light on the crimes of a dictatorship
41980.e: A truth commission collects witness statements and evidence about human rights violations. It is not a court, but its reports often help in later trials.
41980.m: A truth commission sheds light on crimes of the past.

41981.q: The Argentine report on the dictatorship is called “Nunca más”. What does that mean?
41981.e: “Nunca más” means “Never again”. The 1984 report documented thousands of cases of disappeared people.
41981.m: The Argentine report on the dictatorship is called “Never again”.

41982.q: What did the Argentine truth commission collect from 1983?
a: Reports about people who had disappeared
41982.e: The commission under the writer Ernesto Sabato collected witness statements about people who had disappeared during the dictatorship.
41982.m: Argentina's truth commission collected reports about the disappeared.

41983.q: Which subject did the Valech Commission in Chile investigate in 2003 and 2004?
41983.e: The Valech Commission heard tens of thousands of former prisoners of the Pinochet dictatorship. Its report confirmed that torture had been used systematically.
41983.m: The Valech Commission investigated torture in Chile.

41984.q: When did Chile set up its first truth commission?
a: Shortly after the end of the dictatorship
In the middle of the dictatorship
41984.e: In 1990, straight after the end of the Pinochet dictatorship, the commission under Raúl Rettig began work. It investigated deaths and disappearances.
41984.m: Chile investigated the dictatorship's crimes straight after it ended.

41985.q: According to the truth commission in Peru, who were most of the victims of the conflict from 1980?
41985.e: The commission estimated about 69,000 deaths in the war between the state and rebels such as the “Shining Path”. Most of the victims were poor Indigenous farmers.
41985.m: In the conflict in Peru it was mainly poor Indigenous farmers who suffered.

41986.q: What did Brazil's truth commission name in its report on the military dictatorship?
a: The dead, the disappeared and those responsible
The winners of the next election
41986.e: The commission presented its report in 2014. It named 434 dead and disappeared people and many of those responsible.
41986.m: Brazil's truth commission named the victims and those responsible for the dictatorship.

41987.q: Which country set up a famous truth commission under Desmond Tutu that also influenced Latin America?
41987.e: After the end of apartheid the commission investigated the crimes of the past from 1996. It is a well-known example around the world.
41987.m: South Africa had a famous truth commission under Desmond Tutu.

41988.q: According to the truth commission in Guatemala, who suffered especially in the civil war?
41988.e: The 1999 report concluded that the state had committed genocide against Maya communities.
41988.m: In Guatemala's civil war it was mainly the Maya who suffered.

41989.q: Which organisation set up the truth commission for El Salvador?
41989.e: The commission set up by the UN investigated crimes in the civil war from 1980 to 1992. Its 1993 report is called “From Madness to Hope”.
41989.m: The UN investigated the crimes in El Salvador's civil war.

41990.q: Which country did Mobutu Sese Seko rule as a dictator?
41990.e: Mobutu ruled the Congo from 1965 to 1997. From 1971 to 1997 the country was called Zaire.
41990.m: Mobutu Sese Seko ruled the Congo, which he called Zaire.

41991.q: How did Mobutu come to power in 1965?
41991.e: Mobutu was head of the army and seized power in a coup in 1965. After that he allowed no more real elections.
41991.m: Mobutu seized power in a military coup in 1965.

41992.q: Which new name did Mobutu give his country in 1971?
41992.e: Mobutu renamed the country Zaire in 1971, after an old name for the Congo river. Since 1997 it has been called the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
41992.m: Under Mobutu the Congo was called Zaire from 1971 to 1997.

41993.q: Which item of clothing was Mobutu's trademark?
41993.e: Mobutu almost always appeared with a leopard-skin hat and a walking stick. The hat was meant to show strength and African tradition.
41993.m: Mobutu's trademark was a leopard-skin hat.

41994.q: Which famous boxing match took place in Mobutu's capital Kinshasa in 1974?
41994.e: In 1974 Muhammad Ali beat George Foreman in Kinshasa. Mobutu used the fight to make his country known around the world.
41994.m: The “Rumble in the Jungle” took place in Kinshasa in 1974.

41995.q: What did Mobutu do with his country's wealth?
a: He shared it out among the poor
He gave it to the UN
41995.e: Mobutu moved a huge fortune abroad while the people stayed poor. Rule like this is called kleptocracy, “rule by thieves”.

41996.q: How did Mobutu lose power in 1997?
41996.e: Rebels under Laurent-Désiré Kabila captured Kinshasa in 1997. Mobutu fled into exile and died the same year.
41996.m: Mobutu was driven out by rebels in 1997.

41997.q: Why did Western countries such as the USA support Mobutu for a long time?
a: He was seen as an ally against communism
41997.e: During the Cold War the USA and other Western countries saw Mobutu as a partner against the Soviet Union. That is why they overlooked his oppression for a long time.
41997.m: During the Cold War the West backed Mobutu as an opponent of communism.

41998.q: Which country did Robert Mugabe rule?
41998.e: Mugabe was prime minister from 1980 and President of Zimbabwe from 1987 to 2017.

41999.q: Which European country ruled present-day Zimbabwe as a colony?
41999.e: Zimbabwe was a British colony and was called Rhodesia at that time. It became independent in 1980.
41999.m: Zimbabwe was a British colony called Rhodesia.

42000.q: What did Zimbabwe achieve in 1980 after a long war of liberation?
a: Victory at a football World Cup
42000.e: After a long war of liberation Zimbabwe became independent in 1980. Mugabe won the first elections and became head of government.

42001.q: Which economic problem reached its peak in Zimbabwe in 2008?
42001.e: Money lost its value so quickly that there were banknotes of 100 trillion Zimbabwe dollars. In 2009 the country's own currency was abandoned.
42001.m: In Zimbabwe money became almost worthless in 2008.

42002.q: What did Mugabe's government often seize by force from 2000?
42002.e: In the so-called land reform many farms of white large landowners were occupied. After that farming collapsed badly.
42002.m: Mugabe's land reform led to a collapse in farming.

42003.q: How did Mugabe's rule end in 2017?
a: The army forced him to resign
He handed the office to his son
42003.e: In November 2017 the military took control. Mugabe then resigned at the age of 93.
42003.m: Mugabe had to resign in 2017 under pressure from the army.

42004.q: Who became President of Zimbabwe after Mugabe resigned in 2017?
42004.e: Emmerson Mnangagwa had long been Mugabe's vice president. After Mugabe resigned he took over the presidency.
42004.m: Mugabe's vice president became his successor in 2017.

42005.q: What did observers often accuse Robert Mugabe of at elections?
a: Too many candidates on the list
School opening hours that were too short
42005.e: At elections in Zimbabwe opposition figures were threatened and results were doubted. In this way Mugabe's party ZANU-PF stayed in power.
42005.m: Mugabe also held on to power through unfair elections.

42006.q: How long was Robert Mugabe in power altogether?
42006.e: Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe from 1980 to 2017, first as prime minister and then as president.
42006.m: Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for 37 years.

42007.q: What does the Afrikaans word “apartheid” mean?
42007.e: In Afrikaans apartheid means roughly “apartness”. It referred to the legal separation of people by skin colour.
42007.m: Apartheid means separation by skin colour.

42008.q: In which country was there a system of apartheid?
42008.e: Apartheid was the state system of racial segregation in South Africa. A white minority ruled over the black majority.

42009.q: Who held power in South Africa during apartheid?
42009.e: Only white people were allowed to vote for parliament. In this way a small white minority ruled over the black majority.
42009.m: During apartheid a white minority ruled.

42010.q: What were black South Africans not allowed to do during apartheid?
42010.e: Black people had no vote for parliament. They also had to use separate schools, buses and residential areas.
42010.m: During apartheid black people were not allowed to vote.

42011.q: How were schools, buses and residential areas organised during apartheid?
42011.e: White and black people had to use separate schools, buses, beaches and residential areas. The facilities for black people were usually much worse.
42011.m: Apartheid separated people by skin colour.

42012.q: How did many countries around the world react to apartheid?
a: With boycotts and sanctions against South Africa
They praised South Africa for it
