42298.m: Engels described the misery of English workers in a book of his own.

42299.q: How did Engels help the Marx family in London for many years?
a: He paid a large part of their living costs
He gave them a large country estate
He made Marx a factory director
He got Marx a seat in parliament
42299.e: Engels worked in the family business in Manchester and regularly sent Marx money. This meant Marx could work on his books.
42299.m: Without Engels’s money, Marx could hardly have written so much.

42300.q: What did the Irish worker Mary Burns show her partner Friedrich Engels in Manchester?
42300.e: Mary Burns herself lived in Manchester as a worker. She guided Engels through the districts where factory workers lived in great poverty.
42300.m: Mary Burns showed Engels the life of the workers in Manchester.

42301.q: Which task did Engels take on after Karl Marx died in 1883?
a: He published the second and third volumes of ‘Das Kapital’
He burned all of Marx’s letters
42301.e: Engels put Marx’s unfinished manuscripts in order. The second volume came out in 1885, the third in 1894.
42301.m: After his friend’s death, Engels completed ‘Das Kapital’.

42302.q: Which nickname did Engels get because of his great military knowledge?
42302.e: Engels had done military service in Berlin and fought in the Baden-Palatinate uprising of 1849. Later he wrote many articles about wars and armies.
42302.m: Among his friends, Engels was seen as an expert on military matters.

42303.q: To which country did Engels flee in September 1848 because he faced arrest in Cologne?
42303.e: Engels stayed in Switzerland for a few months and helped to set up workers’ associations there. In January 1849 he returned to Cologne.
42303.m: In 1848 Friedrich Engels found refuge in Switzerland.

42304.q: What did Marx mean by the ‘alienation’ of workers?
a: They no longer have any connection to the product of their work
They move to a foreign country
They have to learn a foreign language
42304.e: In a factory, a worker only makes a small part of a product that does not belong to him. Marx thought that this makes him a stranger to his own work.
42304.m: For Marx, alienation means that workers become strangers to their own work.

42305.q: Whom did Marx and Engels mean by the ‘proletariat’?
a: Workers without their own factories or land
42305.e: Proletarians do not own factories or machines. They have to work for others for a wage.
42305.m: For Marx, the proletariat is the working class.

42306.q: Which famous call to action comes at the end of the Communist Manifesto?
42306.e: Marx and Engels wrote the Manifesto in 1848. With this call they wanted to move workers in all countries to fight together.
42306.m: The Communist Manifesto ends with ‘Workers of the world, unite!’.

42307.q: According to Marx, what should no longer exist in the communist future?
42307.e: Marx expected that with common ownership of the means of production, classes would disappear as well. That is why he spoke of a classless society.
42307.m: Marx’s aim was a classless society.

42308.q: According to Marx, what does a proletarian own that he can sell in order to live?
42308.e: According to Marx, a proletarian has no factories or machines of his own. So he has to sell his labour power to an employer for a wage.
42308.m: A proletarian lives by selling his labour power.

42309.q: What did Marx mean by the term ‘surplus value’?
a: The value that workers create beyond their wages
The tax the state puts on goods
The interest a bank pays on savings
42309.e: According to Marx, workers produce more value than they receive in wages. According to his theory, the factory owner keeps this surplus.
42309.m: For Marx, surplus value is the part of work that is not paid as wages.

42310.q: What did Marx understand by the ‘dictatorship of the proletariat’?
a: A transitional period in which the working class holds state power
A king ruling over the workers
A ban on all trade unions
An election in which only rich people take part
42310.e: Marx imagined that after a revolution the workers would take over the state for a while. After that, in his view, the state would gradually become unnecessary.
42310.m: For Marx, the dictatorship of the proletariat was meant as a transition.

42311.q: What does ‘class consciousness’ mean for Marx?
a: Workers recognise their shared situation and interests
Pupils are proud of their school class
Rich people only travel first class
Farmers know the boundaries of their fields
42311.e: According to Marx, workers first have to understand that they are all in a similar situation. Only then can they stand up for their aims together.
42311.m: Class consciousness means recognising your own position in society.

42312.q: Before the rise of the bourgeoisie, which group had the most power in Europe?
42312.e: In the Middle Ages and early modern times, kings and nobles controlled land and politics. With trade and industry, rich townspeople gained more and more influence.
42312.m: Before the middle class, power lay mainly with the nobility.

42313.q: Which language does the word ‘bourgeoisie’ come from?
42313.e: The word was taken from French. In the 19th century it spread all over Europe as a technical term.
42313.m: The word ‘bourgeoisie’ is of French origin.

42314.q: Which English term roughly corresponds to ‘bourgeoisie’?
42314.e: Originally the word meant the inhabitants of a town, the townspeople. In English it is therefore roughly the same as the middle class.

42315.q: What is meant by ‘means of production’?
a: Factories, machines and raw materials used to make goods
The money in a savings account
42315.e: Means of production are everything you need to make goods. According to Marx, whoever owns them belongs to the ruling class.
42315.m: Goods are made with the means of production.

42316.q: What did Marx call the conflict between the bourgeoisie and the proletariat?
42316.e: Marx saw history as a series of struggles between social classes. Under capitalism, in his view, owners and workers face each other.
42316.m: For Marx, history is a history of class struggles.

42317.q: According to Marx, what is the most important aim of an employer under capitalism?
a: To make as much profit as possible
To pay as much tax as possible
To sell as little as possible
To pay the highest possible wages
42317.e: According to Marx, a capitalist has to make a profit to survive the competition. That is why he tries to keep costs low.
42317.m: Under capitalism, an employer strives for profit.

42318.q: Through which revolution did the middle class in France gain political power from 1789?
42318.e: In the French Revolution, the old privileges were abolished and human rights were declared. The middle class became the leading force in the state and the economy.
42318.m: The French Revolution strengthened the middle class.

42319.q: What is the economic system in which companies are private and produce for profit called?
42319.e: Under capitalism, companies belong to private owners, and prices are set on the market. Marx sharply criticised this system.
42319.m: Under capitalism, private companies produce for profit.

42320.q: How long was a working day often in many factories during early industrialisation?
42320.e: In the first factories there were hardly any protective laws. Working days of 12 to 16 hours, six days a week, were common.
42320.m: In the past, factory workers often worked more than twelve hours a day.

42321.q: What do you call the plight of workers in the 19th century and the search for solutions to it?
42321.e: With industrialisation, the number of poor working-class families grew sharply. The debate about wages, housing and protecting workers was called the social question.
42321.m: The social question was about the hardship of workers during industrialisation.

42322.q: Which disease was often spread by dirty drinking water in 19th-century working-class districts?
42322.e: In cramped districts without sewers, germs got into the drinking water. That is why outbreaks of cholera killed many people.
42322.m: Dirty water spread cholera in the cities.

42323.q: Under the Federal Factory Act of 1877, how old did children have to be at least to work in a factory?
42323.e: The Factory Act of 1877 banned children under 14 from working in factories. It was one of the most progressive laws protecting workers in Europe.
42323.m: From 1877, children under 14 were no longer allowed to work in factories in Switzerland.

42324.q: Which canton decided at its Landsgemeinde in 1864 on a factory law with a maximum of 12 working hours a day?
42324.e: The Glarus Landsgemeinde (open-air assembly) even pushed the law through against the will of the cantonal government. It also banned night work.
42324.m: Glarus was a pioneer in protecting factory workers.

42325.q: What were large, crowded blocks of flats for working-class families in cities like Berlin called?
42325.e: In these buildings many families lived in very cramped conditions, often with dark back courtyards. Light, air and sanitation were often lacking.
42325.m: Many working-class families lived crammed together in tenement barracks.

42326.q: Which uprising of 1844 in Silesia became a symbol of the misery of workers?
42326.e: The Silesian weavers suffered from falling wages and hunger. Their uprising was crushed by the army and later portrayed by Gerhart Hauptmann in the play ‘The Weavers’.
42326.m: The weavers’ uprising of 1844 showed the hardship of home workers.

42327.q: What happened in 1832 during the ‘Uster Fire’ in the canton of Zurich?
a: Home weavers set fire to a mechanical weaving mill
Soldiers burned down a farming village
42327.e: The home weavers were afraid of losing their work because of the new weaving machines. In protest, they set the factory on fire.
42327.m: In the Uster Fire, home weavers fought back against the machines.

42328.q: Why did many children work in factories in the 19th century?
a: Families needed the wages, and children were cheap workers
All schools were closed at that time
By law, children were only allowed to work in factories
The children preferred working to playing
42328.e: The parents’ wages were often not enough to live on. Factory owners were happy to employ children because they could pay them less.
42328.m: Poverty forced many children to work in factories.

42329.q: In which country was Robert Owen’s famous model factory?
42329.e: From about 1800 Owen ran the New Lanark cotton mill in Scotland. He turned it into a model business with better living conditions.
42329.m: Robert Owen made a factory in Scotland into a model.

42330.e: Robert Owen was a businessman who ran a large cotton mill. He wanted to show that good working conditions were possible.
42330.m: Robert Owen was a factory owner with social ideas.

42331.q: What did Robert Owen want to try out in a settlement in America in 1825?
42331.e: In New Harmony, Indiana, everyone was supposed to own and work together. The project failed after a few years.
42331.m: Owen tried out an ideal community in America.

42332.q: What did Robert Owen change about working hours in his factory?
a: He introduced night work for children
42332.e: At that time 13 to 14 hours a day were normal. Owen cut working hours to ten and a half hours, and the factory still remained successful.
42332.m: Robert Owen significantly shortened his workers’ working day.

42333.q: Instead of early factory work, what did the workers’ children receive in Owen’s factory village?
42333.e: Owen was convinced that education shapes people. That is why he founded a school for his workers’ children.
42333.m: For Owen, education was more important than early child labour.

42334.q: Robert Owen is seen as the founder of which movement?
42334.e: Owen wanted people to run businesses together and share the profits. His ideas were taken up by workers who founded shared shops and businesses.
42334.m: Robert Owen stood up for running businesses together.

42335.q: Why did Marx and Engels call early socialists like Owen ‘utopian’?
a: They thought their plans were based on wishful thinking rather than analysis
Because these socialists all lived on islands
Because these socialists wrote novels about the future
Because these socialists rejected the workers
42335.e: Marx and Engels thought their own teaching was ‘scientific’. In their view, the older socialists wanted to achieve a fair society only through good examples.
42335.m: Marx and Engels distinguished between utopian and scientific socialism.

42336.q: What did utopian socialists like Charles Fourier want to build?
a: Large communal buildings for living and working together
42336.e: Fourier planned buildings in which around 1600 people were to live and work together. He called them ‘phalanstères’.
42336.m: Utopian socialists dreamed of shared living buildings.

42337.q: Which book by Thomas More from 1516 does the word ‘utopia’ come from?
42337.e: In it, Thomas More described an invented island with an ideal society without private property. The name means roughly ‘no place’.
42337.m: The word ‘utopia’ goes back to a book by Thomas More.

42338.q: Which kind of property did Marx and Engels want to abolish?
a: Private ownership of factories and means of production
All of people’s clothes and furniture
Craftsmen’s tools for their free time
42338.e: Marx and Engels distinguished between personal possessions and ownership of the means of production. According to their teaching, only the latter was to become common property.
42338.m: Marx wanted to abolish private ownership of factories.

42339.q: What did the thinker Proudhon mean by the sentence ‘Property is theft’?
a: Large wealth owned by a few is unfair
Thieves should be allowed to keep property
Everyone should build their own house
42339.e: The Frenchman Pierre-Joseph Proudhon wrote the sentence in 1840. He thought it was unfair that a few people own a lot and others have to work for them.
42339.m: The sentence ‘Property is theft’ criticises unfairly shared wealth.

42340.q: Which fundamental right in the Swiss Federal Constitution protects private property?
42340.e: Article 26 of the Federal Constitution guarantees ownership. Expropriations must be fully compensated.
42340.m: In Switzerland, property is protected by the Constitution.

42343.q: What do you call a business that belongs to its members together?
42343.e: In a cooperative, all members have a say, usually with one vote per person. In Switzerland, many housing and farming businesses are organised like this too.
42343.m: A cooperative belongs to its members together.

42344.q: What did the researcher Elinor Ostrom, who won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2009, show?
a: Communities can manage shared resources well themselves
Only the state can use pastures properly
Fishing grounds are best owned by one person
42344.e: Elinor Ostrom studied pastures, forests and fishing grounds. She showed that communities often manage such resources well themselves, for example Alpine pastures in Switzerland.
42344.m: Elinor Ostrom researched how communities manage common property.

42345.q: What do you call it when the state takes over private companies?
42345.e: In nationalisation, companies become the property of the state. Communist states nationalised almost the whole economy.
42345.m: In nationalisation, a business becomes the property of the state.

42347.q: What does the abbreviation SP stand for in Swiss politics?
42347.e: The Social Democratic Party of Switzerland (in German: Sozialdemokratische Partei, SP) was founded in 1888. It grew out of various workers’ associations.
42347.m: SP stands for Social Democratic Party.

42348.q: How do social democrats want to change society?
a: Through the rule of a king
42348.e: Social democrats rely on elections, parliament and laws. Revolutionary communists, on the other hand, wanted to get rid of the existing order through a revolution.
42348.m: Social democrats want to reach social goals through democratic reforms.

42349.q: Who elects the members of the Swiss Federal Council?
42349.e: The National Council and the Council of States elect the Federal Councillors together. In 1943 they elected the first Social Democrat, Ernst Nobs.
42349.m: The Federal Assembly elects the Federal Council.

42350.q: What is the big strike of 1918 organised by the SP and the trade unions in Switzerland called?
42350.e: In November 1918 around 250,000 people stopped work. The Federal Council sent in the army, and the strike was called off after a few days.
42350.m: The national strike of 1918 was the biggest walkout in Swiss history.

42351.q: Since 1919, how have the seats in the National Council been shared out among the parties?
a: According to their share of the vote
Every party gets the same number
42351.e: Since 1919 proportional representation has applied. Parties receive seats in proportion to their votes. This was one of the demands of the national strike.
42351.m: Since 1919 the National Council has been elected by proportional representation.

42352.q: What is the party colour of the Swiss SP?
42352.e: Since the 19th century, red has been the colour of the workers’ movement. The Swiss SP uses red as well.
42352.m: The colour of the social democrats is red.

42353.q: What is the difference between a reform and a revolution?
a: A reform changes things step by step, a revolution overthrows the order
A revolution always lasts many centuries
42353.e: Reforms change laws step by step, for example through elections. A revolution gets rid of the existing order quickly and often with violence.
42353.m: Social democrats rely on reform rather than revolution.

42354.q: How many of the seven Federal Council seats has the SP held for a long time?
42354.e: Since 1959 the ‘magic formula’ has shared out the Federal Council seats according to party strength. Since then the SP has had two Federal Councillors.
42354.m: The SP has two seats on the Federal Council.

42355.q: What did the first workers’ associations campaign for in the 19th century?
42355.e: Workers joined together to achieve more together. Social democratic parties later grew out of such associations.
42355.m: Workers’ associations were the forerunners of social democracy.

a: A song of the workers’ movement
42356.e: ‘The Internationale’ is the best-known song of the workers’ movement. It is sung all over the world in many languages.
42356.m: ‘The Internationale’ is the song of the workers’ movement.

42357.q: Which country does the song ‘The Internationale’ originally come from?
42357.e: The words and the tune were written in France. From there the song spread all over the world.

42358.q: Which state used ‘The Internationale’ as its national anthem until 1944?
42358.e: The Soviet Union sang ‘The Internationale’ as its anthem until it got its own national anthem in 1944. After that the song remained the party anthem.
42358.m: ‘The Internationale’ was the anthem of the Soviet Union for a long time.

42359.q: Whom does ‘The Internationale’ call on to stand together?
a: The workers and the oppressed of the whole world
The soldiers of a single army
42359.e: The song calls on all workers and oppressed people to work together for a fairer world. That is why it is called ‘international’.
42359.m: ‘The Internationale’ calls on workers of all countries to stand together.

42361.q: Which song did students sing in 1989 during the protests in Tiananmen Square in Beijing?
42361.e: The demonstrators sang the song of the workers’ movement, which the Communist Party of China also uses. In this way they showed that they were appealing to ideals of justice.
42361.m: ‘The Internationale’ was also heard at the protests in Beijing in 1989.

42362.q: Why is the song called ‘The Internationale’?
a: It is meant to unite workers of all countries
It was written at an airport
It is only sung at the Olympic Games
It is only sung in English
42362.e: The workers’ movement wanted to stand together across national borders. That is why the song was translated into very many languages.
42362.m: ‘The Internationale’ is meant to unite workers of all countries.

42363.q: Who joined together in the International Workingmen’s Association in 1864?
42363.e: In 1864, workers’ representatives from various European countries met in London. They wanted to fight together for better working conditions.
42363.m: The International Workingmen’s Association linked workers across national borders.

42364.q: Under which name is the International Workingmen’s Association also known?
42364.e: Because other international workers’ associations were founded later, it is called the First International. It was the first big union of workers across national borders.
42364.m: The International Workingmen’s Association is also called the First International.

42365.q: Which well-known thinker wrote the founding address of the International Workingmen’s Association?
42365.e: Marx sat on the organisation’s leading body and wrote its most important statements, including the founding address.
42365.m: Karl Marx wrote the founding address of the First International.

42366.q: Why did workers’ representatives in the 19th century like to meet in Switzerland, for example in Geneva in 1866?
a: Because there was more freedom there
Because all the workers there were rich
Because there were no factories there
42366.e: In Switzerland people could gather and speak their minds more freely than in many other European countries. That is why the first congress of the First International took place in Geneva.
42366.m: Because of its freedoms, Switzerland was a popular meeting place.

42367.q: What did the delegates of the First International discuss at their congresses, for example in Basel in 1869?
a: Workers’ rights such as shorter working hours
42367.e: The delegates talked about working hours, wages and workers’ rights. In Basel they also argued fiercely about the right path to a fairer society.
42367.m: In 1869 the First International met in Basel.

42368.q: What did the Russian anarchist Mikhail Bakunin reject, which is why he quarrelled with Karl Marx?
42368.e: Anarchists like Bakunin did not want any state at all. Marx, on the other hand, wanted the workers to take over the state first. In 1872 Bakunin was expelled from the First International.
42368.m: Mikhail Bakunin was Marx’s great opponent in the First International.

42369.q: What happened to the First International after its leadership was moved to New York in 1872?
a: It became the biggest party in the USA
It took over the government in America
42369.e: Marx wanted to stop the anarchists from taking over the leadership. But so far from Europe, the organisation soon lost importance and was dissolved in 1876.
42369.m: The General Council of the First International moved to America in 1872.

42370.q: In which region of Switzerland is Saint-Imier, where anarchists met for a congress in 1872?
42370.e: Saint-Imier is in the Bernese Jura. Many watchmakers lived there, some of whom were anarchists. The congress is seen as the birth of the anarchist International.
42370.m: Saint-Imier is an important place in the history of anarchism.

42371.q: In which months of 1871 did the Paris Commune exist?
42371.e: The Commune began with an uprising in Paris on 18 March 1871. It was crushed by government troops on 28 May.
42371.m: The Paris Commune only lasted about two months.

42372.q: After which war did the Paris Commune come about?
42372.e: In 1870/71 France had lost the war against Prussia and its allies, and Paris had been under siege for a long time. Many Parisians were outraged by the peace and the government.
42372.m: The Paris Commune followed a heavy military defeat for France.

42373.q: From which city did the French government under Adolphe Thiers fight the Commune?
42373.e: The government and the National Assembly were based in Versailles. From there, Thiers sent troops against rebellious Paris.
42373.m: During the Commune, Thiers’s government was based in Versailles.

42374.q: What is the last week of fighting of the Paris Commune in May 1871 called?
42374.e: From 21 to 28 May, government troops recaptured Paris barricade by barricade. Thousands of Communards were killed or executed.
42374.m: The Paris Commune ended in a bloody week.

42375.q: Which monument in Paris did the Communards pull down in 1871?
42375.e: The column on the Place Vendôme celebrated Napoleon’s victories. For the Communards it was a symbol of war and imperial rule.
42375.m: The Communards pulled down the Vendôme Column.

42376.q: Which woman fought on the barricades of the Paris Commune and is still well known today?
42376.e: Louise Michel was a teacher and fought with weapons for the Commune. Afterwards she was exiled to the French colony of New Caledonia.
42376.m: Louise Michel is a well-known fighter of the Paris Commune.

42377.q: What did the Paris Commune decide about the relationship between Church and state?
a: The separation of Church and state
The introduction of a state church
The election of the mayor by priests
42377.e: The Commune declared that the state should not favour any religion. In the whole of France, separation was only introduced in 1905.
42377.m: The Commune separated Church and state.

42378.q: What does the ‘Communards’ Wall’ in Paris commemorate?
a: Fighters of the Paris Commune who were shot
The building of the Eiffel Tower
42378.e: On 28 May 1871 the last fighters of the Commune were shot at this wall in Père Lachaise Cemetery. Today it is a place of remembrance.
42378.m: The Communards’ Wall commemorates the end of the Paris Commune.

42379.q: What did workers in the USA go on strike for on 1 May 1886?
42379.e: The American workers’ movement called for a nationwide strike on this day. It wanted to limit daily working hours.
42379.m: 1 May came out of the struggle for shorter working hours.

42380.q: What do trade unions typically demand on 1 May?
a: Better working conditions and fair wages
42380.e: On 1 May, trade unions stand up for the concerns of employees. These include fair wages and good working conditions.
42380.m: On 1 May, trade unions demand better working conditions.

42381.q: Who mainly takes to the streets on 1 May?
42381.e: 1 May is the day of the workers’ movement. Trade unions and employees demonstrate for their rights at rallies.
42381.m: On 1 May, trade unions and employees demonstrate.

42382.q: Which century does 1 May as International Workers’ Day date from?
42382.e: On 1 May 1890, workers in many countries took to the streets together for the first time. There were rallies in Switzerland too.
42382.m: 1 May as Labour Day has existed since the 19th century.

42383.q: In which of these cantons is 1 May a public holiday?
42383.e: 1 May is not a national holiday in Switzerland; the cantons decide for themselves. In Zurich it is treated the same as a Sunday (as of 2026).
42383.m: In Switzerland, each canton decides for itself whether 1 May is a day off.

42384.q: Which flower is a symbol of 1 May in the workers’ movement?
42384.e: Many people at May Day rallies wore a red carnation on their lapel. Red is the traditional colour of the workers’ movement.
42384.m: The red carnation belongs to 1 May.

42385.e: On 1 May, trade unions and employees demonstrate for their concerns. In many countries it is a day off work.

42386.q: In which country did the February Revolution break out in 1917?
42386.e: The unrest began in what was then the Russian capital, Petrograd, today’s St Petersburg. In the end the Tsar had to abdicate.
42386.m: The February Revolution took place in Russia in 1917.

42388.q: On which special day did the women workers’ strikes in Petrograd begin in 1917?
42388.e: On 8 March 1917 (23 February in the old calendar), women textile workers took to the streets on International Women’s Day. Their protests turned into a general strike.
42388.m: The February Revolution began with women’s protests on International Women’s Day.

42389.q: What did people in Petrograd complain about most in the winter of 1917?
a: Taxes on bicycles being too high
A lack of schools in the countryside
42389.e: Because of the First World War there was a shortage of food and fuel, and long queues formed outside the bakeries. Hunger drove many people onto the streets.
42389.m: Hunger and bread shortages set off the protests in Petrograd in 1917.

42390.q: What decided the February Revolution when the soldiers in the capital changed sides?
a: They refused to shoot at the demonstrators
They left the city for the front
They occupied the Kremlin in Moscow
They immediately proclaimed a new tsar
42390.e: Many regiments in Petrograd went over to the rebels instead of shooting at them. This meant the Tsar’s government lost its power in the capital.
42390.m: The revolution won because the soldiers joined the demonstrators.

42391.q: Which government took over the leadership of Russia after the February Revolution?
42391.e: After the Tsar was overthrown, politicians from the Duma formed a Provisional Government, a temporary government. It was meant to govern until elections to a Constituent Assembly.
42391.m: After the February Revolution, a temporary, provisional government ruled.

42392.q: Who overthrew the Provisional Government in Russia in October 1917?
42392.e: The Provisional Government was overthrown by the Bolsheviks under Lenin in the October Revolution. After that the communists took power.
42392.m: The Bolsheviks overthrew the Provisional Government in October 1917.

42393.q: Which important decision did the Provisional Government make about the First World War?
a: It made peace with Germany immediately
It went over to Germany’s side
42393.e: The Provisional Government stuck with its allies and kept fighting against Germany. This made it unpopular with many war-weary soldiers and workers.
42393.m: The Provisional Government lost support because it carried on the war.

42394.q: In which country did Lenin lead a revolution in 1917?
42394.e: Lenin and the Bolsheviks took power in Russia in October 1917. This later led to the Soviet Union.
42394.m: Lenin led the revolution in Russia in 1917.

42395.q: What is the revolution of 1917 that brought Lenin to power called?
42395.e: In October 1917, according to the Russian calendar of the time, Lenin’s Bolsheviks overthrew the government. That is why it is called the October Revolution.
42395.m: Lenin came to power with the October Revolution of 1917.

42396.q: Who ruled Russia before the revolutions of 1917?
42396.e: For centuries Russia was ruled by a tsar. The last tsar, Nicholas II, had to abdicate in 1917.

42397.q: What was the group within the Russian social democrats that Lenin led called?
42397.e: In 1903 the Russian Social Democratic Party split into Bolsheviks (the majority) and Mensheviks (the minority). Lenin led the Bolsheviks.
42397.m: Lenin was the leader of the Bolsheviks.

42398.q: In which Swiss city did Lenin live in exile until 1917?
42398.e: During the First World War Lenin lived in Bern and finally in Zurich on the Spiegelgasse. In April 1917 he travelled from there back to Russia.
42398.m: Before the revolution, Lenin lived in Zurich.

42399.q: With which slogan did Lenin and the Bolsheviks win many supporters in 1917?
42399.e: The Bolsheviks promised peace to the war-weary people, land to the farmers and bread to the hungry. This set them apart from the Provisional Government.
42399.m: With the promise of peace, land and bread, Lenin won many people over.

42400.q: Which new state was founded under Lenin’s leadership in 1922?
42400.e: At the end of 1922 Russia and other Soviet republics joined together to form the Soviet Union. Lenin was its first head of government.
42400.m: The Soviet Union was founded in 1922.

42401.q: With which country did Lenin’s government make the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in March 1918?
42401.e: With the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, Soviet Russia left the First World War. In return it had to give large territories to Germany and its allies.
42401.m: With the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, Lenin ended the war against Germany in 1918.

42402.q: What was the city of Petrograd renamed after Lenin’s death in 1924?
42402.e: A few days after Lenin’s death, Petrograd was given the name Leningrad in his honour. Since 1991 the city has been called St Petersburg again.
42402.m: From 1924 to 1991 St Petersburg was called Leningrad.

42403.q: What is Nicholas II known for in Russian history?
42403.e: Nicholas II ruled from 1894 to 1917. After him there were no more tsars in Russia.
42403.m: Nicholas II was the last tsar of Russia.

42404.q: Which ruling family did Tsar Nicholas II belong to?
42404.e: The Romanovs had ruled Russia since 1613. With Nicholas II their rule ended after more than 300 years.
42404.m: Nicholas II was the last tsar from the Romanov family.

42405.q: Which illness did Alexei, the only son of Nicholas II, have?
42405.e: Alexei suffered from haemophilia, the bleeding disorder: even small injuries could cause life-threatening bleeding. His mother Alexandra had passed the illness on to him.
42405.m: The heir to the throne, Alexei, suffered from haemophilia.

42406.q: Which wandering preacher gained great influence at the Tsar’s court because he could supposedly help Alexei?
42406.e: Rasputin seemed able to calm Alexei’s bleeding and so won the Tsarina’s trust. His influence damaged the reputation of the Tsar’s family; he was murdered in 1916.
42406.m: Rasputin’s influence at court damaged the Tsar’s reputation.

42407.q: What happened on ‘Bloody Sunday’ in St Petersburg in January 1905?
a: Soldiers shot at workers demonstrating peacefully
The Tsar was injured in an attack
A huge fire destroyed the Winter Palace
Japan attacked the city with ships
42407.e: Thousands of workers marched to the Winter Palace with a petition, and soldiers opened fire. After that many people lost their trust in the Tsar, and the Revolution of 1905 began.
42407.m: On Bloody Sunday in 1905 the Tsar lost the trust of many workers.

42408.q: What did Nicholas II have to allow after the Revolution of 1905?
a: The election of the Tsar by the people
42408.e: In the October Manifesto of 1905, the Tsar promised basic rights and an elected parliament, the State Duma. But its power remained limited.
42408.m: After 1905 Russia got a parliament, the Duma.

42409.q: Which fateful decision did Nicholas II make in 1915?
a: He took supreme command of the army himself
He moved the capital to Moscow
42409.e: In 1915 the Tsar went to the front, which made him personally responsible for the defeats. In the capital, the Tsarina and Rasputin now had more influence.
42409.m: As commander-in-chief, the Tsar was blamed for the defeats in the war.

42410.q: What happened to the Tsar’s family in July 1918?
a: They were murdered by the Bolsheviks
42410.e: The Bolsheviks held the family prisoner in Yekaterinburg. There the Tsar, his wife and their five children were shot.
42410.m: The Tsar’s family was murdered in 1918.

42411.q: What did Nicholas II do in March 1917 after unrest and defeats in the war?
42411.e: Because of hunger, strikes and defeats in the First World War, the Tsar lost all support. In March 1917 he gave up the throne, and the rule of the tsars ended.

42412.q: In which part of Zurich did Lenin live in 1916 and 1917?
a: On a farm on the edge of the city
42412.e: Lenin lived at Spiegelgasse 14 in Zurich’s old town. Today a plaque reminds people of this.
42412.m: Lenin lived in Zurich’s old town.

42413.q: Who did Lenin live with in his flat in Zurich?
42413.e: Lenin’s wife, Nadezhda Krupskaya, went with him into exile. She also worked closely with him politically.
42413.m: In Zurich, Lenin lived with his wife.

42414.q: Why did Lenin live in Switzerland during the First World War?
a: Neutral Switzerland gave him protection in exile
He was on a long skiing holiday
42414.e: Lenin was persecuted in Russia and lived abroad. Switzerland was neutral in the war, so many refugees found protection there.
42414.m: Lenin lived in exile in neutral Switzerland.

42416.q: What were the socialists who met Lenin in Zimmerwald near Bern in 1915 against?
42416.e: In 1915 socialists from several countries met in Zimmerwald. They wanted the First World War to stop.
42416.m: In 1915 opponents of the First World War met in Zimmerwald.

42417.q: What did Lenin mainly use his time in Zurich for?
a: He read in libraries and wrote political works
He worked as a teacher at a school
He ran a bank on the Bahnhofstrasse
He studied medicine at the university
42417.e: Lenin spent many hours in Zurich’s libraries. There he read a lot and wrote articles and books.
42417.m: In Zurich, Lenin read and wrote a lot in libraries.

42418.q: After his time in Switzerland, what did Lenin want to achieve in Russia?
42418.e: Lenin returned to Russia in 1917. In the autumn he and the Bolsheviks took power in the October Revolution.
42418.m: Lenin led the revolution in Russia in 1917.

42419.q: How did Lenin travel back from Switzerland to Russia in 1917?
42419.e: In April 1917 Lenin travelled through Germany by train with a group. The Swiss Fritz Platten helped to organise the journey.
42419.m: In 1917 Lenin travelled back to Russia by train.

42420.q: From which Swiss city did Lenin travel back to Russia in 1917?
42420.e: Lenin lived in Zurich during the First World War. In April 1917 he left from there in the sealed train carriage through Germany towards Russia.
42420.m: In 1917 Lenin travelled from Zurich to Russia.

42421.q: Which country did Lenin’s train travel through straight after leaving Switzerland in 1917?
42421.e: The train crossed the border into Germany at Thayngen and Gottmadingen. Russia and Germany were enemies in the war at that time.
42421.m: In 1917 Lenin travelled right across Germany in the middle of the war.

42422.q: Why did the German government let Lenin travel through?
a: It hoped he would weaken Russia
Lenin had paid Germany a lot of money
42422.e: Germany wanted Russia to drop out of the war because of unrest at home. Peace in the East would have freed German troops for the West.
42422.m: Germany helped Lenin because it hoped the war in the East would end.

42423.q: What did it mean that Lenin’s carriage was ‘sealed’?
a: The passengers were not allowed to leave the carriage
The carriage was armoured with lead
The carriage ran without a locomotive
42423.e: Most of the carriage doors were locked, and the Russians were not allowed to get off in Germany. This was so there would be no contact with Germans.
42423.m: In the sealed carriage, the passengers were not allowed to get off in Germany.

42424.q: Roughly how many Russian émigrés travelled in the sealed carriage?
42424.e: Just over 30 people travelled with Lenin, including Grigory Zinoviev and Karl Radek. So it was a small group.
42424.m: A group of about 30 people travelled in the sealed carriage.

42425.q: How did Lenin’s group cross the Baltic Sea on the way to Sweden?
a: By ferry from Sassnitz to Trelleborg
By plane from Berlin to Stockholm
42425.e: From Sassnitz on the island of Rügen, a ferry took the group to Trelleborg in southern Sweden. From there they went on to Stockholm by train.
42425.m: Lenin crossed the Baltic from Germany to Sweden by ferry.

42426.q: In which city did Lenin arrive in April 1917?
42426.e: Petrograd was the capital of Russia at that time. At the station Lenin was welcomed by a large crowd.

42427.q: Which image did Winston Churchill later use to describe Lenin’s journey through Germany?
42427.e: Churchill compared the journey to putting typhoid or cholera germs into a city’s water supply. He meant that Lenin was sent to shake Russia on purpose.
42427.m: Churchill saw Lenin’s journey as a deliberate weapon against Russia.

42428.q: What were the opponents of the Bolsheviks called in the Russian Civil War?
42428.e: The Bolsheviks were called the Reds and their opponents the Whites. The Whites included supporters of the Tsar, officers and liberals.
42428.m: In the Civil War the Reds fought against the Whites.

42429.q: Roughly when did the Russian Civil War last?
42429.e: The Civil War began after the October Revolution and lasted mainly from 1918 to 1921. In the Far East the fighting went on until 1922.
42429.m: The Russian Civil War raged mainly from 1918 to 1921.

42430.q: Which side won the Russian Civil War?
42430.e: The Bolsheviks controlled the heartland with Moscow and Petrograd and had a tightly led army. The Whites were divided and spread over a huge area.
42430.m: The Reds won the Civil War and secured the Bolsheviks’ power.

42431.q: What did the Whites want to prevent in the Russian Civil War?
a: The building of the Trans-Siberian Railway
42431.e: The Whites were very varied, including officers, supporters of the Tsar and liberals. The only thing they had in common was that they fought against the Bolsheviks.
42431.m: The Whites fought against Bolshevik rule.

42432.q: What was the secret police founded by the Bolsheviks in December 1917 called?
42432.e: The Cheka under Felix Dzerzhinsky persecuted political opponents with great harshness. In the Civil War it carried out the so-called Red Terror.
42432.m: The Cheka secret police persecuted the Bolsheviks’ opponents.

42433.q: What was the strict economic policy of the Bolsheviks during the Civil War called?
42433.e: Under war communism, businesses were nationalised and grain was taken from farmers by force. This led to hunger and uprisings.
42433.m: During the Civil War, Soviet Russia had war communism.

42434.q: Which countries sent troops to Russia during the Russian Civil War?
a: Great Britain, France, the USA and Japan, among others
Only the neutral countries Switzerland, Sweden and Norway
Only China, India and the Ottoman Empire
Not a single country; the war stayed purely Russian
42434.e: Several foreign powers landed troops in Russia and partly supported the Whites. But their involvement stayed limited, and they withdrew again.
42434.m: Foreign powers also got involved in Russia during the Civil War.

42435.q: Which terrible disaster struck the regions along the Volga after the Civil War in 1921 and 1922?
a: A plague of locusts from Africa
42435.e: War, forced requisitions and drought caused a famine in which millions of people died. Aid organisations from abroad also tried to help.
42435.m: After the Civil War, millions of people starved to death along the Volga.

42436.q: Where did many Whites who fled Russia after the Civil War live?
a: Abroad, for example in Paris, Berlin or Prague
In Siberia near the Arctic Circle
In the Kremlin fortress in Moscow
In camps on the Crimean peninsula
42436.e: About one to two million people left Russia after the defeat of the Whites. They formed Russian exile communities in many European cities.
42436.m: After the Civil War, many opponents of the Bolsheviks lived in exile.

42437.q: In which year was the Red Army founded?
42437.e: At the beginning of 1918 the Bolsheviks founded the Workers’ and Peasants’ Red Army. It replaced the Tsar’s army, which had fallen apart.
42437.m: The Red Army was founded in 1918.

42438.q: Who built up the Red Army as People’s Commissar for War?
42438.e: Leon Trotsky turned volunteer units into a large, tightly led army. He travelled from front to front in an armoured train.
42438.m: Leon Trotsky is seen as the founder and organiser of the Red Army.

42439.q: Which badge did Red Army soldiers wear on their caps?
42439.e: The red five-pointed star became the badge of the Red Army during the Civil War. It later became a symbol of the whole Soviet Union.
42439.m: The red star was the badge of the Red Army.

42440.q: Which experienced experts did the Red Army leadership bring in, even though they had once served the Tsar?
a: Officers of the old Tsarist army
42440.e: Without experienced officers, the new army could not fight well. So it used thousands of former Tsarist officers as ‘military specialists’.
42440.m: The Red Army used the knowledge of former Tsarist officers.

42441.q: What was the job of the political commissars in the Red Army?
a: They watched over the officers’ loyalty to the Party
42441.e: Next to every commander stood a Party commissar. He checked whether the officers stayed loyal to the Bolsheviks and gave the soldiers political education.
42441.m: Political commissars kept an eye on the officers in the Red Army.

42442.q: What was the famous cavalry force of the Red Army under Semyon Budyonny called?
42442.e: The First Cavalry Army under Semyon Budyonny fought in the Civil War and in the war against Poland in 1920. The Red Army’s pointed cloth cap was called the ‘budyonovka’ after Budyonny.
42442.m: Budyonny’s First Cavalry Army was the best-known cavalry of the Red Army.

42443.q: Against which neighbouring country did the Red Army fight in 1920, losing outside Warsaw?
42443.e: In the Polish-Soviet War the Red Army stood outside Warsaw in 1920. The Polish army drove it back in the Battle of the Vistula.
42443.m: In 1920 Poland stopped the Red Army outside Warsaw.

42444.q: What name did the Red Army get in 1946?
42444.e: After the Second World War the Red Army was renamed the Soviet Army in 1946. It kept this name until the end of the Soviet Union.
42444.m: From 1946 the Red Army was called the Soviet Army.

42445.q: Who introduced the New Economic Policy (NEP) in Soviet Russia in 1921?
42445.e: After the Civil War the country was poor and hungry. So with the NEP, Lenin allowed some private trade again.

42446.q: In which year did Lenin introduce the New Economic Policy?
42446.e: In March 1921 the 10th Party Congress decided on the New Economic Policy. After the Civil War the country was poor and hungry.

42447.q: Which policy did the New Economic Policy replace?
42447.e: War communism had led to hunger and uprisings. With the NEP, Lenin relaxed the harsh forced measures.
42447.m: The NEP replaced harsh war communism.

42448.q: Thanks to the New Economic Policy, what were farmers allowed to do again?
a: Sell their surplus at the market
42448.e: Instead of having to hand over all their grain, farmers paid a fixed tax in kind. They were allowed to sell the rest freely.
42448.m: With the NEP, farmers could sell their surplus again.

42449.q: What stayed in the hands of the state during the New Economic Policy?
a: Heavy industry, banks and foreign trade
42449.e: Small businesses and trade were allowed to be private. The ‘commanding heights’ of the economy, heavy industry, banks and foreign trade, were still controlled by the state.
42449.m: Under the NEP, the state kept the big businesses and banks.

42450.q: What were the traders and businessmen who got rich during the NEP period called?
42450.e: The Nepmen ran shops, trade and small businesses. Many communists were suspicious of them as new capitalists.
42450.m: The successful traders of the NEP period were called Nepmen.

42451.q: How did the economy develop in the first years of the NEP?
a: It was taken over by Germany
42451.e: Farming, trade and crafts recovered quickly, and the shops filled up again. By the mid-1920s production had almost returned to pre-war levels.
42451.m: With the NEP, the Soviet economy recovered.

42452.q: Who ended the New Economic Policy in the late 1920s?
42452.e: Around 1928 Stalin replaced the NEP with Five-Year Plans and the forced collectivisation of farming. Private traders were pushed out again.
42452.m: Stalin ended the NEP and turned to a strict planned economy.

42453.q: In which decade was the Soviet Union founded?
42453.e: The Soviet Union was founded at the end of 1922, a few years after the October Revolution of 1917. It lasted until 1991.
42453.m: The Soviet Union was founded in 1922.

42454.q: What was the full name of the Soviet Union?
42454.e: The abbreviation USSR stands for Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. In Russian the abbreviation was SSSR.
42454.m: USSR means Union of Soviet Socialist Republics.

42455.q: Which was the largest republic of the Soviet Union?
42455.e: Russia was by far the largest and most important republic of the Soviet Union. The capital, Moscow, was also in Russia.
42455.m: Russia was the largest republic of the Soviet Union.

42456.q: Which of the following republics was one of the founders of the Soviet Union?
42456.e: The Ukrainian Soviet Republic signed the founding treaty. The Baltic states were only occupied in 1940, and Kazakhstan later became a union republic of its own.
42456.m: Ukraine was one of the founding republics of the Soviet Union.

42457.q: What did the red flag of the Soviet Union show in the top corner?
a: A hammer, a sickle and a star
42457.e: The flag of the Soviet Union was red and showed a hammer and sickle in the top left, with a red star above them. The hammer and sickle stood for workers and farmers.
42457.m: The hammer and sickle on the red flag stood for workers and farmers.

42458.q: Which city was the capital of the Soviet Union?
42458.e: Moscow was the capital of the Soviet Union from its founding in 1922 until its end in 1991. The government was based there in the Kremlin.
42458.m: Moscow was the capital of the Soviet Union.

42459.q: Which song was the anthem of the Soviet Union from its founding until 1944?
42459.e: The Internationale is the anthem of the workers’ movement and originally comes from France. In 1944 the Soviet Union got its own anthem.
42459.m: The first anthem of the Soviet Union was the workers’ song ‘The Internationale’.

42460.q: What was Switzerland’s relationship with the Soviet Union like in the first decades?
a: For a long time Switzerland had no diplomatic relations with it
The two countries were at war
42460.e: After the murder of a Soviet diplomat in Lausanne in 1923, relations were very bad. Only in 1946 did the two countries establish diplomatic relations.
42460.m: Switzerland and the Soviet Union only established relations in 1946.

42461.q: Where did Lenin move the seat of the Soviet government in March 1918?
42461.e: Because German troops were threatening Petrograd, the government moved to the Kremlin in Moscow. Lenin lived and worked there in the Senate Palace.
42461.m: From 1918 the Soviet leaders governed from the Moscow Kremlin.

42462.q: In general, what is a kremlin in Russian cities?
a: A fortified castle in the city centre
42462.e: Many old Russian cities have a kremlin, for example Novgorod or Kazan. The Moscow Kremlin is the best known.
42462.m: Not only Moscow but many Russian cities have a kremlin.

42463.q: How many towers does the wall of the Moscow Kremlin have?
42463.e: The Kremlin wall is over two kilometres long and has 20 towers. Red stars shine on five of them.
42463.m: The Moscow Kremlin wall has twenty towers.

42464.q: Roughly what shape is the ground plan of the Moscow Kremlin?
42464.e: The Kremlin lies on a hill between the Moskva and the former Neglinnaya river. Its wall encloses an irregular triangle.
42464.m: The ground plan of the Moscow Kremlin is roughly triangular.

42465.q: Roughly how old is the present wall of the Moscow Kremlin?
42465.e: The present wall was built by Italian master builders at the end of the 15th century. So it is over 500 years old.
42465.m: The Kremlin wall is over 500 years old.

42467.q: Which huge gun can you see in the Moscow Kremlin?
42467.e: The Tsar Cannon was cast in 1586 and weighs about 40 tonnes. It was probably never fired in war.
42467.m: The huge Tsar Cannon stands in the Kremlin.

42468.q: What replaced the double-headed eagles on the Kremlin towers in the 1930s?
42468.e: The tsars’ eagles were removed in 1935 and replaced by stars. Since 1937, stars made of ruby-red glass have shone on the towers.
42468.m: On the Kremlin towers, stars replaced the tsars’ eagles.

42469.q: How is Lenin’s body in the mausoleum preserved for visitors?
42469.e: After Lenin’s death his body was embalmed. To this day experts regularly treat it with solutions so that it is preserved.
42469.m: Lenin’s embalmed body is still regularly looked after today.

42470.q: What does the Lenin Mausoleum on Red Square stand next to?
42470.e: The mausoleum stands right in front of the Kremlin wall on Red Square. Behind it are the graves of other Soviet figures.
42470.m: The Lenin Mausoleum stands in front of the Kremlin wall.

42471.q: What was the very first Lenin Mausoleum of 1924 made of?
42471.e: A few days after Lenin’s death a wooden mausoleum was built. From 1930 the present stone building was put up.
42471.m: The first Lenin Mausoleum was built of wood.

42472.q: Which stone is the present Lenin Mausoleum mainly made of?
42472.e: For the stone building of 1930, red granite, black labradorite and other stones were used. The colours match the Kremlin wall.
42472.m: The present mausoleum is built of red and dark stone.

42473.q: On which square is the Lenin Mausoleum?
a: On St Peter’s Square in Rome
On Times Square in New York
42473.e: The mausoleum stands on Red Square in Moscow, right in front of the Kremlin wall. Many people visit it every year.
42473.m: The Lenin Mausoleum is on Red Square.

42474.q: What shape is the Lenin Mausoleum?
42474.e: The mausoleum is built of blocks stacked in steps and looks like a flat stepped pyramid. There is a platform on top.
42474.m: The Lenin Mausoleum looks like a small stepped pyramid.

42475.q: What did the Soviet leadership use the roof of the mausoleum for during parades?
42475.e: During military parades, the Party leaders stood on the mausoleum’s stand. From there they gave speeches and saluted the troops.
42475.m: During parades, the Soviet leaders stood on the Lenin Mausoleum.

42476.q: Whose body lay next to Lenin in the mausoleum from 1953 to 1961?
42476.e: After Stalin died in 1953, his body was also put on display in the mausoleum. In 1961 it was removed and buried by the Kremlin wall.
42476.m: Stalin lay next to Lenin for some years before he was reburied in 1961.

42477.q: Why was Lenin’s body taken out of Moscow during the Second World War?
a: German troops were advancing on Moscow
Lenin was to be buried in Zurich
It was too hot in Moscow
42477.e: In 1941 German troops came very close to Moscow. So the coffin was taken to safety in Siberia and returned in 1945.
42477.m: During the Second World War, Lenin’s body was kept safe in Siberia.

42478.q: What does the Russian word ‘soviet’ mean in English?
42478.e: ‘Soviet’ means council. It referred to assemblies of elected representatives of workers, soldiers and farmers.
42478.m: A soviet is a council of elected representatives.

42479.q: Who sat in the soviets, the councils of the Russian Revolution?
42479.e: In the soviets, elected representatives of the workers, soldiers and farmers met. The first such councils were formed as early as 1905.
42479.m: Representatives of workers, soldiers and farmers sat in the soviets.

42480.q: What was the name of Lenin’s party, which gained more and more influence in the soviets in 1917?
42480.e: The Bolsheviks were Lenin’s party. By the autumn of 1917 they had a majority in many soviets.
42480.m: Lenin’s party was called the Bolsheviks.

42481.q: Who held power in Russia in 1917 after the Tsar was overthrown?
a: A new government and the soviets at the same time
42481.e: After the Tsar was overthrown there was a Provisional Government. At the same time the soviets had great influence. This is called dual power.
42481.m: In 1917 the government and the soviets shared power.

42482.q: What was Lenin’s famous slogan about the councils in 1917?
42482.e: With this slogan Lenin demanded that the Provisional Government be overthrown and power be given to the councils. The Bolsheviks gradually won a majority in many soviets.
42482.m: In 1917 Lenin demanded all power for the soviets.

42483.q: What happened in Petrograd during the October Revolution of 1917?
a: The Tsar returned to the throne
42483.e: The Bolsheviks overthrew the Provisional Government. A congress of soviets then confirmed their seizure of power.
42483.m: In the October Revolution the Bolsheviks came to power.

42484.q: Why did the Bolsheviks dissolve the newly elected parliament in January 1918?
a: Because they did not have a majority there
Because the building had burned down
Because no one had been elected
42484.e: In the election the Bolsheviks only received about a quarter of the votes. After a single day of sitting, they dissolved the parliament.
42484.m: In 1918 the Bolsheviks dissolved the elected parliament and governed through the soviets.

42485.q: From 1936, what was the highest parliament of the Soviet Union called?
42485.e: The Constitution of 1936 created the Supreme Soviet as the highest body of state power. But real power lay with the leadership of the Communist Party.
42485.m: The parliament of the Soviet Union was called the Supreme Soviet.

42486.q: In which present-day country was Joseph Stalin born?
42486.e: Stalin was born in 1878 in the town of Gori in Georgia. At that time Georgia was part of the Russian Empire.

42487.q: Roughly what does the revolutionary name ‘Stalin’ mean?
42487.e: The name comes from the Russian word ‘stal’ for steel. His real name was Ioseb Jughashvili.
42487.m: The name Stalin means something like ‘man of steel’.

42488.q: Which position did Stalin take on in the Communist Party in 1922?
42488.e: In 1922 Stalin became General Secretary of the Party. At first this position was seen as an administrative post, but Stalin used it to build up his power.
42488.m: As General Secretary of the Party, Stalin rose to become the most powerful man.

42489.q: Whose death in 1924 opened the way for Stalin to rule alone?
42489.e: Lenin, the founder of the Soviet Union, died in January 1924. After that a power struggle began over who would succeed him, and Stalin won it.
42489.m: After Lenin’s death in 1924, Stalin won the power struggle.

42490.q: Which revolutionary was Stalin’s greatest rival and was expelled from the Soviet Union in 1929?
42490.e: Leon Trotsky had built up the Red Army and was Stalin’s most important opponent. He was expelled and murdered in Mexico in 1940 on Stalin’s orders.
42490.m: Trotsky lost the power struggle against Stalin and had to go into exile.

42491.q: What did Lenin warn against in his so-called Testament?
a: Against Stalin as too rude and power-hungry
Against the power of the Church
42491.e: Shortly before his death, Lenin wrote that Stalin was too rude and should be removed from his important post. But the letter was kept secret within the Party.
42491.m: Lenin thought Stalin was too rude and warned against him.

42492.q: What is the wave of persecution from 1936 to 1938, in which Stalin had hundreds of thousands killed, called?
42492.e: In the Great Terror, Stalin had supposed enemies arrested and shot, including many Party members and officers. Estimates suggest about 700,000 executions.
42492.m: In the Great Terror, countless people were persecuted and killed.

42493.q: What are the public trials of old Party leaders in Moscow from 1936 called?
42493.e: In the Moscow show trials, the accused had to confess to made-up crimes. The verdicts had been decided in advance.
42493.m: In show trials, the verdict is decided before the trial.

42494.q: Instead of spreading the revolution to many countries, what did Stalin want to do first?
a: Make the Soviet Union strong on its own
Form a union with the USA
42494.e: Stalin called his idea ‘socialism in one country’. His rival Trotsky, on the other hand, wanted to spread the revolution to many countries.
42494.m: Stalin relied on socialism in one country.

a: A labour camp in the north
A farmers’ market in the city
42495.e: In a kolkhoz, farmers had to pool their land, livestock and tools. They worked together according to the state’s targets.
42495.m: In a kolkhoz, farmers worked the land together.

42496.q: Who ordered the forced collectivisation of farms in the Soviet Union?
42496.e: From 1929 Stalin forced farmers to bring their farms into kolkhozes. Lenin was already dead by then.

42497.q: What did the Party call the better-off farmers who were persecuted as enemies?
42497.e: Farmers with a little more land or livestock were seen as kulaks. They were dispossessed, deported or killed.
42497.m: The kulaks were persecuted as class enemies.

42498.q: What did farmers have to give up during forced collectivisation?
42498.e: The farmers had to bring their possessions into the kolkhoz. There everyone worked together according to the state’s targets.
42498.m: In collectivisation, farmers lost their own land.

42499.q: What is the terrible famine of 1932 and 1933 in Ukraine called?
42499.e: Because of collectivisation and high grain quotas, millions of people in Ukraine starved to death. The Ukrainian word Holodomor means roughly ‘killing by hunger’.
42499.m: The Holodomor was a famine in Ukraine with millions of deaths.

42500.q: What did many farmers do in protest before they had to join the kolkhozes?
42500.e: Many farmers did not want to hand over their animals and preferred to slaughter them themselves. As a result, the Soviet Union’s livestock numbers fell sharply.
42500.m: As resistance, many farmers slaughtered their own livestock.

42501.q: What was a terrible consequence of forced collectivisation?
42501.e: The kolkhozes harvested less, and the state took away a lot of grain. That is why millions of people starved to death in the early 1930s.
42501.m: Forced collectivisation led to a great famine.

42502.q: Why did many farmers resist the kolkhozes?
a: They wanted to keep their own land
They wanted to pay more taxes
They did not want to bring in a harvest
42502.e: Many farming families had worked their land for generations. They did not want to give it to a kolkhoz.
42502.m: The farmers did not want to give up their own land.

42503.q: What were the state economic plans that directed industry from 1928 called?
42503.e: From 1928 the state set out in Five-Year Plans what the factories had to produce. The first Five-Year Plan was officially declared fulfilled after just over four years.
42503.m: The Soviet economy was steered by Five-Year Plans.

42504.q: What do you call an economy in which the state sets production and prices?
42504.e: In the Soviet Union, the state planning authority decided what was produced. Supply and demand hardly played a part.
42504.m: In a planned economy, the state decides about production.

42505.q: Which sector had priority in Stalin’s industrialisation?
42505.e: Stalin mainly wanted steel, coal, machines and weapons. Everyday goods such as clothes or furniture stayed in short supply.

42506.q: What was mainly produced in the new industrial city of Magnitogorsk in the Urals?
42506.e: From 1929, Magnitogorsk was built around a huge steelworks. The nearby Magnetic Mountain contained a lot of iron ore.
42506.m: Magnitogorsk was the new steel city in the Urals.

42507.q: Why was the miner Alexei Stakhanov celebrated as a role model in the Soviet Union in 1935?
a: He mined a record amount of coal
He was the first to fly into space
42507.e: In a single shift, Stakhanov mined many times the required amount of coal. The Party made him a role model for all workers.
42507.m: The Stakhanovite movement celebrated workers who achieved record results.

42508.q: Who had to do forced labour on many huge building projects such as the White Sea-Baltic Canal?
42508.e: The canal was built between 1931 and 1933 almost entirely by prisoners. Many thousands died from cold, hunger and exhaustion.
42508.m: Many of Stalin’s big projects were built by Gulag prisoners.

42509.q: Who decided in the Soviet Union what the factories had to produce?
42509.e: The planning authority Gosplan worked out the targets for every business in the country. It drew up the Five-Year Plans in detail.
42509.m: In the Soviet Union, the state planned all production.

42510.q: What was produced at the big Dneproges power station on the River Dnieper?
42510.e: Dneproges was a hydroelectric power station in Ukraine. It started working in 1932 and supplied electricity to new factories.
42510.m: Dneproges was an enormous hydroelectric power station on the Dnieper.

42511.q: Shortly before which event was the Hitler-Stalin Pact signed in 1939?
a: Before the start of the Second World War
Before the end of the First World War
Before the fall of the Berlin Wall
42511.e: The treaty was signed in Moscow on 23 August 1939. On 1 September 1939 Germany attacked Poland, and the Second World War began.
42511.m: The Hitler-Stalin Pact was signed shortly before the war began in 1939.

42512.q: Which two countries signed the Hitler-Stalin Pact?
a: The Soviet Union and the USA
42512.e: Hitler led Germany and Stalin led the Soviet Union. The foreign ministers Ribbentrop and Molotov signed the treaty.
42512.m: The pact was signed between Germany and the Soviet Union.

42513.q: What kind of treaty was the Hitler-Stalin Pact officially?
a: A peace treaty after a war
42513.e: Both states promised not to attack each other. This was surprising, because Nazis and Communists were bitter enemies.
42513.m: In the Hitler-Stalin Pact, both dictators promised not to attack each other.

42514.q: What was settled in the pact’s secret additional protocol?
a: A joint flight to the Moon
42514.e: In the secret protocol, Germany and the Soviet Union divided Eastern Europe into spheres of interest. The Soviet Union denied that the protocol existed until 1989.
42514.m: The secret protocol divided Eastern Europe between Hitler and Stalin.

42515.q: Which country was attacked by Germany in September 1939 and shortly afterwards by the Soviet Union?
42515.e: Germany attacked Poland on 1 September 1939. On 17 September the Red Army marched in from the east.
42515.m: In 1939 Poland was divided between Germany and the Soviet Union.

42516.q: Which three states on the Baltic Sea were occupied by the Soviet Union in 1940?
42516.e: The Baltic states had been given to the Soviet Union in secret protocols. In 1940 they were occupied and made into Soviet republics.
42516.m: The Baltic states lost their independence to the Soviet Union in 1940.

42517.q: How did the Hitler-Stalin Pact end?
a: Germany attacked the Soviet Union in 1941
42517.e: On 22 June 1941 the German army attacked the Soviet Union without a declaration of war. The attack was called “Operation Barbarossa”.
42517.m: Hitler broke the pact in 1941 by attacking the Soviet Union.

42518.q: What happened in the Katyn Forest in 1940?
a: The Soviet secret police shot thousands of Polish officers
Germans and Soviets celebrated the pact
The first Soviet atomic bomb was tested
42518.e: The Soviet secret police, the NKVD, murdered around 22,000 Polish prisoners, many of them at Katyn. The Soviet Union only admitted the crime in 1990.
42518.m: The Katyn massacre was carried out by the Soviet secret police.

42519.q: What did the Soviet Union supply to Germany after the pact until 1941?
a: Raw materials such as oil and grain
42519.e: The pact also included an economic agreement. The Soviet Union supplied raw materials and received machines and industrial goods in return.
42519.m: Soviet raw materials helped Germany in the first years of the war.

42520.e: The city stretches a long way along the west bank of the Volga. The Volga was an important transport route for oil from the south.

42521.e: The city was called Tsaritsyn until 1925 and then Stalingrad. Since 1961 it has been called Volgograd.
42521.m: The former Stalingrad is now called Volgograd.

42522.q: Roughly how long did the Battle of Stalingrad last?
42522.e: The fighting began in summer 1942 and ended at the beginning of February 1943. The city was almost completely destroyed.
42522.m: The Battle of Stalingrad lasted about half a year.

42523.q: What happened to the German army in Stalingrad in November 1942?
a: It was encircled by the Red Army
It went home of its own accord
It was freed by the USA
42523.e: The Red Army attacked north and south of the city. A few days later the ring around the Germans was closed.
42523.m: In Stalingrad the German army was encircled.

42524.q: Why is Stalingrad seen as a turning point of the Second World War?
a: Afterwards the German army in the east was mostly retreating
Afterwards Germany made peace with the Soviet Union
Afterwards the atomic bomb was used
42524.e: After this defeat, Germany lost the initiative in the east. The Red Army then pushed the German army back step by step.
42524.m: Stalingrad became the turning point of the war in the east.

42525.q: Roughly how many German soldiers were taken prisoner at Stalingrad?
42525.e: About 90,000 soldiers were taken prisoner. Only around 6,000 of them returned home years later.
42525.m: Only a few of the prisoners from Stalingrad survived.

42526.q: Which huge statue on Mamayev Kurgan hill commemorates the battle?
42526.e: The statue of a woman with a raised sword was unveiled in 1967. Including the sword, it is about 85 metres tall.
42526.m: The statue “The Motherland Calls” stands in Volgograd.

42527.q: On which peninsula did the Yalta Conference take place?
42527.e: Yalta is a resort on the south coast of Crimea on the Black Sea. The conference met in the Livadia Palace.
42527.m: The Yalta Conference took place in Crimea.

42528.q: When did the Yalta Conference take place?
a: Shortly before the end of the Second World War
After the fall of the Berlin Wall
42528.e: The conference took place in February 1945. The war in Europe was almost over by then.
42528.m: The Yalta Conference took place shortly before the end of the war.

42529.q: Which three statesmen met at Yalta?
42529.e: Franklin D. Roosevelt came for the USA and Winston Churchill for Great Britain. They are also called the “Big Three”.
42529.m: Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin met at Yalta.

42530.q: What did the Allies decide at Yalta for Germany after the war?
42530.e: After victory, Germany was to be divided into occupation zones. France was also to receive its own zone.
42530.m: At Yalta the division of Germany into zones was decided.

42532.q: Which international organisation was partly prepared at Yalta?
42532.e: The three powers agreed on a founding conference in San Francisco. There the UN Charter was signed in June 1945.
42532.m: Yalta prepared the founding of the United Nations.

42534.q: Which Allied conference followed Yalta in summer 1945?
42534.e: In July and August 1945 the victorious powers met in Potsdam near Berlin. Harry S. Truman now came for the USA, because Roosevelt had died in April.
42534.m: After Yalta the victorious powers met in Potsdam.

42535.q: What is meant by a personality cult?
a: The exaggerated worship of a ruler
A religious festival in a village
A census of the whole country
42535.e: In a personality cult, a leader is shown as a hero or almost as a god. Criticism of him is forbidden.
42535.m: A personality cult presents a ruler as someone who can never be wrong.

42536.q: What nickname was Stalin celebrated with in propaganda?
42536.e: Stalin was shown as a caring father of all the peoples of the Soviet Union. Songs, poems and pictures praised him.
42536.m: Propaganda called Stalin the “Father of the Peoples”.

42537.q: What happened on old photos to people who had fallen out of favour with Stalin?
a: They were labelled with their names
42537.e: People who were arrested or executed were often later removed from photos. A well-known example is the secret police chief Nikolai Yezhov.
42537.m: Under Stalin, opponents were later removed from photos.

42538.q: What happened to many cities in the Soviet Union at the time of the Stalin cult?
a: They were sold to the USA
They were given the names of kings
42538.e: Many places bore Stalin’s name in his honour, for example Stalingrad or Stalinabad, today’s Dushanbe.
42538.m: Many cities bore Stalin’s name at the time of the Stalin cult.

42539.q: What was the state prize for art and science named after Stalin called?
42539.e: The Stalin Prize was awarded to artists and scientists from 1941. After de-Stalinisation it was renamed.
42539.m: The Stalin Prize was a high award in the Soviet Union.

42540.q: What did art have to be like under Stalin?
a: Easy to understand and praising socialism
42540.e: Art was supposed to show life under socialism in a positive way. This required style is called socialist realism.
42540.m: Under Stalin, art had to praise socialism.

42541.q: How were Stalin’s birthdays celebrated in the Soviet Union?
a: With huge celebrations across the country
42541.e: For Stalin’s 70th birthday in 1949 there were celebrations across the whole Eastern Bloc. Gifts came to Moscow from many countries.
42541.m: Stalin’s birthdays were marked with huge celebrations.

42542.q: What was the grand avenue in East Berlin that bore Stalin’s name until 1961 called?
42542.e: Stalinallee was built in the 1950s in the style of grand Soviet buildings. Today it is called Karl-Marx-Allee and Frankfurter Allee.
42542.m: There was a Stalinallee in East Berlin.

42543.q: Which people from the Caucasus were almost all deported to Central Asia in February 1944?
42543.e: Stalin accused the Chechens and Ingush of working with the Germans. Within a few days they were taken in goods trains to Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.
42543.m: In 1944 the Chechens were deported as an entire people.

42544.q: Which people were deported from Crimea in May 1944?
42544.e: Almost all Crimean Tatars were taken to Uzbekistan within a few days. Many died during the transport or in the first years afterwards.
42544.m: In 1944 the Crimean Tatars were driven out of Crimea.

42545.q: Which people of German origin lost their autonomous republic in 1941 and were deported?
a: The Danube Swabians of the Banat
42545.e: After the German attack in 1941, the Volga German Republic was dissolved. The people were deported to Siberia and Kazakhstan.
42545.m: In 1941 the Volga Germans were deported to the east.

42546.q: Under which Soviet ruler were entire peoples deported?
42546.e: In the 1930s and 1940s Stalin had entire peoples taken away from their homeland. He distrusted them and accused them of treason.

42547.q: To which areas were most of the deported peoples taken?
42547.e: The deported people had to start again in remote, barren areas. They were not allowed to leave their settlements without permission.
42547.m: The deported people were mostly taken to Central Asia and Siberia.

42548.q: Which authority carried out the deportations?
42548.e: The People’s Commissariat for Internal Affairs organised trains, guards and camps. It was also responsible for the police and the secret police.

42549.q: How were deported people in the Soviet Union usually taken away?
42549.e: People were locked into cramped goods wagons and transported for days. Many did not survive the journey.
42549.m: The deported people were taken away in goods trains.

42550.q: What does it mean when a people is deported?
a: They are forcibly taken away from their homeland
They may travel freely to another country
They are counted in a census
42550.e: In a deportation, people are taken away against their will. In the Soviet Union this happened to entire peoples.
42550.m: To deport means to forcibly take people away from their homeland.

42551.q: Who gave the famous Secret Speech against Stalin in 1956?
42551.e: Khrushchev was First Secretary of the Communist Party at the time. In the speech he settled accounts with Stalin’s crimes.
42551.m: Khrushchev criticised Stalin in his Secret Speech in 1956.

42552.q: Who did Khrushchev give his Secret Speech to in 1956?
a: To the delegates of the Communist Party
To the UN in New York
On television to the whole nation
42552.e: The speech was given in a closed session of the Party Congress. Only Party members were allowed to listen; foreign guests were not admitted.
42552.m: Khrushchev gave the Secret Speech to Party members.

42553.q: What did Khrushchev accuse Stalin of in the Secret Speech, among other things?
a: Letting himself be worshipped like a god
Being too friendly to the USA
42553.e: Khrushchev criticised the personality cult: Stalin had himself celebrated and worshipped everywhere. He also openly named arrests and torture.
42553.m: The Secret Speech criticised the personality cult around Stalin.

42554.q: Roughly how long did the Secret Speech last?
42554.e: Khrushchev spoke for about four hours. Many delegates were shocked, and some collapsed.
42554.m: The Secret Speech lasted several hours.

42555.q: When could people in the Soviet Union officially read the text of the Secret Speech?
a: Only more than 30 years later under Gorbachev
The very next day in all newspapers
A week later on the radio
42555.e: In the West the speech was already known in 1956. In the Soviet Union, however, the text remained secret for a long time and was only printed in 1989 during glasnost.
42555.m: Soviet citizens could only officially read the Secret Speech in 1989.

42556.q: Why is Khrushchev’s 1956 speech called the “Secret Speech”?
a: It was given in a closed session
It was written in a secret code
It was given at night in a forest
42556.e: Khrushchev spoke in a closed session of the Party Congress; foreign guests were not allowed to attend. The text was not meant to become public, but it soon reached the West.
42556.m: The Secret Speech was given in a closed session.

42557.q: Which uprising in autumn 1956 was partly encouraged by the Secret Speech?
a: The East German uprising of 17 June
The fall of the Berlin Wall
42557.e: The criticism of Stalin raised hopes of more freedom in the Eastern Bloc. In Hungary the uprising was crushed by Soviet tanks in November 1956.
42557.m: The Secret Speech encouraged the uprising in Hungary in 1956.

42558.q: What did Khrushchev mainly blame Stalin for in the Secret Speech?
42558.e: Khrushchev spoke about the persecution of loyal Party members and about torture. He kept quiet about his own part in the purges.
42558.m: Khrushchev held Stalin responsible for terror and arbitrary rule.

a: Turning away from Stalin’s methods of rule
A return to rule by the tsars
42559.e: After Stalin’s death, terror and the personality cult were toned down. But the rule of the Communist Party remained.
42559.m: De-Stalinisation ended the Stalin cult, not the Party dictatorship.

42560.q: What is the period of relaxation under Khrushchev called, after a novel by Ilya Ehrenburg?
42560.e: Ehrenburg’s novel “The Thaw” appeared in 1954. The title became the name for the years with more freedom in art and society.
42560.m: The Thaw brought more freedom after Stalin.

42561.q: What happened to Stalin’s embalmed body in 1961?
a: It was removed from the Lenin Mausoleum
It was put on display in a museum
42561.e: Stalin’s body had lain next to Lenin in the mausoleum since 1953. In 1961 it was buried by the Kremlin Wall.
42561.m: Stalin’s body was taken out of the mausoleum in 1961.

42562.q: What happened to many prisoners in the Gulag camps after Stalin’s death?
a: They were released and some were rehabilitated
They were called up into the army
They had to move to collective farms
42562.e: In the 1950s millions of prisoners were released. Many victims were officially declared innocent, often only after their death.
42562.m: With de-Stalinisation many Gulag prisoners were released.

42563.q: What did the Russian writer Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn mainly write about?
42563.e: Solzhenitsyn had been a prisoner in a camp himself. Under Khrushchev, a story of his about everyday life in the camps was allowed to appear for the first time in 1962.
42563.m: Solzhenitsyn described life in the Soviet prison camps.

42564.q: What happened in 1953, shortly after Stalin’s death, to his feared secret police chief Beria?
42564.e: After Stalin’s death Beria was one of the most powerful men. His rivals in the Party leadership had him arrested and shot in December 1953.
