42564.m: Beria was overthrown and executed shortly after Stalin’s death.

42565.q: Which politician replaced Khrushchev as Party leader in 1964?
42565.e: Khrushchev was removed by the Party leadership in October 1964. Under Brezhnev, de-Stalinisation was largely halted.

42566.q: What happened to a large Stalin monument in Budapest in 1956?
42566.e: During the Hungarian Uprising, demonstrators cut through the statue. Only the boots were left standing on the base.
42566.m: In 1956 the Hungarians pulled down the Stalin monument in Budapest.

42568.e: At the beginning of March 1953 Stalin suffered a brain haemorrhage. Because his guards were afraid to check on him for a long time, he only got help late.

42569.q: Where did Stalin suffer his fatal stroke?
a: In his home town of Gori
42569.e: Stalin was found in his country house in Kuntsevo on the edge of Moscow. He spent most of his last years there.
42569.m: Stalin collapsed at his dacha near Moscow.

42570.q: What happened to the leadership of the Soviet Union after Stalin’s death?
a: The Soviet Union was dissolved at once
The USA took over the government
42570.e: At first several politicians led together, including Georgy Malenkov. Over the following years Nikita Khrushchev came out on top.
42570.m: After Stalin’s death several politicians fought for power.

42571.q: What happened at Stalin’s funeral in Moscow?
a: Many people were crushed to death in the crowd
42571.e: Hundreds of thousands wanted to see the dead Stalin. Many people died in the crush; the exact number is unknown.
42571.m: People died in the crush at Stalin’s funeral.

42572.q: Who became First Secretary of the Communist Party in September 1953?
42572.e: After Stalin’s death there was at first a joint leadership of several politicians. Khrushchev came out on top over the following years.

42573.q: Where was Stalin first laid to rest after his death?
a: In the mausoleum next to Lenin in Moscow
42573.e: From 1953 Stalin’s embalmed body lay next to Lenin in the mausoleum. In 1961 it was removed and buried by the Kremlin Wall.
42573.m: Stalin first lay next to Lenin in the mausoleum.

42574.q: What happened to many prisoners in the camps shortly after Stalin’s death?
a: They were sent to the USA
42574.e: As early as March 1953, an amnesty released over a million prisoners with shorter sentences. Political prisoners were mostly released later.
42574.m: After Stalin’s death many prisoners were released.

42575.q: In which year did the Soviet Union explode its first atomic bomb?
42575.e: The test took place on 29 August 1949. This made the Soviet Union the world’s second nuclear power after the USA.
42575.m: The Soviet Union exploded its first atomic bomb in 1949.

42576.q: Where did the Soviet Union test its first atomic bombs?
a: On a remote site in the steppe
42576.e: The Semipalatinsk test site was in the steppe of Kazakhstan. More than 400 nuclear tests took place there until 1989.
42576.m: The Soviet Union tested atomic bombs far away from big cities.

42577.q: Which country was the only one to have atomic bombs before the Soviet Union?
42577.e: The USA built the first atomic bombs in 1945. The Soviet Union caught up in 1949 with its own project led by the physicist Igor Kurchatov.
42577.m: The USA was the first country to have atomic bombs.

42578.q: How did the Soviet Union work on its atomic bomb?
42578.e: The project was top secret and was supervised by the secret police chief Lavrentiy Beria. Prisoners also had to work on the building sites.
42578.m: The Soviet atomic bomb project was top secret.

42579.q: How did the Soviet Union get hold of secrets about the American atomic bomb?
a: Through a treaty with the USA
42579.e: Spies such as the physicist Klaus Fuchs passed on plans from the USA. This helped the Soviet Union build its bomb.
42579.m: Spies gave away nuclear secrets to the Soviet Union.

42580.q: Who ruled the Soviet Union when it exploded its first atomic bomb in 1949?
42580.e: Stalin ruled from the 1920s until 1953. The Americans named the bomb “Joe-1” after him.
42580.m: The first Soviet atomic bomb was made under Stalin.

42581.q: On which two Japanese cities did the USA drop atomic bombs in 1945?
42581.e: In August 1945 two atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The first Soviet bomb was very similar to the Nagasaki bomb.
42581.m: In 1945 atomic bombs fell on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

42582.q: What effect did the Soviet nuclear test of 1949 have on world politics?
a: The US monopoly on nuclear weapons was over
42582.e: Until 1949 only the USA had nuclear weapons. Now an arms race began between the two superpowers in the Cold War.
42582.m: From 1949 two superpowers had nuclear weapons.

42583.q: What did the bomb scientist Andrei Sakharov later campaign for?
a: Human rights and against nuclear tests
42583.e: Sakharov helped build the Soviet hydrogen bomb. Later he fought for human rights and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1975.
42583.m: Andrei Sakharov went from bomb builder to human rights campaigner.

42584.q: Which US president announced the doctrine named after him against the spread of communism in 1947?
42584.e: Harry S. Truman presented the doctrine to the US Congress on 12 March 1947. It is seen as one of the starting points of the Cold War.
42584.m: The Truman Doctrine is named after President Harry S. Truman.

42585.q: Which superpower was the Truman Doctrine aimed at?
42585.e: The USA wanted to stop the Soviet Union from spreading its influence. Greece and Turkey were the first to receive help.
42585.m: The Truman Doctrine was aimed at the Soviet Union.

42586.q: What is the US policy that aimed to stop the spread of communism called?
42586.e: The policy of containment was meant to prevent more countries from becoming communist. The Truman Doctrine put this idea into practice.
42586.m: Containment means not letting the opponent’s influence grow any further.

42587.q: What was the big US aid programme for rebuilding Europe from 1948 called?
42587.e: With the Marshall Plan, the USA helped Western Europe with billions after the Second World War. It complemented the Truman Doctrine.
42587.m: The Marshall Plan helped to rebuild Europe.

42588.q: What is the period of tension between the USA and the Soviet Union after 1945 called?
42588.e: The two superpowers never fought each other directly, but they distrusted each other deeply. The Truman Doctrine of 1947 is seen as one starting point.

42589.q: Before which assembly did Truman present his doctrine?
42589.e: Truman spoke to both houses of the US Congress, because Congress had to approve the money for the aid.
42589.m: The US Congress had to approve the money for the Truman Doctrine.

42590.q: What kind of help did the Truman Doctrine mainly promise?
42590.e: The USA supplied money, weapons and advisers to countries resisting communist pressure. This was meant to support their governments.
42590.m: The Truman Doctrine promised economic and military support.

42591.q: What was the Marshall Plan for, from 1948?
42591.e: After the Second World War many countries in Europe lay in ruins. With the Marshall Plan the USA helped with the rebuilding.
42591.m: The Marshall Plan helped Europe to rebuild.

42592.q: Which country paid for the Marshall Plan?
42592.e: The plan is named after the American politician George C. Marshall. The USA gave Europe a lot of money, food and machines.
42592.m: The USA paid for the Marshall Plan.

42593.q: Which country refused to take part in the Marshall Plan and also kept its allies from joining?
42593.e: The Soviet Union feared the influence of the USA and refused. Poland and Czechoslovakia also had to give it up under pressure from Moscow.
42593.m: Under pressure from the Soviet Union, Eastern Europe received no Marshall Plan aid.

42594.q: What did the countries of Europe receive through the Marshall Plan?
42594.e: With the help, factories, roads and houses could be rebuilt. Food was also delivered.
42594.m: The Marshall Plan brought money, food and machines to Europe.

42595.q: Which prize did George C. Marshall receive in 1953 for his plan?
42595.e: Marshall was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1953. He is still the only US Army general to have received this prize.
42595.m: George C. Marshall received the Nobel Peace Prize.

42596.q: Why did the USA want to help Europe with the Marshall Plan?
a: So that communism would not spread further
So that Europe would become part of the USA
Because Europe owed the USA money
So that Europe would get the Olympic Games
42596.e: The USA feared that poor, destroyed countries would turn to communism. A strong Europe was also meant to be a trading partner.
42596.m: The Marshall Plan was meant to strengthen Europe and slow down communism.

42598.q: What had the Soviet Union secretly stationed in Cuba, which triggered the Cuban Missile Crisis?
42598.e: The Soviet Union set up missiles with nuclear warheads in Cuba that could reach many cities in the USA.
42598.m: Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba triggered the crisis.

42599.q: How did the USA discover the missile sites in Cuba?
a: Through photos from a U-2 spy plane
42599.e: On 14 October 1962 a U-2 reconnaissance plane photographed the missile bases. The pictures were shown to President Kennedy.
42599.m: Aerial photos from a U-2 plane showed the missiles in Cuba.

42600.q: Which Soviet leader was Kennedy’s opponent in the Cuban Missile Crisis?
42600.e: Nikita Khrushchev led the Soviet Union at the time. He and Kennedy exchanged letters during the crisis and finally found a solution.
42600.m: In the Cuban Missile Crisis Kennedy and Khrushchev faced each other.

42601.q: What was President Kennedy’s first response to the missiles?
42601.e: Kennedy had the US Navy seal off Cuba to stop further missile deliveries. He called the blockade a “quarantine”.
42601.m: The USA responded with a naval blockade, which they called a quarantine.

42603.q: Which revolutionary leader ruled Cuba during the Cuban Missile Crisis?
42603.e: Fidel Castro had taken power in 1959 and moved closer to the Soviet Union. He agreed to the stationing of the missiles.
42603.m: Fidel Castro was Cuba’s ruler during the Cuban Missile Crisis.

42604.q: Which country represented US interests in Cuba from 1961, because the two states no longer had relations?
42604.e: In 1961 Switzerland took on a protecting power mandate for the USA in Havana. In this way it helped communication during the Cuban Missile Crisis and kept the mandate until 2015.
42604.m: Switzerland was the protecting power of the USA in Cuba.

42606.q: Which treaty from 1968 is meant to prevent more states from getting nuclear weapons?
42606.e: The Non-Proliferation Treaty was signed in 1968 and came into force in 1970. States without nuclear weapons promise in it not to acquire any.
42606.m: The Non-Proliferation Treaty is meant to stop the spread of nuclear weapons.

42607.q: On which Japanese city did the USA drop the first atomic bomb in August 1945?
42607.e: On 6 August 1945 an atomic bomb destroyed the city of Hiroshima. Three days later a second bomb hit Nagasaki.
42607.m: The first atomic bomb used in war hit Hiroshima in 1945.

42609.q: What does the term “balance of terror” describe?
a: Nobody attacks because both sides could destroy each other
Both sides have the same number of soldiers
One country protects all the others
42609.e: Because both superpowers had enough nuclear weapons, an attack would also have been deadly for the attacker. This deterrence prevented a direct war.
42609.m: The balance of terror was based on mutual deterrence.

42610.q: Which crisis brought the world very close to nuclear war in 1962?
42610.e: In 1962 the Soviet Union set up nuclear missiles in Cuba, close to the USA. After 13 dangerous days the missiles were withdrawn.
42610.m: In the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 a nuclear war threatened.

42611.q: In which Swiss city did Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev hold their first summit in 1985?
42611.e: In November 1985 the two leaders met in Geneva. The meeting started a period of disarmament.
42611.m: Reagan and Gorbachev first met in Geneva in 1985.

42612.q: What did Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev agree on in a treaty in 1987?
42612.e: With the INF Treaty, the USA and the Soviet Union committed themselves to destroying a whole group of nuclear missiles. This was an important step towards disarmament.
42612.m: In 1987 the USA and the Soviet Union agreed to get rid of nuclear missiles.

42613.q: What is a nuclear missile that can fly from one continent to another called?
42613.e: Intercontinental missiles have a range of over 5,500 kilometres. With them, the USA and the Soviet Union could reach each other directly.
42613.m: Intercontinental missiles can reach other continents.

42614.q: In which year was Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, launched?
42614.e: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 into space on 4 October 1957. This marked the beginning of the space age.
42614.m: In 1957 Sputnik 1 became the first satellite in space.

42615.e: Sputnik 1 weighed about 83.6 kilograms. The metal ball had a diameter of about 58 centimetres.
42615.m: Sputnik 1 was a metal ball of about 84 kilograms.

42616.q: Roughly how long did Sputnik 1 take to go once around the Earth?
42616.e: Sputnik 1 orbited the Earth in about 96 minutes. So it flew over the same countries several times a day.
42616.m: Sputnik 1 went round the Earth in about an hour and a half.

42617.q: What is the shock in the West called when the Soviet Union put the first satellite into space?
42617.e: The USA realised that the Soviet Union was ahead in technology. Anyone who can launch satellites can also fire nuclear missiles over long distances.
42617.m: The Sputnik shock showed the West how far ahead the Soviets were.

42618.q: Which space agency did the USA found in 1958 in response to Sputnik?
42618.e: NASA started work in October 1958. It was meant to bring US space activities together and catch up with the Soviet Union.
42618.m: NASA was founded in 1958 as a result of the Sputnik shock.

42619.q: Which animal became the first living creature to go into Earth orbit, on Sputnik 2 in November 1957?
42619.e: The dog Laika flew into space on Sputnik 2 on 3 November 1957. A return to Earth was not planned, and she did not survive the flight.
42619.m: Laika was the first animal in Earth orbit.

42620.q: Which country was the second, after the Soviet Union, to put a satellite into space?
42620.e: At the beginning of 1958 the USA launched its first satellite, Explorer 1, just under four months after Sputnik 1.
42620.m: The USA followed in 1958 with its first satellite.

42621.q: From which spaceport did Yuri Gagarin take off in 1961?
42621.e: Gagarin’s rocket took off from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in the steppe of Kazakhstan. Sputnik 1 had also been launched from there.
42621.m: Yuri Gagarin took off from the Baikonur spaceport.

42623.q: Which day has been a UN day of remembrance for Gagarin’s flight since 2011?
42623.e: The UN declared 12 April the International Day of Human Space Flight. Gagarin took off on this day in 1961.
42623.m: 12 April is the Day of Human Space Flight.

42624.q: Who was the first woman in space in 1963?
42624.e: The Soviet Union sent Valentina Tereshkova into space on Vostok 6. She orbited the Earth for almost three days.
42624.m: Valentina Tereshkova was the first woman in space.

42625.q: Which country also put a person into orbit around the Earth in 1962, one year after Gagarin?
42625.e: The American John Glenn orbited the Earth three times on 20 February 1962. This put the USA almost a year behind the Soviet Union.
42625.m: John Glenn was the first American in Earth orbit.

42626.q: How did Yuri Gagarin get back to the ground when he landed?
a: In the capsule on the sea
In a space plane on a runway
42626.e: Gagarin was ejected from the capsule a few kilometres up and landed with his own parachute. The capsule came down separately.
42626.m: Gagarin landed by parachute, separately from his capsule.

42627.q: Which US president set the goal in 1961 of putting people on the Moon within the same decade?
42627.e: On 25 May 1961 Kennedy announced the Moon goal to Congress. The USA wanted to catch up with the Soviet lead in space.
42627.m: In 1961 Kennedy set the goal of a Moon landing.

42628.q: With which mission did the first people land on the Moon in July 1969?
42628.e: The Apollo 11 lunar module touched down on the Moon in July 1969. With this the USA won the race to the Moon.
42628.m: Apollo 11 took the first people to the Moon in 1969.

42629.q: Who was the first person to step onto the Moon in July 1969?
42629.e: Neil Armstrong was the first to climb out of the Apollo 11 lunar module. Buzz Aldrin followed him a few minutes later.
42629.m: In 1969 Neil Armstrong was the first person on the Moon.

42630.q: What was the first artificial satellite, launched into space by the Soviet Union in 1957, called?
42630.e: Sputnik 1 orbited the Earth in October 1957. The USA was shocked, and the space race really began.
42630.m: The space race began in 1957 with Sputnik.

42632.q: Which animal was the first living creature to orbit the Earth in 1957?
42632.e: The Soviet Union sent the dog Laika into orbit around the Earth on Sputnik 2. Sadly she did not survive the flight.
42632.m: In 1957 the dog Laika was the first living creature to orbit the Earth.

42633.q: Which two countries competed in the space race?
a: The USA and the Soviet Union
42633.e: In the Cold War, the USA and the Soviet Union wanted to show who was technically stronger. So both tried to be first into space and onto the Moon.
42633.m: The space race was between the USA and the Soviet Union.

42634.q: How many people have walked on the Moon so far (as of 2026)?
42634.e: Between 1969 and 1972 six Apollo missions, each with two astronauts, landed on the Moon. That makes 12 people.
42634.m: Twelve astronauts in total have walked on the Moon.

42635.q: Which state completely surrounded West Berlin during the division?
42635.e: West Berlin lay like an island in the middle of East German territory. That is why the Wall surrounded the city on all sides.
42635.m: West Berlin was an island in the middle of East Germany.

42636.q: According to current research, at least how many people died at the Berlin Wall?
42636.e: A research project counted at least 140 deaths at the Berlin Wall between 1961 and 1989. Most died trying to escape.
42636.m: At least 140 people died at the Berlin Wall.

42637.q: Why did people in Berlin in 1961 jump out of the windows of houses right on the border?
a: Because the houses were on fire
Because the stairs were closed off
42637.e: Some houses belonged to the East, but the pavement in front of them was already in the West. So people jumped out of the windows to get to the West.
42637.m: After the Wall was built, people jumped out of windows to escape to the West.

42638.q: Why did East Germany mainly build the Berlin Wall?
a: To stop its own citizens escaping
42638.e: Until 1961 millions of people fled from East Germany to the West, many through Berlin. The Wall was meant to end this exodus.
42638.m: The Wall was meant to stop people fleeing East Germany.

42639.q: Why did the death of 18-year-old Peter Fechter at the Wall in 1962 shock the world?
a: He bled to death in the border strip and nobody helped him
He died in a car accident in West Berlin
He was bitten by a dog
42639.e: Peter Fechter was shot during an escape attempt. He lay in the border strip for a long time until he died, without anyone helping him.
42639.m: The death of Peter Fechter in 1962 shocked the world.

42640.q: What did the pass agreement at the end of 1963 allow West Berliners to do?
42640.e: For the first time since the Wall was built, West Berliners were allowed to visit relatives in the East over Christmas 1963. Hundreds of thousands took the chance.
42640.m: Thanks to passes, many separated families saw each other again in 1963.

42641.q: Which three victorious powers had their sectors in West Berlin?
42641.e: After 1945 Berlin was divided into four sectors. The three western sectors formed West Berlin, the Soviet sector East Berlin.
42641.m: West Berlin was made up of the sectors of the USA, Great Britain and France.

42642.q: Roughly how long did the Berlin Wall stand?
42642.e: The Wall was built in 1961 and fell on 9 November 1989. That is around 28 years.
42642.m: The Berlin Wall divided the city for about 28 years.

42644.q: In which Swiss city was the hotline agreement signed?
42644.e: Representatives of the USA and the Soviet Union signed the agreement in June in Geneva. The city was often a place of negotiations in the Cold War.
42644.m: The hotline agreement was signed in Geneva.

42647.q: Does the hotline between Washington and Moscow still exist today?
a: Yes, as a secure computer link
No, it was switched off in 1964
Yes, but only as carrier pigeon post
No, it was never in use
42647.e: The link has been modernised again and again: first teleprinters, from 1986 fax machines, and since 2008 a secure computer network.

42648.q: What was special about the first test message over the hotline?
a: An English sentence with all the letters of the alphabet
42648.e: The test read “The quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog’s back 1234567890”. It contains all the letters and digits so that the machines could be checked.
42648.m: The line was tested with a sentence full of letters and digits.

42649.q: Which technology replaced the hotline’s old teleprinters in 1986?
42649.e: From 1986 fax machines were used, which could also send pictures and maps. Since 2008 the link has run over a secure computer network.
42649.m: The hotline later switched to fax and then to computers.

42650.q: What is meant by a proxy war?
a: Great powers support other warring parties instead of fighting themselves
Two countries send athletes instead of soldiers
A country fights only with hired mercenaries
A war fought only at the negotiating table
42650.e: In the Cold War the USA and the Soviet Union never fought each other directly. But they helped different sides in other countries’ wars with weapons and money.
42650.m: In proxy wars, others fight for the interests of the great powers.

42651.q: Under the flag of which organisation did the Western troops fight in the Korean War?
42651.e: In 1950 the UN Security Council decided to help South Korea because the Soviet Union was boycotting the meetings. The troops led by the USA therefore fought under UN command.
42651.m: In the Korean War Western troops fought under UN command.

42652.q: What task has Switzerland carried out on the border between North and South Korea since 1953?
42652.e: Swiss officers are part of the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission in Panmunjom. It monitors the ceasefire of the Korean War.
42652.m: Since 1953 Switzerland has monitored the ceasefire in Korea.

42653.q: Which great power supported South Korea in the Korean War?
42653.e: The USA fought on South Korea’s side. North Korea received help from China and the Soviet Union. The border lies roughly along the 38th parallel.
42653.m: In the Korean War the USA supported South Korea.

42654.q: Which city fell to North Vietnam on 30 April 1975, marking the end of the Vietnam War?
42654.e: The Vietnam War ended with the capture of Saigon. Today the city is called Ho Chi Minh City.
42654.m: The fall of Saigon in 1975 ended the Vietnam War.

42655.q: Which politician led communist North Vietnam?
42655.e: Ho Chi Minh fought first against France and then against the USA for a united Vietnam. He died in 1969, before the end of the war.
42655.m: Ho Chi Minh was the leader of North Vietnam.

42656.q: How did the Vietnam War end for the USA?
a: They withdrew their troops without winning
They became allies of North Vietnam
They made Vietnam a US state
42656.e: In 1973 the US combat troops withdrew. In 1975 North Vietnam conquered the South and united the country.
42656.m: The USA left Vietnam without winning the war.

42657.q: Which communist island in the Caribbean was a close ally of the Soviet Union in the Cold War?
42657.e: Cuba became communist under Fidel Castro. Cuban soldiers also fought in proxy wars, for example in Angola.
42657.m: Cuba was an important ally of the Soviet Union.

42658.q: In which year did the Soviet Union invade Afghanistan?
42658.e: At the end of December 1979 Soviet troops moved into Afghanistan. They wanted to support the communist government in Kabul.
42658.m: The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan began in 1979.

42659.q: What were the Afghan fighters who fought against the Soviet troops called?
42659.e: The mujahideen were various groups of resistance fighters. They were supported by the USA and Pakistan, among others.
42659.m: The mujahideen fought against the Soviet occupation.

42660.q: Which Soviet leader withdrew the troops from Afghanistan in 1989?
42660.e: Gorbachev thought the war was hopeless. On 15 February 1989 the last Soviet soldiers left the country.
42660.m: Under Gorbachev the Soviet Union withdrew from Afghanistan in 1989.

42661.q: In which Swiss city were the agreements on the Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan signed in 1988?
42661.e: The Geneva Accords were signed in April 1988. They set out the withdrawal of the Soviet troops.
42661.m: The Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan was agreed in Geneva in 1988.

42662.q: What did the Soviet Union want to achieve by invading Afghanistan?
a: Support the communist government in Kabul
Hand Afghanistan over to the USA
42662.e: Communists governed in Kabul and were threatened by rebels. Under Leonid Brezhnev the Soviet Union decided to send troops.
42662.m: The Soviet Union wanted to support a communist government in Afghanistan.

42663.q: To which two neighbouring countries did millions of Afghans flee during the war?
42663.e: Because of the fighting, several million people fled. Most found refuge in Pakistan and Iran.
42663.m: Most Afghan refugees went to Pakistan and Iran.

42664.q: Which superpower supplied the Afghan fighters with weapons against the Soviet Union?
42664.e: The USA supported the mujahideen with money and weapons, for example from 1986 with Stinger missiles against helicopters.
42664.m: The USA supported the Afghan fighters with weapons.

42665.q: Roughly how long did the Soviet war in Afghanistan last?
42665.e: The war ended in February 1989 with the withdrawal of the last soldiers. It is sometimes called the “Soviet Union’s Vietnam”.
42665.m: The Soviet Union fought in Afghanistan for almost ten years.

42666.q: In which city were the 1980 Summer Olympics held, which many Western countries boycotted?
42666.e: The 1980 Games took place in Moscow. More than 60 countries stayed away.
42666.m: The 1980 Summer Games in Moscow were boycotted by the West.

42667.q: Why did the USA boycott the 1980 Olympic Games?
a: Because of the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan
Because of the building of the Berlin Wall
Because of the Cuban Missile Crisis
Because of doping in the Eastern Bloc
42667.e: President Jimmy Carter demanded the withdrawal of Soviet troops from Afghanistan. Because this did not happen, the USA stayed away from the Games.
42667.m: The 1980 boycott was a protest against the war in Afghanistan.

42668.q: Which US president called for a boycott of the 1980 Games?
42668.e: Jimmy Carter announced the boycott in January 1980. Many allies such as West Germany and Japan joined in.
42668.m: Jimmy Carter led the boycott of the 1980 Games.

42669.q: Did Switzerland take part in the 1980 Olympic Games in Moscow?
a: Yes, but under the Olympic flag
Yes, it was even the host
42669.e: Switzerland sent athletes to Moscow but, as a protest, marched in under the Olympic flag. The cyclist Robert Dill-Bundi won gold there.
42669.m: Switzerland was at Moscow in 1980, but under the Olympic flag.

42670.q: Which Summer Olympics did the Soviet Union and most Eastern Bloc states boycott?
42670.e: In May 1984 the Soviet Union announced it would not take part. Almost all Eastern Bloc states followed its example.
42670.m: In 1984 the Eastern Bloc responded with a boycott of the Games in Los Angeles.

42671.q: Which Eastern Bloc country took part in the 1984 Games in Los Angeles despite the boycott?
42671.e: Romania defied the boycott and sent a team to Los Angeles. It was celebrated for this in the West.
42671.m: In 1984 Romania was the only Warsaw Pact country in Los Angeles.

42672.q: What official reason did the Soviet Union give for its 1984 boycott?
a: Lack of safety for its athletes
Ticket prices that were too high
Weather that was too hot in California
42672.e: The Soviet Union claimed that its athletes would not be safe in the USA. Many saw it as a response to the 1980 boycott.
42672.m: Officially the Soviet Union justified the 1984 boycott with safety concerns.

42673.q: Which animal was the mascot of the 1980 Olympic Games in Moscow?
42673.e: The mascot was Misha the bear. At the closing ceremony a giant picture of Misha shed a tear.
42673.m: Misha the bear was the mascot of the Moscow Games.

42674.q: What were the “Fichen” that caused outrage in Switzerland in 1989?
42674.e: The Federal Police had kept index cards with notes on many people and organisations. Those affected knew nothing about it.
42674.m: The Fichen were secret index cards kept by the Federal Police.

42675.q: Roughly how many secret files (Fichen) had the Swiss authorities created?
42675.e: Around 900,000 files were found. More than 700,000 people and organisations were recorded.
42675.m: The Swiss authorities had created around 900,000 secret files.

42676.q: Who was mainly watched by the Swiss Federal Police during the Cold War?
a: People thought to be left-wing or communist
42676.e: Out of fear of communism, state security watched many left-wingers, trade unionists and peace activists. Often harmless activities were enough for an entry.
42676.m: The secret files mainly concerned people seen as left-wing.

42677.q: Which commission uncovered the secret files affair in 1989?
42677.e: A parliamentary commission of inquiry (PUK) investigated the Department of Justice. In doing so it came across the files.
42677.m: A parliamentary commission of inquiry brought the secret files to light.

42678.q: Why were many people outraged about the secret files?
a: They had to pay back taxes
They were no longer allowed to vote
42678.e: For years the Federal Police had collected notes on many people without them knowing. Many felt their freedom had been violated.
42678.m: The secret files showed that many people had been secretly watched.

42679.q: Which resignation in 1989 led to the inquiry in which the secret files were discovered?
a: The resignation of Federal Councillor Elisabeth Kopp
The resignation of the President of the National Bank
The resignation of the Federal Chancellor
42679.e: Elisabeth Kopp, the first woman on the Federal Council, resigned in January 1989. After that Parliament set up a commission of inquiry for her department.
42679.m: The resignation of Elisabeth Kopp started the inquiry.

42680.q: After the secret files scandal, what did people mean by the word “Schnüffelstaat” (snooping state)?
a: A state that secretly watches its citizens
A state with lots of police dogs
42680.e: With “Schnüffelstaat”, people criticised the fact that the state had secretly watched them. In March 1990 tens of thousands demonstrated against it in Bern.
42680.m: A snooping state secretly watches its citizens.

42681.q: What could citizens apply for after the secret files scandal?
42681.e: Many people asked to see their file. Names of other people in it were often blacked out.
42681.m: After the scandal you could ask to see your own file.

42683.q: What did the East German leadership under Walter Ulbricht have built in August 1961?
42683.e: Construction of the Berlin Wall began on 13 August 1961. It was meant to stop more people fleeing from East Germany to the West.
42683.m: The Berlin Wall was built under Ulbricht in 1961.

42684.q: In which city did Walter Ulbricht live in exile from 1938?
42684.e: After the Nazis took power, Ulbricht fled via Prague and Paris and lived in Moscow from 1938. He returned from there in 1945.
42684.m: Ulbricht spent the war years in exile in Moscow.

42685.q: Which state did Walter Ulbricht lead as Party leader?
42685.e: Walter Ulbricht was head of the ruling party, the SED, from 1950 to 1971. That made him the most powerful politician in East Germany.

42686.q: Which structure did the East German leadership under Walter Ulbricht have built in Berlin in 1961?
42686.e: In August 1961 East Germany had the Berlin Wall built. In this way it wanted to stop even more people fleeing to the West.
42686.m: The Berlin Wall was built under Ulbricht in 1961.

42687.q: Which party did Walter Ulbricht lead in East Germany?
42687.e: The SED was the ruling party of East Germany. Walter Ulbricht was at its head for many years.
42687.m: Walter Ulbricht was head of the SED.

42688.q: Who pushed Walter Ulbricht out of the Party leadership in 1971 with Soviet approval?
42688.e: On 3 May 1971 Ulbricht officially resigned “for health reasons”. His successor as Party leader was Erich Honecker.
42688.m: Erich Honecker replaced Ulbricht at the head of the Party in 1971.

42689.q: What did Walter Ulbricht claim in June 1961: “Nobody intends to ...”?
42689.e: In June 1961 Ulbricht said nobody wanted to build a wall. Two months later construction of the Berlin Wall began.
42689.m: Ulbricht denied plans for the Wall shortly before it was built.

42690.q: In 1945 Ulbricht said: “It must look democratic, but we must have everything in our hands.” What did he mean?
a: The Communists only wanted to appear to share power
All parties should have equal power
The people should decide everything themselves
The Soviet Union should withdraw at once
42690.e: From the outside it was meant to look as if there was democracy. In reality the Communists wanted to fill all the important posts themselves.
42690.m: Ulbricht wanted to show democracy on the outside but keep all the power.

42691.q: Which measure by the East German government triggered the uprising of 1953?
42691.e: Workers were supposed to produce about 10 per cent more for the same pay. In practice this was a pay cut and made many people angry.
42691.m: Higher work quotas triggered the 1953 uprising.

42692.q: In which country did the uprising of 17 June 1953 take place?
42692.e: On 17 June 1953 hundreds of thousands of people went on strike and demonstrated against the government all over East Germany.
42692.m: The uprising of 17 June 1953 took place in East Germany.

42693.q: Who started the protest that grew into the 1953 uprising?
42693.e: On 16 June 1953 building workers on Stalinallee in East Berlin stopped work. The next day the strike spread to the whole of East Germany.
42693.m: The uprising began with building workers in East Berlin.

42694.q: Who crushed the uprising of 17 June 1953 with tanks?
42694.e: The Soviet occupying power declared a state of emergency and sent in tanks and thousands of soldiers. Many people were killed.

42695.q: How did many people in East Germany learn about the strikes in other towns in 1953?
a: From a radio station in West Berlin
42695.e: The station RIAS in West Berlin reported in detail on the strikes. So people all over East Germany heard about them.
42695.m: A radio station from West Berlin spread the news of the uprising.

42696.q: How did West Germany remember 17 June 1953 until 1990?
a: With a ban on talking about it
With a military parade in East Berlin
42696.e: In West Germany, 17 June was a public holiday called “Day of German Unity” until 1990. Since 1990 it has been 3 October.
42696.m: In West Germany, 17 June was a public holiday until 1990.

42697.q: Which street in Berlin commemorates the 1953 uprising?
42697.e: The West Berlin Senate renamed the street from the Brandenburg Gate to Ernst-Reuter-Platz as early as 22 June 1953.
42697.m: The Strasse des 17. Juni commemorates the uprising.

42698.q: What did people in East Germany do on 17 June 1953?
a: They went on strike and demonstrated
42698.e: In many towns workers stopped work and demanded free elections. Afterwards the writer Bertolt Brecht mocked the government in a poem.
42698.m: On 17 June 1953 many people in East Germany went on strike and demonstrated.

42699.q: What happened to many of those involved after the uprising of 17 June 1953?
a: They were allowed to travel freely to the West
42699.e: More than 15,000 people were arrested. At least 55 people died in the uprising.
42699.m: After the uprising many people were arrested.

42700.q: What does the abbreviation FDJ stand for?
42700.e: The FDJ was the only state-recognised youth organisation in East Germany. It was closely linked to the SED.
42700.m: The FDJ was the youth organisation of East Germany.

42701.q: Which item of clothing did FDJ members wear at official events?
42701.e: The “blue shirt” was the mark of the FDJ; girls wore a blue blouse. The badge was sewn onto the sleeve.
42701.m: The blue shirt was the mark of the FDJ.

42702.q: Which symbol was shown on the FDJ badge?
42702.e: The rising sun stood for a new start and a bright future. It was yellow on a blue background.
42702.m: The rising sun was the symbol of the FDJ.

42703.q: From what age could you join the FDJ?
42703.e: At 14, young people usually moved from the Pioneers to the FDJ. Membership was officially voluntary.

42704.q: Was membership of the FDJ officially compulsory?
a: Yes, but only in East Berlin
42704.e: Officially the FDJ was voluntary. But anyone who did not join often had disadvantages, for example when looking for an apprenticeship or a university place.
42704.m: The FDJ was officially voluntary, but almost all young people joined.

42705.q: Who was the first chairman of the FDJ, from 1946 to 1955?
42705.e: Honecker led the FDJ from its founding on 7 March 1946 until 1955. Later he became head of state and Party leader of East Germany.
42705.m: Erich Honecker was the first leader of the FDJ.

42706.q: Which party was the FDJ closely linked to?
42706.e: The SED was the ruling party of East Germany. The FDJ was meant to bring up young people in line with its ideas.
42706.m: The FDJ was the youth organisation of the SED.

42707.q: In which state was the FDJ the state youth organisation?
42707.e: The FDJ was the only state-recognised youth organisation in East Germany. Almost all young people from 14 were members.
42707.m: The FDJ was the youth organisation of East Germany.

42708.q: Which communist politician was East Germany’s Pioneer organisation named after?
42708.e: Ernst Thälmann was leader of the KPD and was murdered in Buchenwald concentration camp in 1944. East Germany honoured him as a role model.
42708.m: East Germany’s Pioneers bore the name of Ernst Thälmann.

42709.q: What colour was the neckerchief of the Young Pioneers from Year 1 to Year 3?
42709.e: Young Pioneers in their first three years at school wore a blue triangular neckerchief. It was tied with a knot at the front.
42709.m: Young Pioneers wore a blue neckerchief.

42710.q: What colour was the neckerchief of the Thälmann Pioneers from 1973?
42710.e: From December 1973 Thälmann Pioneers wore a red neckerchief like the Pioneers in the Soviet Union. Before that it had been blue.
42710.m: You could recognise Thälmann Pioneers by their red neckerchief.

42711.q: What was the reply to the Pioneer greeting “Be prepared!”?
42711.e: When greeting, the children raised their right hand flat above their head. To “Be prepared!” they replied “Always prepared!”.
42711.m: The Pioneer greeting was “Be prepared!”, “Always prepared!”.

42712.q: What was the Ernst Thälmann Pioneer Organisation?
42712.e: Almost all schoolchildren in East Germany were Pioneers. They wore neckerchiefs, went to camps and were meant to be brought up in line with the Party’s ideas.
42712.m: The Pioneers were East Germany’s children’s organisation.

42713.q: What was the popular monthly children’s magazine for Pioneers called, whose name stood for “Be happy and sing”?
42713.e: “FRÖSI” (from the German “Fröhlich sein und singen”) was published from 1953 to 1991. It contained stories, puzzles, cut-out craft sheets and comics.

42714.q: What did many East German children experience in the holidays at Pioneer camps?
a: Holidays with games, sport and political education
English lessons for a trip to the USA
42714.e: At Pioneer camps children spent several weeks with sport, outings and campfires. Roll calls and education in line with the state were also part of it.
42714.m: Pioneer camps offered holidays and political education.

42715.q: What percentage of schoolchildren were Pioneers in 1989?
42715.e: In 1989 almost two million children belonged to the Pioneer organisation. Anyone who did not join stood out in class.
42715.m: Almost all schoolchildren in East Germany were Pioneers.

42716.q: What was there in the Pioneer Palace in Berlin’s Wuhlheide, opened in 1979?
42716.e: The “Ernst Thälmann” Pioneer Palace had a swimming pool and a cosmonaut training centre, among other things. Today the site is called FEZ.
42716.m: At the Pioneer Palace children could train like cosmonauts.

42717.q: What was called “Republikflucht” (fleeing the republic) in East Germany?
a: Moving to another town in East Germany
42717.e: Anyone who left East Germany without state permission was committing a crime. The official term was “illegal border crossing”.
42717.m: Fleeing the republic meant leaving East Germany without permission.

42718.q: What did people in East Germany face if they were caught trying to escape?
42718.e: Escaping was a crime in East Germany. Anyone caught went to prison, in serious cases for up to eight years.
42718.m: In East Germany an escape attempt was punished with prison.

42719.q: Roughly how many people fled from East Germany to the West between 1949 and the building of the Wall in 1961?
42719.e: By 1961 about 2.7 million people had left East Germany, many of them young and well trained. This exodus badly weakened the economy.
42719.m: Millions of people fled East Germany before 1961.

42720.q: How did two families manage to escape from Thuringia to Bavaria in September 1979?
a: Through a tunnel under the border
42720.e: The Strelzyk and Wetzel families sewed a big balloon out of strips of fabric. After a flight of about half an hour they landed near Naila in Bavaria.
42720.m: In 1979 two families escaped in a home-made balloon.

42721.q: What did West Germany pay so that political prisoners from East Germany could leave for the West?
a: Money or goods to East Germany
42721.e: Through the so-called buying free of prisoners, East Germany received around 3.4 billion Deutschmarks between 1964 and 1989. In this way about 34,000 political prisoners were released.
42721.m: West Germany bought the freedom of political prisoners from East Germany.

42722.q: What was the application called with which East German citizens officially asked for permission to move to the West?
42722.e: Anyone who made an exit application often had to expect disadvantages at work and at school. Until early 1989, refusals did not have to be explained.
42722.m: With an exit application people asked to leave legally.

42723.q: What happened to Peter Fechter at the Berlin Wall in 1962?
a: He was shot while escaping and bled to death
42723.e: Peter Fechter was shot during an escape attempt on 17 August 1962 and was left lying in the death strip. He died in front of many onlookers.
42723.m: The death of Peter Fechter in 1962 shocked many people.

42724.q: Where were many East German refugees first taken in when they arrived in West Berlin?
42724.e: At the Marienfelde emergency reception camp, refugees were registered and looked after. Today there is a memorial there.
42724.m: Many East German refugees first came to an emergency reception camp.

42725.q: What did East German border soldiers receive when they stopped refugees at the border?
42725.e: Border soldiers who prevented escapes received bonuses, extra leave or medals. They were under orders to stop escapes with their weapons if necessary.
42725.m: East Germany rewarded border soldiers who prevented escapes.

a: A gift parcel from relatives in West Germany
A parcel of weapons for the army
A delivery from the Soviet Union
A school pack from the FDJ
42726.e: Many West Germans regularly sent parcels to their relatives in East Germany. They contained things that were in short supply in the East.
42726.m: Western parcels brought sought-after goods from the West into East Germany.

42727.q: Which drink was especially often found in Western parcels?
42727.e: Real coffee was expensive and scarce in East Germany. Around 1,000 tonnes of coffee were sent by parcel every year.
42727.m: Coffee was a classic in the Western parcel.

42728.q: Why were families in East Germany so pleased about Western parcels?
a: Many goods were scarce in East Germany
Parcels were banned in East Germany
They got paid by the state for them
42728.e: In East Germany many things such as real coffee, chocolate or fashionable clothes were rarely available. That is why Western parcels were so popular.
42728.m: Western parcels brought goods that were scarce in East Germany.

42729.q: What were you not allowed to send to East Germany in a Western parcel?
42729.e: Cash was banned in Western parcels, as were tapes and war toys. Parcels were checked and sometimes opened.
42729.m: Money was not allowed in a Western parcel.

42730.q: Roughly how many Western parcels were sent to East Germany each year?
42730.e: On average there were around 25 million parcels a year. They also contained about five million items of clothing.
42730.m: Every year millions of Western parcels went to East Germany.

42731.q: Which baked treat did East German families often send back to the West as a thank you?
42731.e: Dresden stollen was a popular return gift at Christmas. Sometimes it was baked with ingredients from the Western parcel.
42731.m: A stollen was often the thank you for a Western parcel.

42732.q: What advantage did senders in West Germany have when they sent parcels to East Germany?
a: They could deduct the costs from their taxes
They got free holidays in East Germany
42732.e: West Germany supported the parcels by letting people deduct the costs from their taxes. This was meant to strengthen the ties between families.
42732.m: Western parcels could be deducted from taxes.

42733.q: Why were Western parcels sometimes opened in East Germany before they arrived?
a: For checks by customs and the secret police
Because the post office was nosy
To check their weight for the railway
42733.e: Customs and the Stasi searched for banned things such as money, tapes or writings. Some contents were confiscated.
42733.m: Western parcels were often checked in East Germany.

42734.q: What could you pay with in an Intershop?
a: Western money such as the Deutschmark
42734.e: In Intershops only freely exchangeable money such as the Deutschmark was accepted. The East German mark was not accepted.
42734.m: In the Intershop you paid with Western money.

42735.q: Why did East Germany run the Intershops?
a: To get hold of foreign currency
To strengthen the East German mark
42735.e: The state needed foreign currency to buy things in the West. From 1985 the Intershops took over a billion Deutschmarks a year.
42735.m: Intershops brought East Germany valuable foreign currency.

42736.q: Who ran the Intershop shops in East Germany?
42736.e: The Intershops belonged to a state trading company of East Germany founded in 1962. The state wanted to earn Western money with them.

42737.q: Who were the first Intershop stalls meant for?
42737.e: The first stalls at Friedrichstrasse station in East Berlin were aimed at travellers from the West. They were meant to spend their Western money there.
42737.m: The Intershop started at Friedrichstrasse station.

42738.q: What was forbidden for East German citizens until 1974?
42738.e: Until 1974 East German citizens were not allowed to own Western money such as the Deutschmark. After that they could also use it to shop in most Intershops.
42738.m: From 1974 East German citizens were allowed to own Western money.

42739.q: What did East German citizens have to use instead of Western money in the Intershop from 1979?
42739.e: From April 1979 East German citizens had to exchange their Deutschmarks for Forum cheques. Only with these could they keep shopping in the Intershop.
42739.m: From 1979 Forum cheques replaced Western money in the Intershop.

42740.q: Roughly how many Intershop shops were there in East Germany in 1988?
42740.e: The number of Intershops grew from 271 in the 1970s to 416 in 1988. There were shops in towns, on motorways and at border crossings.
42740.m: At the end of the 1980s there were over 400 Intershops.

42741.q: Which goods could you typically buy in an Intershop?
a: Western brand goods such as cosmetics and chocolate
42741.e: The Intershop sold goods from the West that were otherwise hard to get in East Germany. These included sweets, cosmetics, clothing and electronics.
42741.m: In the Intershop you bought sought-after Western goods.

42742.q: What does the abbreviation VEB stand for?
42742.e: A VEB (Volkseigener Betrieb) officially belonged to the people but was controlled by the state. Most businesses in East Germany were VEBs.

42743.q: Who officially owned a People’s Own Enterprise?
42743.e: Officially a VEB was the property of the people, but in reality the state decided about it. A works manager ran it together with the SED party organisation.
42743.m: A VEB was officially the property of the people.

42744.q: Which well-known car did a People’s Own Enterprise build in Zwickau?
42744.e: The Trabant was built at VEB Sachsenring in Zwickau. Many VEBs were grouped together into large combines.
42744.m: The Trabant came from a People’s Own Enterprise.

42745.q: What happened to many People’s Own Enterprises after 1990?
a: They were sold or closed down
They were given to the Soviet Union
42745.e: The Treuhand agency sold the businesses to private companies or closed them. Many people in eastern Germany lost their jobs as a result.
42745.m: After 1990 the VEBs were privatised or closed.

42746.q: Where did most people in East Germany work in 1989?
42746.e: Around 80 per cent of all employees worked in a VEB. There were almost no private businesses left.
42746.m: Most people in East Germany worked in a VEB.

42748.q: What did East Germany do with most private companies?
a: It sold them to the USA
It left them as they were
42748.e: East Germany nationalised companies step by step. In 1972 almost all remaining private businesses became VEBs.
42748.m: Almost all companies in East Germany were nationalised.

42749.q: Who decided in East Germany how much a People’s Own Enterprise should produce?
42749.e: In the planned economy, the State Planning Commission set targets for the businesses. Anyone who exceeded the plan was praised.
42749.m: In East Germany the plan decided what businesses produced.

42750.q: What was the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance (CMEA)?
a: An economic alliance of communist states
42750.e: In the CMEA the Soviet Union and other communist states worked together economically. In the West it was called Comecon.
42750.m: Comecon was the economic alliance of the Eastern Bloc.

42751.q: Which grouping in the West was the economic counterpart to Comecon?
42751.e: In the West several countries worked together in the European Economic Community, which later became the EU. NATO, on the other hand, was a military alliance.
42751.m: Comecon was the counterpart to the Western economic community.

42752.q: In which city was the Comecon secretariat based?
42752.e: The Comecon secretariat was in Moscow. The Soviet Union was the most important member.

42753.q: In which year was Comecon dissolved?
42753.e: Comecon was dissolved on 28 June 1991. After the end of the communist governments it no longer had a purpose.

42754.q: Which Caribbean state joined Comecon in 1972?
42754.e: Cuba became a member in 1972 and mainly supplied sugar to the other states. Later Vietnam joined as well.

42755.q: Which Asian country became a member of Comecon in 1962?
42755.e: Mongolia joined on 6 July 1962. It was the first member state outside Europe.
42755.m: Mongolia was the first non-European country in Comecon.

42756.q: What did the Soviet Union mainly supply to the other Comecon states?
42756.e: The Soviet Union had huge reserves of oil and natural gas. Oil reached other Eastern Bloc states through pipelines such as the Druzhba pipeline.
42756.m: In Comecon the Soviet Union mainly supplied oil and gas.

42757.q: What does the name of the “Druzhba” oil pipeline, which carried oil from the Soviet Union to other Comecon states, mean?
42757.e: “Druzhba” is the Russian word for friendship. From the 1960s the pipeline supplied oil to countries including East Germany.
42757.m: The Druzhba pipeline bore the name “Friendship”.

42758.q: What does the East German traffic light man (Ampelmännchen) wear on his head?
42758.e: The East German Ampelmännchen can be recognised by his hat and his round shape. This makes him different from the West German traffic light man.
42758.m: The East German Ampelmännchen wears a hat.

42759.q: Who was the East German Ampelmännchen designed for?
42759.e: The traffic psychologist Karl Peglau designed the Ampelmännchen in 1961. Pedestrians were meant to understand the lights more quickly and safely.
42759.m: The Ampelmännchen shows pedestrians when they may cross.

42760.q: In which part of Berlin did the Ampelmännchen with a hat first light up?
42760.e: In 1969 the figures were introduced at a crossing in East Berlin. From 1970 they were standard throughout East Germany.
42760.m: The Ampelmännchen with a hat comes from East Berlin.

42761.q: What does the red East German Ampelmännchen do with his arms?
a: He stretches them out to the sides
He holds them behind his back
42761.e: With his arms spread out, the red figure clearly shows “Stop”. The green figure, on the other hand, walks with big strides.
42761.m: The red Ampelmännchen spreads his arms out.

42762.q: What happened when the Ampelmännchen were to be replaced by West German figures after 1990?
a: There were protests and they were kept
42762.e: Many people fought against the change. That is why the East German Ampelmännchen now light up in many towns in both eastern and western Germany.
42762.m: Protests saved the East German Ampelmännchen.

42763.q: How can you recognise the traffic light woman found in some German cities since 1996?
a: By her hat and walking stick
42763.e: The traffic light woman was designed in 1996 as a counterpart to the Ampelmännchen. She wears plaits and a skirt.
42763.m: As well as the Ampelmännchen, there is also a traffic light woman.

42764.q: Why was the East German Ampelmännchen designed to be so round and easy to recognise?
a: So that pedestrians understand the lights quickly
So that they would look funny
42764.e: The figure was meant to help prevent accidents. Children and older people can also recognise a clear figure quickly.
42764.m: A clear traffic light sign makes the roads safer.

42765.q: What is the East German Ampelmännchen especially known for in Berlin today?
a: As a popular souvenir and landmark
As the logo of the federal government
As the mascot of the German army
As a stamp of Swiss Post
42765.e: Today the Ampelmännchen can be seen on mugs, bags and postcards. He is seen as a symbol that has survived from East German times.
42765.m: The Ampelmännchen became a cult symbol of Berlin.

42766.q: What does the Russian word “samizdat” mean in translation?
42766.e: In samizdat, people spread banned texts themselves, without a state publisher. They were passed on in secret.

42767.q: How were samizdat texts often copied in the Soviet Union?
a: With a typewriter and carbon paper
42767.e: With carbon paper you could type several copies at once. Readers often typed out the texts again and passed them on.
42767.m: Samizdat was made with typewriters and carbon copies.

42768.q: Why did people in the Soviet Union spread some texts in secret?
a: Because the state banned critical texts
Because books were too heavy to carry
42768.e: The government decided what could be printed. So critical texts were typed out secretly and passed on.
42768.m: Banned texts were spread in secret in the Soviet Union.

42769.q: How did people in the Soviet Union spread banned songs?
42769.e: Concerts by singer-songwriters were secretly recorded and copied onto tapes. Later cassettes were used as well.
42769.m: Banned music was passed on secretly on tape.

42770.q: Which famous work about the Soviet prison camps was spread in samizdat?
42770.e: In it Solzhenitsyn described the system of the Gulag camps. The book was banned in the Soviet Union.
42770.m: Solzhenitsyn’s “The Gulag Archipelago” circulated secretly in samizdat.

42771.q: Which secret police in East Germany hunted down people who produced banned magazines?
42771.e: The Stasi watched opponents of the government. In 1987, for example, it confiscated printing equipment belonging to opposition groups.
42771.m: In East Germany the Stasi hunted down secret magazines.

42772.q: In which country were there especially many secret newspapers of the Solidarity trade union in the 1980s?
42772.e: In Poland a great many banned newspapers and books appeared in the 1980s. This was called the “second circulation”.
42772.m: There were especially many secret publications in Poland.

42773.q: What punishment did people in the Soviet Union often face for spreading samizdat?
42773.e: Spreading it counted as anti-Soviet agitation. The punishment was labour camp, exile or loss of citizenship.
42773.m: Anyone spreading samizdat risked the labour camp.

42774.q: In which East German city did the Monday demonstrations begin?
42774.e: After the peace prayers in Leipzig’s St Nicholas Church, people gathered every Monday for demonstrations.
42774.m: The Monday demonstrations began in Leipzig.

42775.q: Which chant became the best-known phrase of the Monday demonstrations in 1989?
42775.e: With this chant people showed that the people, not the Party, should decide. Later many chanted “We are one people!”.
42775.m: “We are the people!” was the chant of the Monday demonstrations.

42776.q: Which slogan was meant to stop the demonstrations from becoming violent?
42776.e: The demonstrators chanted “No violence!” and often carried candles. In this way they wanted to show that they were peaceful.
42776.m: “No violence!” was the most important rule of the demonstrations.

42777.q: What did well-known people in Leipzig want to prevent with an appeal for calm on 9 October 1989?
42777.e: The government had police and soldiers ready. The appeal, made among others by the conductor Kurt Masur, helped everything stay peaceful.
42777.m: On 9 October 1989 the demonstration in Leipzig stayed peaceful.

42778.q: When did the big Monday demonstrations in Leipzig take place?
42778.e: From September 1989 more people demonstrated every Monday. In November the Berlin Wall then fell.
42778.m: The Monday demonstrations took place in autumn 1989.

42779.q: What did many demonstrators carry in their hands as a sign that they were peaceful?
42779.e: Anyone carrying a candle needs both hands and cannot throw stones. The candle became the symbol of the Peaceful Revolution.
42779.m: Candles were the sign of the peaceful protests.

42780.q: Roughly how many people took part in the Monday demonstration in Leipzig on 23 October 1989?
42780.e: The demonstrations grew bigger every week. On 23 October there were over 300,000 people, more than ever before in Leipzig.
42780.m: The Leipzig demonstrations grew hugely in autumn 1989.

42781.q: Thanks to glasnost, what happened to books that had long been banned in the Soviet Union?
a: They were allowed to be printed
They were only shown to children
42781.e: With glasnost, censorship was relaxed. So, for example, the novel “Doctor Zhivago” by Boris Pasternak was finally allowed to appear in the Soviet Union in 1988.
42781.m: With glasnost, previously banned books were allowed.

42782.q: Which Soviet politician made glasnost his programme?
42782.e: Mikhail Gorbachev was head of the CPSU. He relied on glasnost to renew the rigid system.
42782.m: Gorbachev brought glasnost to the Soviet Union.

42783.q: What was Gorbachev’s programme for restructuring the economy and the state, alongside glasnost, called?
42783.e: Perestroika means “restructuring” or “reshaping”. It was meant to modernise the planned economy, while glasnost brought openness.
42783.m: For Gorbachev, perestroika and glasnost went together.

42785.q: Thanks to glasnost, what were newspapers in the Soviet Union increasingly allowed to do?
42785.e: With glasnost, censorship was relaxed. The media could report on corruption, environmental problems and government mistakes.
42785.m: Glasnost relaxed censorship of the media.

42786.q: Thanks to glasnost, what happened to many critics of the government in the Soviet Union?
a: They were released or allowed to return
They had to leave the country
42786.e: With glasnost many political prisoners were released. The well-known civil rights campaigner Andrei Sakharov, for example, was allowed to return from exile to Moscow at the end of 1986.
42786.m: Glasnost brought freedom to many critics of the government.

42787.q: Which award did Mikhail Gorbachev receive in 1990?
42787.e: Gorbachev received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990. He was honoured for his role in the peaceful end of the Cold War.
42787.m: Gorbachev received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990.

42788.q: Thanks to glasnost, which chapter of Soviet history could be talked about more openly?
42788.e: Under Stalin millions of people were persecuted, locked up in camps or killed. With glasnost these crimes were openly examined in the Soviet Union.
42788.m: Glasnost made it possible to come to terms with Stalin’s crimes.

42789.q: On what date did the Chernobyl nuclear disaster happen?
42789.e: In the night of 26 April 1986, reactor 4 at the Chernobyl power station exploded. It was the worst accident at a nuclear power station up to that time.

42790.q: In which Soviet republic of the time was the Chernobyl nuclear power station?
42790.e: Chernobyl is in the north of today’s Ukraine, near the border with Belarus. In 1986 Ukraine was part of the Soviet Union.

42791.q: Which town near the power station was completely evacuated after the disaster?
42791.e: Pripyat was a town for the power station workers with around 49,000 inhabitants. It was evacuated the day after the accident and is still abandoned today.
42791.m: Pripyat has been a ghost town since 1986.

a: A reactor at a nuclear power station
42792.e: During a test a reactor at the nuclear power station went out of control and exploded. A lot of radioactivity escaped into the air.
42792.m: In 1986 a nuclear reactor exploded in Chernobyl.

42793.q: In which country abroad was the increased radioactivity first measured?
42793.e: At the Swedish Forsmark nuclear power station the measuring devices went off on 28 April 1986. In this way the world learnt early on how serious the accident was.
42793.m: Sweden was the first country to detect the radiation from Chernobyl.

42794.q: Which region of Switzerland was most affected by the radioactive fallout from Chernobyl?
42794.e: When the radioactive cloud passed over Switzerland, it rained especially heavily in Ticino. That is why the most radioactivity reached the ground there.
42794.m: Ticino was the most heavily contaminated by Chernobyl.

42795.q: What are the helpers called who cleaned up after the Chernobyl accident and contained the radiation?
42795.e: Hundreds of thousands of soldiers, firefighters and workers were sent in as liquidators. Many of them received high doses of radiation.
42795.m: The clean-up helpers at Chernobyl were called liquidators.

42796.q: How did the Soviet leadership react in the first days after the accident?
a: It kept quiet about how serious it was
It immediately asked the USA for help
42796.e: At first the authorities gave hardly any information; even the May Day celebrations in Kyiv went ahead. The disaster showed how much more openness was needed and strengthened glasnost.
42796.m: The silence after Chernobyl showed how important openness is.

42797.q: What level did Chernobyl receive on the International Nuclear Event Scale (INES)?
42797.e: The INES scale runs from 0 to 7. Chernobyl was rated at the highest level, 7, as a “major accident”.
42797.m: Chernobyl is classed as a nuclear accident at the highest level, 7.

42798.q: Where did Lech Wałęsa work as an electrician?
42798.e: Wałęsa worked at a big shipyard in Gdańsk where ships were built. There he led a big strike in 1980.
42798.m: Lech Wałęsa worked at a shipyard.

42800.q: What is a trade union like the Polish Solidarity?
a: An association of workers for their rights
42800.e: In a trade union, workers join together. Together they campaign for better pay and working conditions.
42800.m: A trade union stands up for workers.

42801.q: How did Poland’s communist government react to Solidarity in 1981?
a: It banned it and locked up its leaders
It invited it to a party
42801.e: In December 1981 martial law was declared in Poland. Solidarity was banned and Lech Wałęsa was detained.

42802.q: Which prize did Lech Wałęsa receive in 1983?
42802.e: Wałęsa received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983 for his non-violent campaign for workers’ rights. His wife accepted the prize in Oslo because he feared he would not be allowed back into Poland.
42802.m: Wałęsa was honoured with the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983.

42804.q: Which office did Lech Wałęsa hold from 1990 to 1995?
42804.e: In December 1990 the Polish people elected Wałęsa as President. He stayed in office until 1995.
42804.m: Wałęsa was President of Poland from 1990 to 1995.

42805.q: What became clear in the partly free elections in Poland on 4 June 1989?
a: Solidarity won almost all the freely contested seats
The Communists won all the seats
42805.e: In the seats that were freely contested, Solidarity won almost everywhere. Shortly afterwards Tadeusz Mazowiecki became the first non-communist head of government in the Eastern Bloc.
42805.m: The election of June 1989 was a big victory for Solidarity.

42806.q: Which country did Pope John Paul II come from?
42806.e: John Paul II’s real name was Karol Wojtyła, and he was born in Poland in 1920. Before his election he was Archbishop of Kraków.
42806.m: John Paul II came from Poland.

42807.q: Which office did John Paul II hold from 1978?
42807.e: In 1978 Karol Wojtyła was elected Pope. As Pope you are the head of the Catholic Church.
42807.m: John Paul II became Pope in 1978.

42808.q: What was special about the election of John Paul II?
a: He was the first non-Italian in over 450 years
He was the youngest pope of all time
He was the first pope from America
He had been a politician before
42808.e: Before him, all popes since 1523 had been Italian. The fact that a Pole from a communist country now became Pope caused a sensation around the world.
42808.m: John Paul II was the first pope from Poland.

42809.q: What effect did Pope John Paul II’s visit to Poland in 1979 have?
a: It gave many Poles courage against the communist state
The churches in Poland were closed
The Pope became President of Poland
42809.e: Millions of people came to his Masses. The visit strengthened people’s sense of togetherness and gave many the courage to stand up to the communist government.
42809.m: The Pope’s visit in 1979 strengthened the Poles’ courage.

42810.q: What happened in St Peter’s Square in Rome on 13 May 1981?
a: An assassination attempt on the Pope
The Pope was made a saint
42810.e: The attacker Mehmet Ali Ağca shot at John Paul II and badly injured him. The Pope survived and later visited the attacker in prison.
42810.m: John Paul II survived an assassination attempt in 1981.

42811.q: Which Swiss troop protected John Paul II in the Vatican?
42811.e: The Pontifical Swiss Guard has guarded the Pope since 1506. Its soldiers are young Swiss Catholics.
42811.m: The Swiss Guard protects the Pope.

42812.q: Which Swiss city did John Paul II visit in June 2004 for a youth meeting?
42812.e: In June 2004 the already seriously ill Pope travelled to Bern and met thousands of young people there. It was his last trip to Switzerland.
42812.m: John Paul II visited Bern in 2004.

42813.q: In which year did John Paul II die?
42813.e: John Paul II died in Rome on 2 April 2005. In 2014 he was declared a saint.

42814.q: On which border did the Pan-European Picnic take place?
42814.e: The picnic took place near Sopron (Ödenburg) on the border between Hungary and the Austrian region of Burgenland. A border gate was open there for a short time.
42814.m: The Pan-European Picnic took place on the Hungarian-Austrian border.

42815.q: On what date did the Pan-European Picnic take place?
42815.e: On 19 August 1989 a border gate was opened during the event. Many East German citizens took the chance to escape.
42815.m: The Pan-European Picnic was on 19 August 1989.

42816.q: Who mainly used the Pan-European Picnic to escape to the West?
42816.e: Many East Germans were on holiday in Hungary in summer 1989. They had heard about the picnic and escaped through the open gate to Austria.
42816.m: East Germans escaped to Austria at the picnic.

42817.q: Roughly how many people escaped across the border at the Pan-European Picnic?
42817.e: Between 600 and 700 East Germans crossed the border in several groups. It was the biggest mass escape since the Wall was built in 1961.
42817.m: 600 to 700 people escaped at the picnic.

42818.q: What was special about the Pan-European Picnic in 1989?
a: A border gate to the West was briefly opened
42818.e: On the border between Hungary and Austria a gate was opened for a short time. Hundreds of East Germans took the chance to escape.
42818.m: At the Pan-European Picnic a border gate to the West opened.

42819.q: How did the Hungarian border guards react when East Germans escaped through the gate at the picnic?
a: They shut the gate at once
42819.e: The gate was only meant to be open as a symbol for three hours. The Hungarian border guards did not step in when hundreds of people ran to Austria.
42819.m: The Hungarian border guards let the refugees go.

42820.q: What did the foreign ministers of Hungary and Austria do at their shared border in June 1989?
a: They cut through the border fence
42820.e: In front of the cameras, the two foreign ministers cut through a piece of the border fence. The pictures went around the world and showed that the Iron Curtain was getting holes in it.
42820.m: In 1989 the border fence between Hungary and Austria was cut through.

42821.q: From what date were East German citizens officially allowed to leave for the West via Hungary?
42821.e: In the night of 11 September 1989 Hungary opened its border to East Germans. Tens of thousands then travelled via Austria to West Germany.
42821.m: Hungary opened its border to East Germans on 11 September 1989.

42822.q: In which state was Günter Schabowski an important politician?
42822.e: Schabowski was part of the leadership of the SED, the ruling party of East Germany. In autumn 1989 he was spokesman for the Party leadership.
42822.m: Schabowski was an East German politician.

42823.q: What did Schabowski announce at a press conference on the evening of 9 November 1989?
42823.e: Schabowski read out a note with a new travel regulation. After that, East German citizens could apply for trips to the West without special reasons.
42823.m: On 9 November 1989 Schabowski announced a new travel regulation.

42824.q: What did Schabowski answer when asked when the new regulation would come into effect?
42824.e: Schabowski said: “As far as I know, that takes effect... immediately, without delay.” In fact the regulation was only meant to apply from the next day.
42824.m: Schabowski’s words “immediately, without delay” opened the Wall.

42825.q: Which structure fell in the night after Schabowski’s press conference?
42825.e: After the announcement, thousands of East Berliners streamed to the border crossings. The crossings were opened that same night, and the Wall had fallen.
42825.m: The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989.

42826.q: What did the border guards do in the night of 9 to 10 November 1989 because so many people came?
42826.e: Thousands of East Berliners pushed towards the border. At Bornholmer Strasse an officer had the barrier opened at about 11.30 pm, and the other crossings followed.
42826.m: In the night of 9 November 1989 the border crossings opened.

42827.q: How did many East German citizens learn about the new regulation on the evening of 9 November?
42827.e: The press conference was broadcast live, and the Western channels reported on it in detail that evening. Many people then set off for the border straight away.
42827.m: Television spread the news of the border opening.

42828.q: How long had the Berlin Wall stood when it fell in 1989?
42828.e: The Wall was built from 13 August 1961. By November 1989, 28 years had passed (1989 minus 1961 equals 28).
42828.m: The Berlin Wall stood from 1961 to 1989.

42829.q: In which country did the Velvet Revolution take place in 1989?
42829.e: The Velvet Revolution ended communist rule in Czechoslovakia in November and December 1989. It was largely non-violent.
42829.m: The Velvet Revolution happened in Czechoslovakia.

42830.q: Why is the revolution in Czechoslovakia called “velvet”?
a: Because it happened almost without violence
Because it took place in winter
Because it lasted only one day
42830.e: Velvet is a soft fabric. The name shows that the change of power was gentle and happened without bloodshed.
42830.m: The Velvet Revolution was gentle and non-violent.

42831.q: With which event did the Velvet Revolution begin on 17 November 1989?
42831.e: On 17 November 1989 students demonstrated in Prague and were brutally attacked by the police. After that, hundreds of thousands took to the streets every day.
42831.m: A student demonstration in Prague sparked the Velvet Revolution.

42832.q: Which writer and civil rights campaigner became President of Czechoslovakia at the end of 1989?
42832.e: Václav Havel was a playwright and one of the best-known critics of the regime. On 29 December 1989 he was elected President.
42832.m: Václav Havel became President of Czechoslovakia in 1989.

42833.q: Who mainly led the Velvet Revolution in Czechoslovakia?
a: Students, artists and civil rights campaigners
42833.e: Students, actresses, writers and civil rights campaigners organised the protests. They founded the Civic Forum in Prague.
42833.m: Ordinary citizens led the Velvet Revolution.

42834.q: What did the demonstrators in Prague do as a sign that the government should go?
42834.e: On Wenceslas Square hundreds of thousands jingled their bunches of keys. It was meant to say: you can lock up now and go home.
42834.m: Jingling keys became the symbol of the Velvet Revolution.

42835.q: What did the Prague Spring of 1968 want to achieve in Czechoslovakia?
a: More freedom in the communist state
42835.e: Alexander Dubček wanted “socialism with a human face”. Warsaw Pact troops ended the attempt. In 1989 Dubček returned as Speaker of Parliament.
42835.m: The Prague Spring of 1968 wanted more freedom.

42836.q: Which two states were formed from Czechoslovakia on 1 January 1993?
42836.e: Czechoslovakia was peacefully divided into two states. Because the split was peaceful, it is called the “Velvet Divorce”.
42836.m: Since 1993 there have been Czechia and Slovakia.

42837.q: What happened in Romania in May 1990, a few months after Ceaușescu was overthrown?
42837.e: After the revolution several parties were allowed to stand again in Romania. In May 1990 Ion Iliescu was elected President.
42837.m: In 1990 Romania held multi-party elections again.

42838.q: In which month of 1989 did the revolution in Romania take place?
42838.e: The protests began on 16 December 1989 in Timișoara. Shortly before Christmas Ceaușescu was overthrown.
42838.m: The Romanian Revolution was in December 1989.

42839.q: What triggered the first protests in Timișoara in December 1989?
a: A pastor was to be forcibly moved
42839.e: The pastor László Tőkés criticised the government and was to be moved because of this. Many people stood in front of his house to protect him, and this turned into big protests.
42839.m: A dispute over a pastor sparked the revolution in Romania.

42840.q: What happened at Ceaușescu’s last big speech in Bucharest on 21 December 1989?
a: He resigned of his own accord
42840.e: Instead of cheering, the crowd whistled and booed. The TV broadcast was cut off, and the whole world saw him losing power.
42840.m: Ceaușescu was booed at his last speech.

42841.q: How did Ceaușescu flee from Bucharest on 22 December 1989?
42841.e: Ceaușescu and his wife fled from the roof of the Party building in a helicopter. A little later they were caught.

42842.q: How was the revolution in Romania different from most of the other upheavals of 1989?
42842.e: Around 1,100 people died in the fighting in Romania. In most other Eastern Bloc states the change in 1989 was peaceful.
42842.m: Romania’s revolution of 1989 was the bloodiest in the Eastern Bloc.

42843.q: What was the feared secret police under Ceaușescu called?
42843.e: The Securitate watched the population in Romania. During the revolution, parts of it fought against the rebels.
42843.m: The Securitate was Ceaușescu’s secret police.

42844.e: On the Baltic Way people held hands and formed a long chain. In this way they peacefully demanded independence for their countries.
42844.m: The Baltic Way was a peaceful human chain.

42845.q: In which year did people in the Baltic states form the “Baltic Way” human chain?
42845.e: The Baltic Way took place in August 1989. The Berlin Wall also fell in the same year.

42846.q: Which three countries did the Baltic Way link?
42846.e: The chain stretched from Tallinn through Riga to Vilnius. These three countries were part of the Soviet Union at the time.
42846.m: The Baltic Way linked Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

42847.q: Roughly how many people took part in the Baltic Way?
42847.e: Over two million people took part. That was a large part of the population of the three countries at the time.
42847.m: Around two million people formed the Baltic Way.

42848.q: Roughly how long was the human chain of the Baltic Way?
42848.e: The chain was about 650 kilometres long; some sources say 675 kilometres. That is much further than the distance from Geneva to Romanshorn.
42848.m: The Baltic Way was around 650 kilometres long.

42849.q: Which treaty from 1939 did the Baltic Way commemorate?
42849.e: In the secret protocol of the Hitler-Stalin Pact, the Baltic states were given to the Soviet Union. In 1940 they were occupied.
42849.m: The Baltic Way commemorated the Hitler-Stalin Pact of 1939.

42850.q: What is the peaceful freedom movement in the Baltic states called, in which singing together played a big part?
42850.e: In Estonia in 1988 hundreds of thousands gathered at song festivals and sang banned folk songs. In this way they peacefully showed their wish for freedom.
42850.m: In the Baltic states people fought for their freedom with songs.

42851.q: How did people protest on the Baltic Way?
42851.e: People stood peacefully side by side and held hands. This created a huge human chain through three countries.
42851.m: On the Baltic Way people held hands.
